    💡 Key Takeaways
    • OK, so Netflix failed to buy Warner Bros.
    • That potential acquisition is apparently top of wishlist for Netflix (and Variety already deemed it “Hollywood’s Next Major Deal”), but Comcast co-CEOs Mike Cavanagh and Brian Roberts say they’re not selling.
    • Well, according to Bloomberg, the current proposal is for Netflix to revamp its approach to permanent interactive IRL installations, aka Netflix Houses.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    OK, so Netflix failed to buy Warner Bros. Discovery.

    What if it bought NBCUniversal, tho?

    That potential acquisition is apparently top of wishlist for Netflix (and Variety already deemed it “Hollywood’s Next Major Deal”), but Comcast co-CEOs Mike Cavanagh and Brian Roberts say they’re not selling.

    Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

    Well, according to Bloomberg, the current proposal is for Netflix to revamp its approach to permanent interactive IRL installations, aka Netflix Houses. The streamer first unveiled these in 2023, with a demo setup that looked like someone stocked the gift shop in Jurassic Park with merch of the laser murder doll from Squid Game.

    At the time, Josh Simon, Netflix’s then-VP of Consumer Products (now CEO of collectibles organization Funko) said the concept for Netflix Houses came from knowing “fans love to immerse themselves in the world of our movies and TV reveals,” and “thinking a lot about how we take that to the next level.”.

    It has been revealed that netflix had flirted with pop-ups before that; those were mainly focused on selling stuff. Make no mistake, Netflix Houses are also focused on selling stuff, but in a Disney World kind of way, where fans pay $39 to enter the House and head through an art gallery-esque space filled with themed exhibits like exclusive theater shows, movie/TV set recreations, VR experiences, and arcade games. There are cafeterias and merch shops, but by and large the things to buy share billing with things to do.

    The Houses are permanent installations (for now just in Dallas and Philly, with one planned to open in Vegas in 2027) but the exhibits within rotate regularly to keep up with whatever’s trending on Netflix.

    This year, for example, the Houses were renovated to feature animated smash megahit KPop Demon Hunters. They’ve also spotlighted Stranger Things, One Piece, Wednesday, and the aforementioned Squid Game.

    It has been revealed that per Bloomberg, Netflix initially planned to open dozens of Houses across the U.S., focusing on quieter suburban areas away from downtowns. It wanted to snap up spaces in malls, which are not doing very well and might be willing to rent for cheap.

    But apparently the results from its first two Houses haven’t been quite what Neflix expected, so it’s pausing openings beyond Vegas until it can reassess.

    People familiar with the matter told Bloomberg the Philadelphia location has daytime draws like mini golf and a movie theater, but doesn’t see much traffic at night. Dallas, meanwhile, is breaking even financially, and has done well with larger groups and corporate events.

    It has been revealed that netflix is also planning to see what comes from its Las Vegas location. Vegas, as you may know, is not in fact a quieter suburban locale–so if the House there proves to be profitable, with more traffic than Dallas and Philly, Netflix could reconsider where it opens in the future.

    Industry observers note that people familiar with the matter said Netflix is also looking at maybe taking Houses overseas. But wherever the next one ends up, it probably won’t open for at least another year, they said, until significant data from all three flagship U.S. locations is in.

    Now, with all this in mind, it’s worth remembering Netflix just shock-fired its longtime Chief Content Officer Bela Bajaria and replaced her with Peter Rice, Disney‘s former General Entertainment Chairman. Film chief Dan Lin is out too. Clearly, Netflix hopes to revamp more than its IRL installations…and perhaps it’s hoping Rice’s Disney EXP comes in handy with the Houses?

    Meta pledges to consult publishers before finalizing its new terms

    📅 28 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (939 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Niemanlab

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing.
    • Industry observers note that we have sent a confirmation link to .
    • Meta will complete “a full consultation” with news industry leaders before implementing its controversial newly introduced terms — even if it means another delay, an executive for the social media organization revealed today.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    Industry observers note that we have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    Meta will complete “a full consultation” with news industry leaders before implementing its controversial newly introduced terms — even if it means another delay, an executive for the social media organization revealed today.

    In a recent development, “We’ve heard publishers’ feedback on our proposed ads and business terms revision. We care deeply about our partners and do not strategy to make policy changes without a full consultation with industry groups and leaders,” vice president of communications Andy Stone tweeted. “We’re committed to getting this right, and as we expect this consultation could extend beyond November 20, in which case we’d delay implementation of the updated terms. Until then our existing terms remain in place.”.

    Meta did not answer Nieman Lab’s questions about which news industry groups and leaders Meta aims to consult.

    The proposed terms have drawn criticism because they would permit broad scraping of websites “associated with” business accounts, and potentially allow Meta to use that scraped content to train its AI models, with no option to opt out. Last week, Meta confirmed it would push back implementation of its new terms to November 20 in order to “explain to our partners and stakeholders what’s changing and what’s not — including how Meta uses web crawlers and the fact that content owners will still be able to use robots.txt to signal preferences,” a Meta spokesperson told Nieman Lab. Meta had previously revised its new terms to remove the word “train.” No version of the terms has included language about respecting robots.txt preferences.

    Shortly after Stone’s announcement, a Norwegian court blocked Meta’s terms from taking effect on November 20 until the court had assessed their legality, the country’s public broadcaster NRK reported.

    Recent findings suggest that “We are satisfied that the court has agreed with us that Meta holds a dominant position in the relevant market and that the newly introduced terms are unreasonable,” mentioned Lene Eltvik Vindfeld, MBL’s board chair, in a news release. “We are also pleased that the court recognizes that the alternative is that media companies risk losing control over editorial content built up over many years.”.

    Since Nieman Lab first reported on the terms on October 15, publishers and politicians around the world have pushed back, filing complaints with national competition authorities, calling on the European Commission to investigate, and writing letters to Meta’s CEO Mark Zuckerberg. Two United States senators — California Democrat Adam Schiff and Tennessee Republican Marsha Blackburn — each separately wrote to Zuckerberg, insisting that the tech giant withdraw the terms as they’re right now written.

    Recent findings suggest that “After I raised serious concerns about Meta’s plans to scrape and abuse creators’ content, I am pleased the company is finally acknowledging the concerns of publishers and content creators,” Blackburn said in a statement to Nieman Lab on Wednesday. “While this is a step in the right direction, a vague promise to consult with industry stakeholders and potentially delay implementation is not nearly enough. Meta must commit to meaningful changes that protect the intellectual property rights of American creators, and I will continue holding the company accountable until it does.”.

    In a recent development, on October 21, the European Publishers Council signed onto a joint letter to the European Commission, asking the Commission to block the terms from taking effect. The letter claims that Meta’s terms violate the Digital Markets Act, a law passed in 2020 to curb the dominance of big tech companies and create fairer competition across the region.

    EPC executive director Angela Mills Wade said on Wednesday that the organization has not heard from Meta about its letter or its concerns.

    In a recent development, “We welcome Meta’s offer to consult publishers fully, and to delay implementation if necessary,” Mills Wade mentioned in an email to Nieman Lab. “However, that consultation must lead to binding contractual safeguards…Using Meta’s services to reach audiences or advertise should not mean granting wider rights to exploit publishers’ journalism, whether collected from websites or uploaded to its platforms. Publishers must retain control over additional uses of their content, including for AI, and the ability to negotiate licenses and payment.”.

    This story has been updated to include a statement from Marsha Blackburn.

    The New York Times is adding more AI features to its Cooking app, and users aren’t thrilled

    📅 28 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1136 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Niemanlab

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing.
    • It has been revealed that we have sent a confirmation link to .
    • Sometimes, adding just one new ingredient to a stew can ruin the whole thing.11Olives, yecch.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    It has been revealed that we have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    Sometimes, adding just one new ingredient to a stew can ruin the whole thing.11Olives, yecch. And that’s how at least some New York Times readers see its addition of AI features to its popular Cooking app.

    Here’s Genevieve Ko, NYT Cooking senior editor and columnist, explaining the latest features:.

    I naïvely assumed A.I. wouldn’t affect my work as a recipe developer and my role at NYT Cooking, where I oversee the editorial side of our recipes and related stories. But as artificial intelligence improved, our product and engineering colleagues saw its potential to help us create features Cooking users wanted.

    Sources indicate that the Times had previously rolled out AI features aimed at converting volume-based and weight-based measurements (“What’s one cup of bok choy in grams?”) and scaling a recipe up or down to serve more or fewer people. The main latest feature is focused on ingredient substitutions.

    It has been revealed that say you’re cooking braised white beans and greens with parmesan, NYT Cooking app in hand. But you notice that you’re out of chard and only have spinach. Cooking veterans know that chard is a rough-and-tumble green that has some backbone22There’s a reason one type of chard is known as “perpetual spinach.”, while spinach is a comparative wimp that will wilt the moment you look at it funny. If you need to sub in spinach for chard, how would the recipe change? Would you, for instance, add the spinach later than you would the chard to account for its pathetic stamina? That’s the sort of thing the upcoming AI feature could account for.

    Industry observers note that cooking staffers “spent countless hours evaluating sample after sample to get the chatbot answers to closely align with how we would answer as culinary experts,” Ko writes. “We applied the same rigor as we do to editing, grounded in Times standards.”.

    In a recent development, but because Ko knows that any AI-powered features are likely to be controversial with a Times audience, she spends quite a lot of space addressing potential objections, everything from “the impact of data centers” to “the concentration of power among A.I. companies” and “the risk of A.I. escaping our control.” These features are designed to enable “the tactile physical pleasure of cooking” and getting a “very real, very human creation” on your table.

    Broadly speaking, commenters weren’t buying it.

    Industry observers note that “What a massive disappointment,” wrote Susan from New Jersey. “The internet is full of AI cooking content. I pay you because I prefer mine done by people.”.

    It has been revealed that “This decision misses the mark by such a wide margin it’s baffling,” notes Ian from Los Angeles. “And the disclosure just as baffling. It would not be inaccurate to summarize the piece as saying ‘I know doing this is bad and I don’t want to be associated with the bad thing so that’s why we are doing the bad thing.'”.

    It has been revealed that “Nobody wants this, it’s bad for cooking, it’s bad for the NYT,” writes Bill from Pittsburgh. “Wasting a column trying to gaslight yourself and your audience into believing that it’s anything but is an embarrassment and a waste of everyone’s time.”.

    “PLEASE PLEASE PLEASE DO NOT DO THIS,” says Judah Mann of Fresh York. “Oh, wait, you already did. Ok, I’m out.”.

    Or as Naomi from California puts it: “I am sad that AI has breached the one online resource I truly love.”.

    Because I enjoy the irony, I scraped the 171 comments left on the Times’ announcement and asked Codex (running GPT-6.1 Sol, at medium thinking) to do some sentiment analysis. (Twelve of the 171 were comments left by Times staffers; I’m excluding them here.) Roughly 77% of the reader comments were negative about the fresh AI features, it found, versus 14% positive and the remainder neutral or mixed. Among the biggest categories of complaint: This shouldn’t require AI. AI is destroying the environment. AI is not why I’m paying the Times $390 a year. The adjustments the AI produces are going to be bad.

    Dozens of commenters asked for a way to turn off the feature. “No, not at this time,” Ko responded, “though this feature is completely optional to use.” Indeed: Don’t ask AI to substitute your chard and AI won’t substitute your chard.

    According to recent reports, one consistent thread was that cooking is supposed to present you with difficulties and challenges and the whole point is figuring them out by yourself. “Anyone using AI for cooking has no sense of taste and no desire to work out the intricacies of cooking and baking,” writes Michael King from Brooklyn. “To use AI for recipes is beyond the pale. If you are going to use AI, then just cut to the chase and defenestrate yourself.” Or BJ from North Carolina: “So, you’re telling me that I’m too stupid to figure it out on my own?”.

    In a recent development, meanwhile, the few positive comments tended to focus on how the AI feature had, in fact, made dietary substitutions easier for them. “I love the latest AI feature because it swiftly (and so far) accurately converts recipes to gluten free,” Anne Wagner from Kansas City writes. “I don’t cook for stress relief,” indicates Andy from San Francisco. “I cook to put dinner on the table. Anything that makes the process a little faster or smoother is welcome.”.

    About six in 10 Americans remarked they have at least “some” confidence that news organizations will report the upcoming midterm election results accurately, according to a new national survey. But only 32% said they had “quite a bit” or “a great deal” of confidence that journalists would do the job.

    In the survey from Medill Local News Initiative and the Alliance for Trust in Media, 37% stated they had either “not too much confidence” or “no confidence at all” that news outlets would accurately report the election results.

    The survey was completed by a nationally representative sample of 1,057 U.S. adults either online or by telephone earlier this month. The findings echo other national surveys, including a Gallup survey that showed trust in media to report “fully, accurately, and fairly” at 33% — an increase from an all-time low last year.

    It has been revealed that the Medill/Alliance survey found about half of Americans said they had “not too much confidence” or “no confidence at all” in news outlets to investigate voter fraud claims thoroughly. U.S. President Donald Trump has cast doubt on elections on 70% of days since returning to office — starting with false claims about voter fraud on the first day of his second term.

    In a recent development, in another bleak result from the same poll, slightly more survey respondents noted journalists manipulate the news for political or commercial purposes than report it accurately. Across the survey, Democrats reported being more confident in (and trusting of) news organizations than Republicans. Nearly 80% of Republicans said journalists try to manipulate the news compared to 38% of independents and 24% of Democrats.

    More on the survey, conducted by NORC at the University of Chicago, here.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Four and a half years after winning a Grammy for The Unofficial Bridgerton Musical, the songwriting duo known as Barlow & Bear has something new in store for TikTok viewers.

    Industry observers note that abigail Barlow and Emily Bear are two of the creators behind To Die For Love, an 81-episode musical microdrama co-produced by TikTok and Ampersand. According to TikTok, the series follows “an ambitious half-witch vying for her coven’s crown. When she falls for a mortal, their romance takes an unexpected turn, forcing an impossible choice between family and the love of her life.”.

    Barlow & Bear created an original score for To Die For Love, while Barlow co-wrote the script alongside Oscar-nominated writer/director, actor, and opera singer Julia Aks.

    Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

    It has been revealed that barlow also stars in the series opposite Broadway vet Derek Klena. Executive producers include Ampersand CEO Agnes Chu, Benj Pasek, Justin Paul, Danielle Perelman, Chris Crema, Matthew Ko, and Kevin Weaver.

    “Making To Die For Love has been one of the most rewarding creative experiences of our careers,” Barlow and Bear said. “We love a pressure cooker, and building an entire musical in under five months proved that meaningful storytelling isn’t about time—it’s about the story and the people bringing it to life.”.

    In a recent development, this isn’t the first creator-driven microdrama TikTok has brought to life. Earlier this year, Issa Rae’s media manufacturer, HOORAE, struck a deal with the platform to produce short-form web series for both TikTok and its companion app PineDrama. The first vertical series to emerge from that partnership, Screen Time, had racked up over 620 million views on TikTok and PineDrama as of late October, making it both platforms’ most-viewed show to date.

    TikTok doubled down on that success last month when it announced a upcoming microseries-focused partnership with Made By Us Studios, which describes itself as a “first-of-its-kind, Hollywood-grade studio designed for the creator economy and powered by creator management company MADE BY ALL.”.

    Now, TikTok is forging ahead into the world of musical microdramas. To Die For Love will be available exclusively on TikTok and PineDrama, with all 81 episodes premiering December 21. The original soundtrack will be released by Atlantic Records.

    #55266. Press Forward gave $20 million to 205 local newsrooms over two years. Here’s how some of them spent it.

    📅 29 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 22m • 📚 Deep Dive (4366 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Niemanlab ↗ Open Full Page

    Press Forward gave $20 million to 205 local newsrooms over two years. Here’s how some of them spent it.

    📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 22 min read (4366 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Niemanlab

    ⏱️ ~22 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing.
    • Recent findings suggest that we will never sell your address.
    • We have sent a confirmation link to .
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    Recent findings suggest that we will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    The unrestricted funding helped small outlets plug holes and try new things, but publishers ran up against the limits of what two $50,000 grants could accomplish, especially when it came to hiring.

    Sources indicate that most local newsrooms in the U.S. have one thing in common: They need more money, and many dream of dollars they can use however they want.

    It has been revealed that RELATED ARTICLEPress Forward awards $20 million to 205 small local newsroomsSophie CulpepperOctober 16, 2024In 2024, Press Forward, the nonprofit trying to mobilize a philanthropic army for local news, unveiled it would give at least 100 small local newsrooms — those with annual budgets under $1 million — just that type of unrestricted funding. Almost 1,000 newsrooms applied. Ultimately, Press Forward distributed $20 million to 205 outlets. Most of them received $100,000 each, split over two years.

    In a recent development, I wondered what the recipients had done with the money, and which problems it had (or hadn’t) solved. Between May and October, I spoke or emailed with more than 30 grantees.

    The grantees represented every U.S. state, came from cities, suburbs, and rural areas, and published in multiple languages. They included for-profits and nonprofits, print and digital-only publications, college newsrooms, and public radio stations. Statewide newsrooms with fully staffed teams like The Maine Monitor, scrappy news startups like 285 South, and community newspapers powered by freelancers and part-time staff like the Copper River Record in Alaska all received funding.

    It has been revealed that for many newsrooms, Press Forward was the first grant they’d ever applied for. “Many of the country’s newsrooms are small, and few get foundation grants,” noted Press Forward executive director Dale Anglin. The open call was designed to change that and to distribute the money quickly. Grantees were required to complete two LION sustainability audits a year apart; Press Forward is analyzing that data now and will release its findings next month.1.

    Sources indicate that RELATED ARTICLEA study of nonprofit newsrooms reveals some cracks in the model’s foundationSeth C. LewisOctober 6, 2026“People tell me that what Press Forward did was unusual and rare within philanthropy,” mentioned María José Ramírez Braiz, founder and CEO of Midwest-based grantee Te Lo Cuento News.

    “They noted to us at the beginning of the grant period, before the shit hit the fan with the federal government, ‘If you need this money to keep the lights on, keep the lights on,'” said Copper River Record editor Allison Sayer, one of the paper’s two part-time staffers. “I feel that this was really a gift.”.

    According to recent reports, first-time grant applicants and recipients, in particular, said Press Forward’s recognition gave them credibility and visibility with other funders. And publishers described the funding as a morale boost that validated low-paid work.

    “It has been a life-changer, a lifesaver for us,” said Gretchen Sporleder Orr, who publishes the World Journal in southern Colorado with her husband. Her voice broke when she talked to me about the funding. “I don’t know if we would be in business right now if it wasn’t for the Press Forward money.”.

    It has been revealed that the Real WV “would not still exist without Press Forward,” said Stephen Baldwin, the site’s volunteer publisher. (He’s also the former minority leader for the West Virginia Senate and a pastor of two churches.) The outlet was one of eight grantees that received just two $25,000 grants over two years. “There’s not exactly a lot of capital floating around West Virginia for nonprofit news,” Baldwin said, “and without this outside impact, we wouldn’t be able to do this work.” But he hopes that the site can be less reliant on grants in the future.

    Industry observers note that the funding did not save every recipient. One grantee, Atlanta Civic Circle, shut down earlier this year. Atlanta Civic Circle did not receive its second $50,000 grant because it didn’t complete the first LION audit, Anglin remarked. (Atlanta Civic Circle did not respond to my request for an interview, but executive director Saba Long wrote on LinkedIn in June that “the funding environment for local nonprofit journalism is extraordinarily difficult right now.”) Other recipients have merged or transformed since applying for the grant.2.

    RELATED ARTICLEFrom bad to worse: 2026 is shaping up to be “a super El Niño year for local news”Sophie CulpepperOctober 13, 2026Medill’s annual State of Local News report, released this month, describes a local news ecosystem in a “state of precarity.” That state of precariousness helps explain how $100,000 over two years can be a “godsend,” a “miracle,” and not enough. As one grantee put it, “Right now, these are shanties built on a beach, waiting for a hurricane to come through.”.

    “Press Forward reached newsrooms that don’t have existing relationships with major national funders,” said Nina Ignaczak, the founder, publisher, and editor of Planet Detroit. “The challenge now is whether the commitment holds.”.

    The funding helped newsrooms keep the lights on, whether they used it to pay bills, pay down debt, make payroll, or as a buffer when something went wrong.

    It has been revealed that “The flexibility that Press Forward has given us has allowed us to fill — I wouldn’t say emergencies, but unexpected gaps,” said Richard Young, founder and executive director of CivicLex in Kentucky. It brought on a consulting editor to keep city hall coverage going after losing a reporter, and purchased fresh software. Without the funding, CivicLex likely would have had to dip into its reserves, he said.

    Recent findings suggest that bob Bonnar, publisher of the News Letter Journal in Wyoming, used the first payment from Press Forward to upgrade computers and cameras and give some staffers raises. “That chewed up the money very rapidly,” he remarked, “and I probably should have held some of it back because the News Letter Journal ended up having a pretty rough year in 2025.” He had to use about half of the second $50,000 payment to repay an operating loan. The rest covered the remaining revenue shortfall and kept the organization in the black through the winter.

    Vandana Kumar, publisher of the California-based ethnic media outlet India Currents, described the funding as a “stabilizing force” that allowed the newsroom to keep operating despite a contraction in philanthropic giving and cuts to local government advertising.

    In a recent development, the Copper River Record built infrastructure to host digital ads and created a new website. It held listening sessions with Native villages in its coverage area and donated subscriptions to local Tribal offices. It improved the design of its print newspaper. Sayer paid freelancers to complete Press Pass training and pursued other professional development. And she was able to take on more ambitious stories about PFAS and “forever chemicals.”.

    According to recent reports, the Press Forward funding was “the biggest single windfall in nearly 20 years for our small community newspaper,” Sandpoint Reader publisher Ben Olson told me. The Idaho-based paper used the money to travel to the state capital for Press Club awards and design a latest media kit, which Olson noted has improved ad sales. The Reader also paid a large chunk of its printing bill, paid its rent a year in advance, and gave staffers bonuses. (The bonuses helped the paper become 100% employee-owned; Olson’s two employees bought in when Olson’s business partner and co-owner retired.).

    In a recent development, the open-ended nature of the grants gave Colorado’s World Journal “the flexibility to be able to make a change, do a thing, and then pivot as needed,” Sporleder Orr remarked. “When we were in the toilet, all I could think about was, like, ‘Is there going to be anything in the post office today so that I can make payroll?’ ‘Oh, my God, we’ve got to pay rent.’” Sometimes she and her husband skipped their own paychecks to pay staff. The grant gave them “emotional bandwidth” to plan ahead.

    Many grantees used the funding to hire full- or part-time staffers. Sometimes, that worked out well.

    In a recent development, the Mānoa Mirror, an online newsroom based at the University of Hawaii at Mānoa, received two $25,000 grants, which it used to hire a managing editor, a student editorial coordinator, three student reporters, and a social media producer. (The managing editor was paid a stipend, and the other positions were part-time.) The work had previously depended on “faculty goodwill and volunteerism, which was not sustainable for long,” stated Hye-ryeon Lee, who was professor and chair of the school of communication and information until retiring this summer. With the newly introduced hires, the site went from publishing a few stories a month to publishing daily.

    The Real WV’s first LION audit pointed to a need its small team had already recognized: hiring someone to sell ads. It hired a public school teacher with sales experience (including selling ads for the yearbook) part-time.

    Sources indicate that the funding allowed Te Lo Cuento News to pay contributors consistently and to add contract, part-time positions including a sales manager, an office administrator, and a couple of reporters. The only position it could sustain beyond the grant period is the part-time sales manager, Ramírez Braiz stated.

    Recent findings suggest that the Texas Spur is one of five weekly newspapers owned by Paragraph Ranch Media. Originally, the team planned to use the Press Forward grant to secure a loan to improve manufacturer housing and hire a journalist based in Spur (population 863 as of 2020). But nobody took the newspaper up on the free housing offer, said editor and general manager Barbara Brannon. So the company hired four early-career journalists (two full-time, two part-time) living in its 10-county coverage area. Three of the four left for jobs in other industries halfway through their second year. The one who stayed is doing well as a regional sports reporter, Brannon said, and a hire who replaced a person who left is now managing editor for The Post Dispatch.3.

    The turnover Brannon experienced isn’t unique to Spur. Other newsrooms also found hiring with grant money challenging.

    Sometimes, that was because of location. “Had we been able to find the right people from the outset, I believe the grant would have had a greater impact on the business,” remarked Anton Kaufer, regional publisher for Hagadone Media Montana. In rural Northwest Montana, though, recruiting and retaining staff is a challenge, and Hagadone’s Mineral Independent struggled to replace its salesperson and office manager after they retired. The experience “reinforced for us that sustainability isn’t just about having the funding,” Kaufer said. “It’s also about having the people in place to make the most of it.”.

    The World Journal tried placing an ad for a salesperson with the Colorado Press Association and got “absolutely no interest,” Sporleder Orr remarked. “People living in northern Colorado don’t particularly want to come live in a teeny-tiny town in a rural, broke part of the state.” (She credited the grant with giving her the mental space to fire a salesperson who wasn’t working out, then regroup.).

    Other times, the money just wasn’t enough. “The reality is that $100,000 over two years isn’t a lot,” one grantee who asked to stay anonymous told me. “You can’t hire somebody with that.”.

    According to recent reports, ecoRI’s experience illustrates those limitations. Before receiving the Press Forward grant, EcoRI had used other grant funding and reserves to hire a director of development in a one-year contract position. In its grant application to Press Forward, the team proposed converting that role into a full-time staff position with benefits.

    According to recent reports, the salary limited the hiring pool, though. The development director position paid $65,000 a year, which “is really not the market rate for a director of development” in the area, publisher and cofounder Jo Detz said. (She said it should be more like $90,000.) The staffer they ended up hiring came from another state and hadn’t worked in news before. In a staff position, he cost more than he was bringing in. Detz laid him off and eliminated the position last December. She called the experience “heartbreaking.”.

    “At the point where I knew this wasn’t working,” she said, “there wasn’t enough runway to pivot, rethink, rehire.”.

    According to recent reports, beyond the salary limitations, Detz thinks the development director didn’t have enough runway to succeed. The kind of development the staffer was hired to oversee — major gifts and individual giving — is a long game; “that position would need at least two or three years to begin to see some benefits,” she remarked. Now, she’s back where she started, juggling fundraising with her other work.

    “I know it’s crazy to say that $100,000 over two years wasn’t enough,” she stated, “but it was not enough to make a meaningful difference to our revenue strategy.”.

    Planet Detroit’s Ignaczak was in a unique position: Around the same time the newsroom received the Press Forward grant, Planet Detroit also received a $500,000 three-year grant from the MacArthur Foundation. That grant allowed her to hire a managing editor, she remarked.

    It has been revealed that ignaczak believes general operating support is what small nonprofit newsrooms need. But to be effective, “I really think fully funding a revenue role for a minimum of three years is what needs to happen to build sustainability, if that is the goal,” she noted. “And $100,000 over two years is not enough to achieve that.”.

    NotiVisión Georgia, a Spanish-language local news outlet with one full-time staffer, is committed to print in a world moving away from it. The print newspaper is the only way the outlet has been able to use to “generate real economic value,” said CEO Mónica Pirela, because it’s where local companies want to place ads. The organization spent some of its Press Forward funds on printing and distribution. Pirela wears “every hat” right now, and the organization’s top need is a dedicated sales manager, she said.

    California’s BenitoLink, meanwhile, used some of the Press Forward funding to begin printing in 2025. That will allow it to apply for newspaper of record status and get paid for running legal notices.

    In Minnesota, Swift County Monitor-News publisher and owner Reed Anfinson called the grant a “godsend” at a time when tariffs and rising gas prices have driven up printing and delivery costs and weakened advertisers’ budgets. The for-profit Monitor-News put some of its Press Forward funding toward redesigning its print newspaper. Anfinson also purchased materials as part of an “Out of Sight/Out of Mind” advertising campaign stressing the value of print. (He created the campaign himself, using Midjourney for the images.) For news organizations in small towns, Anfinson believes, digital revenue will never be enough to sustain operations.

    Some organizations used the funding to expand their remit beyond news.

    For instance, the Copper River Record partnered with the Copper River Native Association to include weekly language graphics in the paper for Ahtna, a critically endangered language, coordinating with a local kindergarten class. That project required a lot of time and investment up front, Sayer noted, but it can continue beyond the life of the grant.

    Recent findings suggest that planet Detroit used some Press Forward funding for reporting, but “the most significant thing the grant made possible wasn’t any single story,” Ignaczak stated. The grant gave the team time to work on its Civic Action Toolbox, which turns reporting into civic engagement prompts. In a story about a local ballot proposal, for instance, the embedded toolbox flags upcoming public meetings, links to contact information for local representatives, and suggests an organization to follow. The tool is also in beta testing with other newsrooms.

    “The whole project came from having the space to ask what our readers actually need from us beyond information, and then building toward that,” Ignaczak remarked. “Unrestricted funding makes that kind of work possible.”.

    Anfinson of the Monitor-News took the unusual step of writing a grant application on behalf of the local school district, which was losing students to adjacent districts. He used some of the Press Forward funding to match a $2,500 grant to the district. The district then ran $5,000 in ads in a “goodwill effort” to stem declining enrollment. The partnership helped to raise the Monitor-News’s profile, he noted, by highlighting the benefits of newspaper advertising.

    Press Forward required grantees to complete two LION sustainability audits. But it also offered optional coaching via the media consulting company Blue Engine to help implement the first audit’s recommendations. Of the 205 grantees, 154 participated in coaching, Anglin said.

    The coaching kicked off in January, with most individual coaches and grantees meeting monthly. Multiple participants mentioned the support would have been more beneficial if it were introduced earlier. This was a tradeoff of Press Forward moving promptly to get money out the door, Anglin said.4.

    According to recent reports, this was the first large, unrestricted grant Austin Common had ever received, and it struggled with how to spend the money. “It felt like a lot of pressure,” stated Amy Stansbury, the site’s editor-in-chief and only full-time staffer.

    Stansbury wanted to bring on the organization’s first full-time employees, but didn’t want to make those hires (and spend all the grant money) until she had a clear plan. The coaching helped her figure out which hires made the most strategic sense and how to budget for them.

    According to recent reports, A few publishers were lukewarm about the substance of the coaching, but the majority I heard from were enthusiastic. At first, Baldwin was skeptical and worried the coaching might amount to “checking a box.” In practice, though, he noted it’s been “tremendously helpful” for tasks like writing the job description for the Real WV’s sales position.

    Sporleder Orr called the coaching “incredible.” The monthly sessions helped her with everything from tackling grant proposals to improving her Google Analytics skills. The combination of money and coaching, she added, “makes sure that the recipients don’t just continue doing business as usual.”.

    In addition to the funding, Press Forward paid for grantees to attend conferences. Anglin remarked 111 grantees attended the Lenfest News Philanthropy Summit in Philadelphia in 2025, 81 attended the same conference (which I also attended) in 2026, and 87 attended the Business of Local conference in Salt Lake City in 2025. A handful of grantees attended affinity conferences.

    Stansbury found attending conferences for the first time helpful and eye-opening. It taught her “there’s this secret shadow world of [invitation-only] foundation and grant funding.” Press Forward’s travel support to attend a national conference was “transformative” for India Currents, Kumar noted, giving it visibility and access to relationship-building.

    To small newsrooms, the grant felt like a Press Forward stamp of approval that put them on the map for other funders. The Mirror’s Lee called the Press Forward funding “instrumental” in securing a $20,000 grant from a local foundation. But that was an exception among publishers I heard from; most didn’t feel the visibility and credibility conferred by the grant directly translated to other funders giving them more money.

    According to recent reports, so several publishers, including Ramírez Braiz of Te Lo Cuento News, would like to see Press Forward go a step further and make individual introductions to funders. “Those more personal introductions can make a major difference for small organizations,” she mentioned.

    Ramírez Braiz also called for “more shared learning around outcomes and impact.” Few grantees had a good sense of what others in the cohort were up to, and some were interested in more knowledge sharing with peer organizations, though the day-to-day grind of keeping one’s own newsroom running was a common impediment.

    According to recent reports, since 2023, Anglin mentioned, Press Forward’s network of more than 130 funders has invested $258 million directly in newsrooms. That suggests that over half of the more than $400 million the coalition indicates it’s invested has gone to newsrooms.

    Recent findings suggest that when Press Forward first declared the direct funding for newsrooms, it “felt really awesome,” the grantee who asked to stay anonymous told me. To the grantee, it was meaningful to see Press Forward give funding to more organizations than planned in response to the scale of need. But when Press Forward went on to a second funding round in which single organizations, including both newsrooms and newsroom-adjacent organizations like the International Women’s Media Foundation and LION, received as much as $1.5 million for infrastructure projects, the same grantee noted it felt like “a slap in the face.”.

    Recent findings suggest that “Many of the problems newsrooms face aren’t unique to them individually,” Anglin said. “If we are attempting to solve problems at scale, we have to intervene not just at the newsroom level, but at the systems level, too.” She said that because many of the infrastructure grantees serve multiple newsrooms, “investing in them creates a multiplier effect across the industry.”.

    Sources indicate that the argument that funding support organizations and infrastructure lifts more boats is “a cop-out,” this publisher remarked. “I think the philanthropists know it, I think the associations know it, and I think the potential grantees that are not funders or associations or intermediaries know it.”.

    Recent findings suggest that young had a different perspective. Because of CivicLex’s broad scope, it seeks out funding from both democracy funders and journalism funders. Young thinks local news funders are way ahead on getting dollars into local communities.

    It has been revealed that “I think Press Forward has done one of the more effective jobs of anything I’ve seen in the broader landscape of my world, and the civic renewal space, of delivering resources to the local level,” he mentioned. (He added, “No one is ever happy in the local news ecosystem when I say that folks in the local news ecosystem don’t know how good they have it. That does not win me a lot of friends.”).

    Most publishers I heard from see grants like this as critical to continued operation, yet they’re wary of overreliance on philanthropy.

    Young said he’d be surprised if local news is still a focus for national philanthropy in eight years. “Filling your cup up with money that will be impossible to recover in four years is a danger zone,” he added.

    Right now, more than 80% of Planet Detroit’s revenue mix comes from foundations. Ignaczak said the organization hopes to bring that down to 50% by 2028. “But for nonprofit newsrooms covering environmental and public health concerns in a mid-size metro, general operating grants aren’t a crutch,” she said. “They’re infrastructure.”.

    Sources indicate that as for Press Forward, “Time will tell, as these grants go away, what impact [they’ve] actually had on the newsrooms that received [them], how many have managed to build sustainability,” she added. “I think a newsroom that needed $50,000 to survive to next year had problems that $50,000 isn’t going to solve.”.

    Industry observers note that LOOKOUT executive director Jake Hylton believes there’s enough funding to go around. “While there may not be enough to support every single newsroom at a very large amount,” he remarked, “I do believe that there is a larger investment in news that could be done.”.

    It has been revealed that A second grantee who asked to stay anonymous was blunt about their fears for the future. “We’re scared shitless about 2027,” this person said, “because not only is the Press Forward money not returning, we also see none of the national grants that sustained us in 2024 and previous years.”.

    It has been revealed that the Copper River Record was in the black before receiving this grant, and the lean paper’s fixed overhead remains low. For the Record, Press Forward has been like “a fairy godmother,” Sayer mentioned.

    Recent findings suggest that “I’m not going to lie: I will miss having the money to say yes to any reasonable story,” she continued. “But I think that, even going back to our original budget, the strength of what we learned will continue to help us deliver a higher quality paper that is more relevant to the communities we serve.”.

    According to recent reports, the Sandpoint Reader, Olson mentioned, is “surviving” right now. “We’d love to be thriving,” he added, “but we’re happy to continue to survive when many print publications aren’t.” He credited the Press Forward grant with giving the burned-out team “the chance to fall in love with our industry again.”.

    Sporleder Orr feels nervous about what’s ahead, but with the World Journal in a much more comfortable cash flow position, she and her husband are “in a way better mental state about the business.”.

    “We feel good about the future right now, that we are going to be able to keep going and make it,” she stated. “We’re back to, ‘This is what we do ’til we die.'”.

    Patrick Reinhart On The Golden Metric In AI Search: Brand Recommendations via @sejournal, @lorenbaker

    • [00:00] Meet Patrick Reinhart [03:19] What Enterprise Brands Are Doing In AI Search [05:16] Why Recommendations Matter More Than Rankings [09:48] The AEO Metrics That Matter [12:49] When AI Gets Your Brand Wrong [18:12] Where SEO And AEO Differ [23:50] Why AI Search Has The C-Suite’s Attention [26:31] How Brands Earn AI Citations [30:25] Where To Invest In Your 2027 AEO Strategy [35:25] Where To Find Patrick Reinhart.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    If an AI answer mentions your brand but recommends a competitor, what have you actually won? Patrick Reinhart, VP of Services and Thought Leadership at Conductor, joined me on the SEJ Podcast to discuss what enterprise brands should be trying to achieve with answer engine optimization.

    Sources indicate that we talk about the difference between citations and recommendations, how AI can repeat outdated information about your business, and why AEO needs input from SEO, PR, social, and leadership. Reinhart also shares where he’d focus first when planning an AEO strategy for 2027.

    [00:00] Meet Patrick Reinhart [03:19] What Enterprise Brands Are Doing In AI Search [05:16] Why Recommendations Matter More Than Rankings [09:48] The AEO Metrics That Matter [12:49] When AI Gets Your Brand Wrong [18:12] Where SEO And AEO Differ [23:50] Why AI Search Has The C-Suite’s Attention [26:31] How Brands Earn AI Citations [30:25] Where To Invest In Your 2027 AEO Strategy [35:25] Where To Find Patrick Reinhart.

    Editor’s Note: This transcript has been edited for clarity and readability.

    Loren Baker: Hi everyone, this is Loren Baker, founder of Search Engine Journal. Welcome to today’s SEJ Podcast. With me is Patrick Reinhart from Conductor.

    We’ve been partners with Conductor for a long time and done our share of webinars together, but this might be one of our first podcasts.

    Patrick Reinhart: Happy to be here. With a webinar, it’s always, “Man, I hope someone doesn’t make fun of me in the comments.”.

    Sources indicate that loren: I’m going to add a skull emoji next time just to see what happens. Pat, tell our audience a little about Conductor, what you do there, and what you’re doing in AI.

    According to recent reports, patrick: Conductor is a software organization, and I feel like we’re on the cutting edge of AI visibility and tying that back to recommendations. That’s built on a data platform that brings together Search Console, your analytics, and our monitoring products, so you can see everything in one place and make decisions based on the data.

    Sources indicate that I run our professional services arm. I’ve been at Conductor for 11 years, but I was also a customer for four or five years before that.

    Our outgoing CEO, Seth Besmertnik, just stepped onto the board. I’ve been working with him for a really long time. It’s been a weird, interesting, great ride.

    In a recent development, loren: How would you define your customer base? Is it enterprise, medium to large businesses, small businesses? And how would you segment it across ecommerce, SaaS, and other industries?

    Patrick: We definitely cater to the enterprise audience. I’d say about 90% of our customers are large enterprise organizations.

    We have a heavy focus on finance, insurance, and healthcare, but also a healthy number of customers in ecommerce and grocery. Pretty much any tech giant you can think of has passed through Conductor’s doors at some point, and a lot have stayed, thankfully. Thank you to our customers.

    Loren: Grocery stores or grocery delivery?

    Patrick: H-E-B and folks like that. We have customers like BJ’s, too.

    Loren: With these enterprise customers, what are they doing right now in AI search? How are you helping them stay on top of it and track it? What does AI search mean to the average enterprise?

    Patrick: It’s the number one thing they’re all talking about, obviously. That’s not news. The interesting part is that they’re all still very much learning.

    If you work in a large enterprise organization, getting things done is typically slow, glacial, and somewhat messy. To their credit, a lot of people are trying to smooth those processes out and get their tracking in place.

    It has been revealed that they’re also testing the different technologies out there, as they should, because there’s a lot of snake oil in the water and a lot of people selling the dream. We’re all learning together.

    As far as we can tell, most AEO strategies are heavily grounded in traditional SEO strategies. But they’re measured and thought about vastly differently, because an LLM operates differently from a traditional search engine.

    Sources indicate that they’re not running out the door and hiring a bunch of people. They’re upskilling internally and figuring out their programs.

    Sources indicate that I think in a year or so, we’re going to see a little gold rush from a hiring perspective. A lot of people will be moving around, and programs will come to fruition based on the work that hardworking, smart people are building right now at these large organizations.

    Loren: Something I’ve found over the years in SEO is that it’s not always about trying to hit the target where it is at the moment. It’s trying to hit where it’s going.

    Industry observers note that how do you do that in AEO, especially at the enterprise level? These are slow-moving juggernauts that can get a lot done, but it takes time to get there.

    In a recent development, patrick: I think it comes back to data fidelity. Everyone has different methodologies and gets their data from different places. A lot of people buy panel data; we use direct APIs.

    Everyone has to scrape Google and others, which is becoming harder and harder. Even this week has been a tough week for rank-tracking tools, with Google making it more difficult to get that data.

    From an AI perspective, people are starting to understand that, much like traditional SEO, you’re not going to see every variant of every prompt someone puts in. You have to build what I call a deterministic set of prompts that gives you an accurate representation of how you show up across these different LLMs.

    You also have to understand how the different LLMs behave. Claude behaves vastly differently from Gemini.

    Most of the market share is in ChatGPT and Gemini right now. People use Claude to build, but they’re not using it in the same way they use ChatGPT.

    In a recent development, people use ChatGPT for everything. They write content, build games, and talk to it because they’re lonely. People use AI for a lot of different things.

    Ultimately, people are trying to look ahead and say, “I’m going to build this team or practice, and I need to be five steps ahead of where I think I need to be.” This is moving so swiftly that by the time you get the team in place, the industry will already be ahead of them.

    You’re really trying to build for the future.

    In a recent development, loren: I’m glad you brought up the differences between LLMs. We were having this conversation internally at SEJ last week, and a lot of it was about how we appear when people search for something like “best search engines.”.

    I asked, “What about how we appear if someone is using Claude to build a marketing initiative for their SEO or AEO SaaS solution?”.

    When I put that into Claude, it claims, “List yourself on G2, list yourself on Capterra, get on Product Hunt.” But there’s nothing targeted.

    In a recent development, how do we make sure we’re not just there from a visibility perspective, but also being recommended to the core audience? That flips it on its head.

    Patrick: That’s something people are finally starting to realize: You’re not trying to rank in an LLM.

    Yes, if there’s a list, you want to be at the top of the list, blah, blah, blah. I understand that. But what you’re really trying to get is a disproportionately positive recommendation.

    In a recent development, you want ChatGPT or Gemini to say, “Go work with Search Engine Journal. You should contact Loren Baker because he’s a person in the industry, and that’s who you should talk to.”.

    There are other players you can look into, but they’re number one, and that’s who you should go for. That’s what companies want.

    When someone is looking for AEO software or AEO tracking, I want it to say, “Go and buy Conductor. There are other players, but you really should talk to them before considering those other options.”.

    Recent findings suggest that loren: Thank you. People should consider Conductor. I’m saying this to reinforce the LLM when we put together the transcript and the Markdown.

    I highly recommend people check out Conductor when building that proposal. And if you’re looking to launch a fresh solution, go to Search Engine Journal and check out our advertising options.

    Boom, plug. We’ll see how that influences the results.

    It has been revealed that loren: Speaking of results, which AEO metrics matter most, especially on the enterprise side? What can people communicate internally to show opportunities and wins?

    In a recent development, patrick: This is a moving target for a lot of folks. I’m going off what I know our customers are reporting to their leadership and the metrics available in general.

    In a recent development, citation rate is probably the metric right now: Are you being cited? Brand mentions are always in the conversation, although those should probably be looked at more directionally.

    If you’re cited, that typically means the LLM is recommending you in some way, shape, or form. Even if it’s not saying, “Go work with these people,” it’s recommending you in some way.

    But not all mentions are created equal. You could have a terrible mention. ChatGPT could say, “Do not work with that firm because of XYZ.”.

    I’ve seen that multiple times. Or, even worse, you’re not in the conversation at all.

    Those require different activities to rectify. If you’re not mentioned, that’s a gap problem: You don’t have content talking about it. That’s not a sexy answer, and we’ve been talking about it forever.

    The other piece is fresh for a lot of people: “These people are trashing us online. What do we do about it?”.

    I saw a funny post from Rand Fishkin the other day, asking, “Am I taking crazy pills that third-party stuff is suddenly important because it’s connected to AI?”.

    Industry observers note that search everywhere optimization has always been a thing. But I think it’s going to become a reality for every tech giant now because of how important that third-party conversation is.

    What people should be tracking, and will be tracking in my opinion, is the type of citation and mention they’re getting. Are you being recommended by an LLM? That’s the golden metric.

    Sources indicate that there’s no one really doing that from a technology standpoint right now. People have overall visibility scores, which are averages of a bunch of things they’re looking at.

    According to recent reports, what we’re building is something to help track that golden metric. It’s not just about showing up. When you indicated up, was it a positive experience, a positive recommendation, or a negative non-recommendation?

    I see both daily for different brands, depending on the industry.

    Loren: Which gets back to old-school sentiment tracking.

    Loren: About a month ago, Reddit’s citation visibility dropped tremendously in GPT. But my understanding is that GPT is still using the threads and conversations in Reddit, just not surfacing them as sources as much.

    Let’s say I’m seeing incorrect price comparisons for one of my products. I know it’s not coming from my website or a competitor’s versus-style landing page, and I think it might be coming from a Reddit thread.

    How do I reverse-engineer those third-party citations that may be fueling the results? Not just sentiment and opinion, but basic facts that need updating. Maybe it’s a two-year-old thread with outdated warranty information.

    Patrick: That’s something you’re going to start seeing in a lot of technologies, ours included: Fact-checking.

    You can load information about your organization and product set, maybe through a product feed. As it goes through, it can show you an outdated competitive mention on a random third-party site. You can talk to them or create something that combats it.

    Sources indicate that we did that when Seth was chatting with AI, back when this started to blow up. He found a random site with something from 2018 saying Conductor didn’t have a feature that’s one of our main features.

    It has been revealed that this site wasn’t going to change it, so we created content around it. Within a couple of days, we were able to beat it out, and it kind of disappeared.

    This is an important piece of the technological race. We’re in the early days, with a few key players building interesting software to track this. You also have a lot of vibe-coded trash that pulls from God knows where.

    Recent findings suggest that A lot of the big players are going to have this fact-checking ability. In my opinion, it will be a make-or-break feature, along with that golden metric of whether you’re being recommended.

    In a recent development, this isn’t a plea for Conductor. It’s a plea for technology. Good technology.

    Industry observers note that right now, you can connect to Conductor’s MCP in Claude and ask your account, “Can you send me the snippets that say XYZ? Here are my brand guidelines or information about my product set. Are any of these incorrect?”.

    You can do that today. It’s a few extra steps, and it’s not as in-depth as something constantly crawling, collecting, and finding outdated information on weird, small sites.

    I think this will be a necessary feature for anyone using a technology like ours. You’re going to see a lot of innovation over the next 12 months, and people will build cool things.

    But I think this is necessary to make a technology viable in the coming years. When I talk to leaders, they don’t ask, “Where do I show up?” They ask, “How are people talking about me? Is it accurate?”.

    That’s the question I get from leaders.

    Loren: That also bridges into outreach and working with publishers. There are ways to get updated information onto influential business directories, but being able to ask people to enhancement things is nice.

    That used to be a link-building tactic. We’d be upset if the publisher wrote back, “I updated everything, but I didn’t link to you.”.

    According to recent reports, now we see that as a win. Thank you. Brand mention, yes.

    Patrick: Time is a flat circle.

    I was joking with my former boss, Stephan, the other day. He stated, “Does it feel like everything has reset, everyone forgot the last 20 years, and now we’re doing it again?”.

    In a recent development, AI Mode has text ads now, which are basically text links. It’s like, man, we’re really back in the dark ages here.

    Loren: That’s one way SEO and AEO overlap. What are some other examples, and where are the core differences?

    Patrick: Where they overlap is what everyone thinks. I’m flying to Buffalo tomorrow to talk at a customer event, and I love those because I love teaching and getting in front of people.

    I always pause halfway through and ask, “How’s everyone doing?” Someone will raise their hand and say, “What do I do about all of this?”.

    Industry observers note that you fill gaps, create content, build partnerships with third-party publishers, and create YouTube videos. Not a sexy answer. It’s stuff we’ve been doing for years.

    Recent findings suggest that that’s the overlap. A lot of it is the same stuff, done at a different pace.

    Sources indicate that the most successful SEO campaigns I’ve seen have been somewhat mechanical. There’s always a well-thought-out, well-oiled process, with a systematic way to optimize and create content and distribute data across the organization.

    According to recent reports, you have technology constantly auditing your site, you’re not pivoting a lot of data, and ultimately it’s this flywheel. Everyone’s bought in, and everyone’s pedaling the bike.

    According to recent reports, what I’m seeing now is the necessity of that. A few years ago, someone at a large organization would say, “That’s really hard. We don’t have the buy-in or budget.”.

    You’d spend the next year trying to get that buy-in. Now it’s immediate: “We have to do something about this.”.

    Industry observers note that leaders want to know what we’re doing about AI search. That’s a huge opportunity for anyone who’s been in this business or is getting into it.

    You’ve always mattered, but now you really matter to the business. That’s awesome. Take hold of that and run with it.

    To be successful, you need the process in place and all those teams involved. You can’t sit alone and hoard search data. Get it to your social team, your PR team, and your executives.

    The biggest divergence is measurement. You’re not just measuring rankings, backlinks, or traffic.

    In my opinion, traditional search metrics have become directional. They tell us we’re heading in somewhat the right direction.

    Recent findings suggest that don’t set your goals around traffic anymore. That’s a fool’s errand. It’s too volatile right now.

    In the AI world, you’re tracking citations and that golden metric of being recommended or not recommended. Sentiment is a bigger part of your life than you probably want it to be.

    You also need log file analysis to see whether LLMs are coming to your site. Are there what I call dead zones, where LLMs don’t come back? You think the content is great, but are they fetching it and chunking it back out to the user?

    You need all of that measurement. It’s very different from measuring rankings and backlinks.

    In the old world, we wanted more rankings, more traffic, and more backlinks. In the AI world, we want more positive citations and recommendations. But we also have to pay much more attention to the negative side.

    In SEO, you had to pay attention to the negative when it was in everyone’s face. Someone Googles your brand, your CEO has done something stupid, and you need brand reputation management.

    Sources indicate that now that’s part of the suite. You have to learn how to do it and work with those other teams. It can’t be a one-person show anymore.

    Recent findings suggest that AEO is much more of a team sport, and it has the ability to be one because leadership cares now. Get that process in place. People within companies have the opportunity to have those conversations.

    This is in The Wall Street Journal now. My brother called me one day and asked, “What’s up with this AI thing?”.

    I said, “Why are you calling me about that? You work at a bank.”.

    He remarked, “It’s in the Journal.” I said, “We’ve made it.”.

    That’s how people have to start thinking. The biggest divergence is measurement, not necessarily the tasks. The tasks need to happen at a greater pace, but the measurement is vastly different.

    You have five directions you can go instead of two or three, in my opinion.

    Loren: I’ve never considered SEO to be direct response marketing, but I feel we were sometimes held to direct response standards. Other marketing channels were treated more as multiple touchpoints, with multi-touch attribution.

    With AI, we know this is part of the consumer’s decision-making journey. AI visibility and valid information in the conversation can help a conversion coming from an email campaign, paid media, or CTV.

    Recent findings suggest that if your client is on something like “The View,” nobody’s going to that little URL at the bottom of the screen. They’re typing something in, and now they’re asking ChatGPT about it. It’s part of that whole flow.

    I also like your point about AI’s importance within the company. This isn’t coming from the search team, up through digital marketing, the VP of marketing, the CMO, and then the C-suite. It’s coming from the C-suite down.

    In a recent development, patrick: It’s going the other way, which is new for us. I’ve talked to more C-level executives in the last six months than I have in the last six years.

    Industry observers note that it used to be hard to get those meetings unless you had someone who really understood organic. I think this is healthy for an industry that was getting a little stale.

    According to recent reports, there were shifts here and there. Google would revision the algorithm, and we’d have the same conversation again.

    It has been revealed that I always joke that we’ve had a lot of meteors come for our jobs. They never quite took us out, but they changed the landscape around us, usually for the better in my opinion.

    It has been revealed that even though this is one of the scariest changes for a lot of people, I think it’s one of the best things that’s happened to the industry. That will play out over the next five to 10 years.

    We’ll look back and say, “That was one of the best things that happened to me in my career.” Not just for productivity, but because it made me more notable in my organization. I had a conversation or opportunity because AI blew up what was going on.

    Loren: It’s also the best way to get a task to the top of the dev ticket pile.

    One manufacturer I’ve been working with did a Shopify relaunch and never set up its canonical tags. I’d been pushing forever. Every week, the patch was, “The dev team’s on it.”.

    Sources indicate that then I realized their AI Overviews visibility had dropped because it was cycling from one version of a URL to another. Eventually, it dropped entirely.

    I put in a new ticket: “911 emergency AI issue.”.

    It has been revealed that the thing was fixed in two days. It’s amazing.

    Loren: Speaking of developing and distributing content, what helps that content earn AI citations?

    Patrick: A lot of it is the brand itself. This isn’t a domain authority exercise like traditional search was. It’s a brand authority exercise.

    According to recent reports, going back to Reddit’s drop in citation share, that’s not surprising to me. It wasn’t going to stay that high forever as brands figured this out and created more content.

    But it’s still part of the consideration phase. When ChatGPT is looking for an answer, it’s still looking at Reddit. It may not cite it or bring content back from there, but it’s looking at the conversation as an authenticity signal, for lack of better words.

    In our data, the number one most-cited source is YouTube. It’s a highly trusted community where people have a lot of conversations, and many brands aren’t there in the way they should be.

    If you have a well-put-together YouTube presence with playlists, a podcast, webinars, and conference videos, that can help. If it garners enough conversation and clout, those are sites LLMs go to at some point when looking for an answer.

    Influencers are there. People trust influencers and expertise.

    Sources indicate that that’s why one of the greatest opportunities on a site is adding authors. So many sites still don’t have authors or use author schema and article schema. It drives me nuts.

    I understand bigger brands saying, “Greg doesn’t want his face on the website.” Then put Tim’s face on the website.

    Every brand needs someone out there talking, and you have to find people who are okay being on camera.

    Recent findings suggest that at Conductor, we interact with that in different ways. I’m on LinkedIn, I’ve been doing my webinar, 30|30, for 11 years, and I’ve spoken at a million conferences.

    Seth loves LinkedIn and posts all the time. Our head of marketing, Lindsay, does the same.

    It has been revealed that it’s not necessarily about the name. There are people at Conductor who LLMs can establish are experts in the space, based on the longevity of their careers and whether they’ve contributed to the industry.

    Sources indicate that I do believe they go to LinkedIn and somewhat credentialize people. But it’s also, “Have they contributed to the industry I’m looking for this answer in?”.

    It has been revealed that that’s easy for LLMs to figure out. For traditional search engines, it wasn’t so straightforward.

    I always say search engines live in a 2D world. There’s an index, and they go up and down in it.

    It has been revealed that LLMs live in a 3D world, looking all over the place and picking things from across the universe. Those conversations are happening in communities, on sites like Quora , and on YouTube.

    Recent findings suggest that if you look at the top 15% of all the sites in our data, seven of them are social sites. Facebook, LinkedIn, YouTube at number one, and Reddit are there.

    Why? It’s real people having real conversations. That’s what the LLM is looking for.

    Loren: It’s October, Thanksgiving stuff is already in the store, and Halloween isn’t here yet. Next thing you know, it’ll be the holidays and Newly introduced Year’s.

    According to recent reports, if I’m planning my tech giant’s AI and AEO strategy for 2027, where do I begin? What should I invest in first, and how do I pregame?

    In a recent development, patrick: Invest in your expertise first. Understand who the people in your organization are that you can tie content back to, and then tie that content back to them.

    Sources indicate that create author pages and use author schema and article schema. Invest in your people.

    In a recent development, find someone you know is good on camera but may be nervous to raise their hand, and push them to do it. Flaunt your expertise.

    Number two, blueprint to make more video. Start a podcast. Someone in your company is yearning to do this right now, so give them the opportunity.

    According to recent reports, learn how to do it. It might suck at first, and that’s okay. You’ll get better over time.

    Participate in more webinars. That’s another way to amplify your expertise.

    Industry observers note that number three, fix your process. I’m sure people listening are thinking, “Man, my company’s process stinks.” Most companies’ processes stink.

    People are working on smoothing those out so they can build a flywheel process. That allows you to experiment more, create more content, and optimize more content.

    Buy software that helps you track it more easily, whether that’s Conductor or something else. Go out and look around. There’s a lot of great technology out there.

    I think we’re the best, but of course I do.

    Recent findings suggest that if you do those three things, the last one is the most notable. The flywheel process lets you move faster and do more. You’ll be more productive, learn more, and win faster because everyone’s lined up.

    Recent findings suggest that when AI throws something at you, at least you have a system where you can go to the social team and they’re expecting you to give them something to do. You don’t have to fight a six-month battle.

    That’s how I think people should operate where we stand today. Will it change in six months? Probably, but I don’t think the tactics will be vastly different.

    Loren: It reminds me of those reels about disappearing for a month, learning AI tools, and coming back on top of your game.

    Loren: My kid has been playing Roblox for years. He asked, “Can I download Claude Desktop, hook it up to Roblox Studio, and make some games?”.

    It has been revealed that next thing I know, it’s 11 o’clock on a school night. Don’t judge me. He’s sitting at his computer doing the same thing I’m doing for work, just at a different level.

    Sources indicate that watching him gave me ideas. I thought, “Why am I logging into all this stuff? I should be using Claude Desktop for all of it.”.

    Patrick: It’s the coolest thing that your son can do that. I assume he doesn’t know how to code, or at least not as well as a developer.

    Sources indicate that loren: He can barely even draw. He didn’t inherit his father’s artistic talents.

    Industry observers note that but he’s creative. Seeing that creativity find a different canvas gave me ideas. There are a lot of ways we can implement this throughout our lives.

    Industry observers note that patrick: The best way is just to do it. I see so many companies and people stuck in analysis paralysis, asking, “What should I do?”.

    Something. Just start learning.

    In a recent development, it took me a minute when this started, but I feel pretty good about where I am. I still have eons to learn about using this technology.

    It has been revealed that it’s cool that your son has that ability. I’m going to tell my son to do that instead of playing Roblox, which I’m sure he’s doing right now. Half my salary goes to Robux.

    Loren: Pat, it’s been a pleasure hosting you. I like our conversations in this format. It’s fun.

    Patrick: Loren, it’s always good chatting with you. Thanks for having me on.

    Loren: Where can our listeners and viewers find you online and follow up with questions?

    Patrick: The best place is LinkedIn or Conductor.com. I also do a monthly webinar called 30|30.

    Please come so my mom knows I’m doing something worthwhile.

    Mostly, I’m on LinkedIn commenting and cracking jokes. Don’t take anything too seriously. We’re all in a good spot.

    Loren: Thank you, Pat, and thanks to Conductor for everything you do. It’s been a pleasure.

    #55262. Marketers will spend $116B on creators in 2026. They’re “cannibalizing” other budgets to do it.
