    Marketers will spend $116B on creators in 2026. They’re “cannibalizing” other budgets to do it.

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (471 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Tubefilter

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Marketers are investing more money into the creator economy—and reallocating their existing advertising budgets to pay for it.
    • According to a recent report from strategic advisory, consulting, and research firm Madison and Wall, marketer spend on creators is set to grow “+15% in 2026 to $116 billion globally, up from $101 billion in 2025.”.
    • Based on that trajectory, the report predicts that the advertiser-funded creator economy will hit $178 billion by 2030.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Marketers are investing more money into the creator economy—and reallocating their existing advertising budgets to pay for it.

    According to a recent report from strategic advisory, consulting, and research firm Madison and Wall, marketer spend on creators is set to grow “+15% in 2026 to $116 billion globally, up from $101 billion in 2025.”.

    Based on that trajectory, the report predicts that the advertiser-funded creator economy will hit $178 billion by 2030.

    Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

    Recent findings suggest that madison and Wall compiled its study by isolating marketing funds dedicated to “creator related activity” (i.e., “spending deployed to creators, agencies, platforms, technology vendors, and media networks to achieve marketing, commerce, or brand objectives”). Other forms of creator income—such as subscriptions, merch, and platform payouts—weren’t taken into account.

    The report further separated creator marketing spend into five distinct categories: audience-led spend, media-led spend, asset-led spend, infrastructure-led spend, and miscellaneous.

    Of those categories, Madison and Wall found that media-led spending—aka “the paid amplification of creator content”—accounts for the largest piece of the pie at 44% (or $52 billion) of 2026 spend.

    Audience-led spending (“the traditional sponsored-post and ambassador model”) ranks second at 28%, while asset-led spending (“where brands pay for content rather than reach”) accounts for 12% of the market. Infrastructure-led spending (net revenue kept by agencies, managers, and platforms) and miscellaneous (events, gifting, licensing, etc.) bring up the rear at 8% and 7% respectively.

    On a global scale, Madison and Wall found that the U.S. was responsible for 43% of creator spending in 2025, well above its ~35% share of global advertising. The closest runners-up were the UK (which accounts for 5% of global creator spending) and Germany (4%).

    One of the key takeaways of Madison and Wall’s report concerned the origin of marketing funds dedicated to creator advertising.

    The firm noted that “creator growth is largely funded by reallocation rather than new money. Interviews with stakeholders across the ecosystem point to three sources: traditional media, notably TV; digital performance media, including paid social, programmatic and search; and creative production budgets. Because creators draw on several existing budget pools at once, the creator economy can keep outgrowing advertising without marketers creating new budgets.”.

    One senior operations executive told Madison and Wall that “80% of the time we are cannibalizing another budget, whether it’s TV or [something else].”.

    Overall, the firm found that creator spending grew at an 18% compound annual growth rate (CAGR) between 2020 and 2025, as compared with 12% for advertising.

    That gap doesn’t seem likely to close anytime soon. According to the firm’s projections, creator spending is set to grow ~12% a year through 2030—putting it well ahead of the 6% growth expected for the advertising economy.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers. We provide a complete backend solution including Database, Auth, Storage, Edge Functions, Realtime, and Vector Search. All services are deeply integrated and designed for growth.

    In a recent development, we are looking for a Senior Contracts Manager to take ownership of vendor contracting at Supabase. You will be the go-to contracts partner for everything we buy.

    This is a hands-on, high-autonomy role with real ownership, for an experienced negotiator who takes pride in making procurement faster while managing risk. You will negotiate directly, build the playbooks and workflows that let the business self-serve on low-risk deals, and escalate the right concerns to Legal at the right time. We work AI-first in Legal: you will use Claude and Ironclad every day to move faster and with greater accuracy. Your work will shape how procurement and vendor contracting scale as Supabase grows.

    Own vendor contracting end to end.

    Review, draft, and negotiate a high volume of vendor agreements, including MSAs, order forms, SOWs, SaaS and cloud subscription terms, DPAs, and NDAs.

    Recent findings suggest that serve as the single point of contact for all vendor contracting matters raised by FinOps, IT, Security, and business owners, from intake through signature, renewals, amendments, disputes, and offboarding. As capacity allows, you will also support the broader Commercial Legal team on other matters.

    Apply and further build out our playbook and risk framework independently, and escalate to the Assistant General Counsel, Commercial where a deal falls outside approved positions or raises novel legal risk.

    Negotiate data, privacy, and security terms (DPAs, security exhibits, cross-border transfers) within the Security team’s playbook, and bring in the AGC, Commercial or Privacy for anything outside it.

    Review AI vendor terms, such as training on our data, output ownership, and model changes.

    Build and scale vendor contracting operations.

    Build out and maintain our vendor playbook in Claude, so the whole team works from the same guidance and low-risk deals move without bottlenecks.

    Design and improve intake, triage, and approval workflows with FinOps.

    In a recent development, own the vendor and procurement workflow in Ironclad, including intake, templates, approvals, and the repository, working with Legal Ops, who own the platform. Use it to track renewals and notice windows with FinOps and flag spend concentration risks.

    Create training and self-serve resources for business partners, and raise the visibility of the contracts function as a business enabler.

    6 to 8+ years of experience negotiating procurement, vendor, or technology transactions contracting, ideally buy-side at a U.S. SaaS or technology firm, with deep knowledge of SaaS, cloud, and software licensing terms.

    A track record of negotiating directly with vendors and their counsel, independently and at pace.

    Strong working knowledge of privacy, data protection, and security terms in commercial contracts, including DPA negotiation and international data transfers.

    Experience designing contracting processes that are consistent, transparent, and easy for the business to follow.

    Clear writing and speaking, with the ability to explain legal and commercial risk plainly and the judgment to know when to hold a position, approve a reasonable risk, or escalate.

    Comfort using AI tools, Claude in particular, with sound judgment about when to rely on outputs, how to verify them, and how to protect confidential information.

    A degree in a relevant field (for example, law, economics, or political science), though we value experience over the specific degree.

    Sell-side experience negotiating customer, partner, or reseller agreements for a SaaS or technology tech giant, which helps you see vendor terms from the other side.

    Hands-on experience with Ironclad or a similar CLM tool (Juro, Docusign CLM) or building AI-assisted legal workflows, ideally with some exposure to AI governance.

    Experience working across jurisdictions or with distributed, international teams.

    Experience at a fast-growing, developer-focused, cloud, security, or open source company.

    Industry observers note that we hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

    In a recent development, every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the manufacturer. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

    Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

    Industry observers note that supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are important to us.

    Once a year, the entire manufacturer gathers in a new city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

    We operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

    Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

    Supabase was born-remote and open-source-first. We believe our globally distributed team is our secret weapon in building tools developers love.

    Over $1B raised (including our $500M Series F).

    We move fast, build in public, and use what we ship. If it’s in your project, we probably use it in ours too. We believe deeply in the open-source ecosystem and strive to support—not replace—existing tools and communities.

    #55260. AI Visibility Data: Avoid 4 Traps & Prioritize The Right Work

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (970 w)

    AI Visibility Data: Avoid 4 Traps & Prioritize The Right Work

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (970 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • This post was sponsored by TransPerfect Digital.
    • According to recent reports, your AI visibility dashboard shows brand mentions, sentiment scores, and frequently cited sources.
    • Which data sources actually help increase AI visibility?
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    This post was sponsored by TransPerfect Digital. The opinions expressed in this article are the sponsor’s own.

    According to recent reports, your AI visibility dashboard shows brand mentions, sentiment scores, and frequently cited sources. But what do they tell you?

    Which data sources actually help increase AI visibility?

    AI tools show 72% visibility; is this good?

    What strategies does AI visibility data inform?

    As you can imagine, the logical next steps are to choose KPIs that reflect your business goals, then use your AI visibility data to identify the next best steps.

    However, the challenge is understanding what to measure, how to analyze, and which online tips are helpful, useless, or harmful.

    These myths and misinterpretations that can steer your generative engine optimization (GEO) work toward the wrong priorities.

    The four traps below will help you interpret those signals before changing your content, channel strategy, or budget.

    Not sure which AI visibility findings deserve your team’s time?

    TransPerfect Digital explains how its team ranks AI search opportunities by business impact and the effort each change would take.

    The first trap is treating AI visibility tracking like a keyword-ranking report.

    A score is only useful if the questions being measured reflect the people you want to reach.

    Instead, choose prompts that reflect your customers’ questions across buying stages, markets, and AI platforms before deciding what to change.

    It has been revealed that imagine a tool reports 72% visibility. That number could look reassuring while describing a narrow set of branded, informational questions from one customer group, market, and AI platform.

    If you cannot tell whether that score includes the questions your buyers ask when comparing options, it cannot tell you which content needs attention.

    To assess our example 72% score, check whether it represents the customers and buying decisions that matter to your business, using a consistent set of prompts for comparison.

    In a recent development, that means checking coverage before setting a target or commissioning content. Use the prompt-library checks below to find which audiences, questions, or markets are missing.

    Sources indicate that pro Tip: Before relying on a visibility score, check whose questions it represents. See how we choose prompts for each audience and buying stage.

    To determine if your AI visibility score is helpful, check its coverage:.

    Pro Tip: Be sure to analyze each individual model, not overall LLM performance, as each retrieves and cites differently.

    Use first-party data to map actual user behavior to your objectives and ICPs, then add questions from sales conversations, customer support, and local teams.

    Adapt the questions to each market’s language and customer needs rather than translating one country’s list.

    Recent findings suggest that list the audiences, products and services, markets, and AI platforms your business needs to monitor. Choose a tool that meets those requirements, and check its visibility definition before comparing scores between tools.

    According to recent reports, prompt wording varies and results can be personalized, so one answer is not a stable ranking. Use these checks to identify recurring patterns per topic cluster, category, or product line before assigning work:.

    The second trap is accepting a headline metric without checking what it means for your business. Visibility scores, sentiment labels, and citation counts need context: your positioning, goals, customers, and products.

    Consider an illustrative example: a tool labels a luxury brand negatively because answers describe its products as expensive.

    That description may reinforce premium positioning. But an answer saying the product is poor value, unreliable, or unsuitable for its intended buyer would raise a different problem.

    In a recent development, before creating a corrective task, connect the metric to your business goal and read the underlying answers. For the sentiment example, ask:.

    Match your response to what the answer actually indicates:.

    Apply this business-context check to every headline metric, not just sentiment, so you do not miss opportunities or spend time correcting something that supports your strategy.

    It has been revealed that the third trap is turning every finding into a to-do or adopting a fashionable GEO tactic without checking its strategic value. A frequently cited source can reveal an information need without dictating a channel.

    Suppose Reddit keeps appearing in answers about your product category. Before adding Reddit activity to your proposal, examine the cited discussions.

    Recent findings suggest that A task such as “post on Reddit” names a channel without explaining the customer need. Identifying that need first makes it easier to choose where and how to contribute.

    According to recent reports, prioritize findings that reveal an important customer need and support your business goals; defer those that do not. Apply that test to Reddit:.

    See how we prioritize changes to content, technical SEO, and third-party sources when several findings compete for the same team’s time.

    The fourth trap is treating visibility as the business goal, then assigning it a precise revenue contribution the evidence cannot support.

    A recorded AI referral and an AI-influenced decision are not the same thing. Someone may discover, compare, or shortlist a brand in an AI answer without clicking through to its website.

    Sources indicate that low recorded referral traffic does not establish low influence. Equally, rising branded search does not prove AI caused the increase.

    Keep these signals distinct in your reporting:.

    Choose business measures that fit your goal, such as qualified inquiries or sales, and show them alongside visibility signals without claiming a causal connection you have not established.

    Before assigning work, review these four questions:.

    Those checks help you decide what to investigate, what to change, and what to leave alone.

    #55259. Elon Musk’s Grokipedia is littered with mistakes. But Wikipedia could still learn some things from it.

    📅 02 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 26m • 📚 Deep Dive (5103 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Niemanlab ↗ Open Full Page

    Elon Musk’s Grokipedia is littered with mistakes. But Wikipedia could still learn some things from it.

    📅 02 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 26 min read (5103 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Niemanlab

    ⏱️ ~26 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing.
    • Recent findings suggest that we have sent a confirmation link to .
    • Grokipedia highlights that AI is actually pretty good at finding tidbits in the far corners of the internet.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    Recent findings suggest that we have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    Grokipedia highlights that AI is actually pretty good at finding tidbits in the far corners of the internet.

    It has been revealed that when I saw Grokipedia’s articles about me, the memories came rushing back: my 19 years in minor league baseball, including that impressive season with the Montgomery Rebels when I hit 20 home runs. I was lean back then — 6 feet tall and 168 pounds — and earned a career batting average just under .300. I became a minor league coach and managed the Chicago White Sox for a short stint in 1970, which Grokipedia stated “highlighted [my] readiness for higher-level responsibilities.”.

    I then attended Arizona State University, switched to a career in journalism, created the fact-checking site PolitiFact, won a Pulitzer Prize, and now teach journalism at Duke University.

    Ah, the memories!…except that I never played minor league baseball, never managed the White Sox, and can only dream about being 6 feet tall. (I’m 5’8″.) Grokipedia, the AI-written encyclopedia of Elon Musk, has confused me with Marion Danne “Bill” Adair, who died in 2002.

    Sources indicate that that article and another one about “Bill Adair (journalist)” — which really is me — illustrate the many flaws of Grokipedia, which launched a year ago. The articles are littered with mistakes and superfluous details. They are terribly written and ridiculously long. If Grok, the AI engine that wrote this turgid prose, were a student in one of my writing courses, I would give it a D. (Editor’s note: After this article was published, someone updated the inaccurate Grok pages. The original versions are linked here.).

    According to recent reports, still, the articles provide valuable lessons for Wikipedia editors who are debating how and when to use AI. Grokipedia adds new content and context that Wikipedia often lacks. It shows that AI is actually pretty good at finding tidbits in the far corners of the internet and summarizing them in sweeping prose. It can also provide balance to articles that need it.

    Grok can’t write worth a lick, but it indicates how Wikipedia can take advantage of AI at a time when overworked editors are trying to keep the encyclopedia alive.

    Musk introduced Grokipedia as an alternative to Wikipedia, which he said was too liberal. (He called it “Wokepedia.”) Still, he trusted it enough to have Grok copy hundreds of thousands of its articles, which is permitted under Wikipedia’s Creative Commons license, and then add content from elsewhere on the internet. With his usual bluster, Musk said his encyclopedia used a new version of his large language model that was good at “cogent analysis.” He said programmers told it to “cycle through the million most popular articles in Wikipedia and add, modify, and delete.” When Grokipedia launched, Musk said he had major aspirations to overtake Wikipedia, which has 68 million articles in more than 300 languages. He said his encyclopedia would be more complete and more balanced and would make smarter use of images and video. Maybe someday. For now, Grokipedia is a massive collection of overly long articles that are often out of date. Its flaws have been well-documented: Articles are littered with mistakes, peddle conspiracy theories, rely on low-credibility sources, and sometimes skew to the right. And although Grokipedia shows edit requests from readers and whether they are approved, the site is not as transparent as Wikipedia, which reveals details about its editors and every change they make. Last spring, Grokipedia mysteriously stopped updating, according to a report by researchers Renée DiResta and Ronald Robertson. It resumed in late September, still a hot mess, but with a more colorful homepage that always seems to feature its article about Musk. Grokipedia has two articles about me: the conflated baseball player one and “Bill Adair (journalist),” the real one, which is incredibly boring, even to me. Both borrow heavily from Wikipedia’s articles about us and enrich them with details found on assorted websites. Wikipedia’s article about me is nicely concise — just 700 words. It is written in the encyclopedia’s signature dry style and doesn’t contain any errors. The article recounts my career, some of the major news events I’ve covered, the two books I’ve written, and the awards I’ve won. But it highlights trivial events from my career, fails to emphasize larger ones, and lacks any criticism of my work. (I have not tried to improve the article because Wikipedia’s conflict of interest policy prohibits people from editing their own bios.) By contrast, Grokipedia’s “Bill Adair (journalist)” is painfully long — 5,600 words. Its greatest value would be to help someone suffering from a sleep disorder. Like a college student trying to meet a word count, Grok stuffed the article with needless details and redundant descriptions. The article tells you about my work with PolitiFact and then tells you again and again. It explains the site’s rating scale eight times and mentions my academic title four times. Despite labels that say “fact-checked by Grok,” both articles had lots of errors. I spotted 32 in the journalist one and so many in the baseball mashup that I couldn’t count them all. Mistakes are not surprising in AI writing, but I discovered interesting patterns that reveal the weaknesses of large language models. In the article about the real me, only seven of the errors were hallucinations in which Grok seemed to create a detail out of thin air. No, I did not win an award from Manhattan College, and no, PolitiFact did not begin by fact-checking the Tampa mayor’s race. Five other errors showed Grok was a lazy researcher that did not look broadly enough to check a claim. Grok said I am the director of Duke’s journalism program, but I left that job five years ago. The sources cited in the article don’t explain Grok’s mistake, so it seems likely it remembered an old announcement and failed to see a newer one that named my successor. The most prevalent errors were in a broad category I’d all cluelessness. These mistakes showed Grok didn’t fully understand what it read, like someone who skimmed an article too rapidly. My favorite in this category was when I got credit for a big scoop in 2000 that George W. Bush had a DUI conviction, which the Grokipedia article said had an impact on “late-election discourse.” I wish! Yes, I was among the many journalists who covered that story, but I had no scoop. Together, the errors reveal that Grok is a knucklehead. It doesn’t know what’s important and what’s not. It is simply mashing together details from many web articles about me. Grok only knows what it found on the internet and it lacks experience and perspective to sort out what’s important. The writing is dreadful. The articles read as if Grok was trained on too many online resumes and corporate memos. Grok uses words and phrases like “commenced” and “transitioned” and “multidisciplinary practicum” and “hypotheses on fact-check efficacy.” A typical sentence: “Adair’s approach in this position reflected a commitment to undiluted sourcing and causal analysis of policy impacts, influencing subsequent innovations in political journalism.” Take a close look at that sentence and you’ll see it’s just a mush of buzzwords. I don’t know what “undiluted sourcing” is and have never used the phrase, nor would I refer to “causal analysis”…of anything. Grok is trying to impress us with an MBA vocabulary but is really just an epic bullshitter. Bernadette Meehan, CEO of the Wikimedia Foundation, which provides money and technical infrastructure for the encyclopedia, has called AI “an existential threat” to Wikipedia. The 25-year-old encyclopedia has long been a source and beneficiary of Google searches. Wikipedia provides the answers and in turn benefits from readers clicking through to read articles. But when people make a query to a chatbot, they often get the answer they need in an AI summary and don’t click through to read the encyclopedia article. That threatens donations because fewer readers see Wikipedia’s fundraising pitches. Wikipedia has banned content generated by LLMs, but that hasn’t stopped many contributors — some well-intentioned, some not — from dumping an avalanche of AI-written content on the site. That has put a huge burden on the site’s “New pages patrol,” the editors who approve articles, because they must weed out the lousy content. (Wikipedia has a helpful guide of LLMs’ favorite words and phrases, such as “tapestry” and “meticulously” and sentences that start with “additionally.”) Still, terrible as it is, Grokipedia offers lessons in how AI can help Wikipedia. Grok’s voracious internet searches sometimes find things that human editors don’t. The long article about me includes a substantive discussion of my research about lying in politics and my work with fact-checkers around the world, neither of which are in the Wikipedia version. Grokipedia also provides some welcome balance. When it offers context, Grokipedia can be a little heavy with hype (“His work has been lauded for innovating transparency in media…”) But it also included a “Criticisms and Controversies” section that details complaints that PolitiFact is biased against Republicans. That section has a healthy back and forth about the critiques and my response. That kind of balance could be helpful for Wikipedia, which has taken heat from Musk and others for being too lefty. Musk’s encyclopedia also has a playful spirit that Wikipedia could learn from. Grokipedia’s homepage features random samples of recent edits that provide a glimpse at how the site is being improved. Another Grokipedia feature reads articles aloud in an AI voice you select: Eve, who sounds like a BBC anchor; Ara, a serious woman with crisp diction; Leo, who might have been a professor at Oxford; and Sal, whose name suggests a sports bar but whose voice is NPR. My big takeaway from Grok is the importance of human judgment in curating knowledge. Grok is a bot trying to behave like a human editor. Its many mistakes and lousy writing show that AI is not ready to replace Wikipedia’s talented volunteers. Still, Grok shows that AI can be a tool that helps them research and write better articles. After seeing an AI encyclopedia up close through my experiences with Grok, I come away with hope. Yes, AI can be a sloppy researcher and an awful writer. But Grok’s performance, shaky as it was, highlighted AI’s readiness for higher-level responsibilities. Bill Adair, the Knight Professor of the Practice of Journalism and Public Policy at Duke University, is writing a book about how Wikipedia editors are adapting to the age of AI.

Grok uses words and phrases like “commenced” and “transitioned” and “multidisciplinary practicum” and “hypotheses on fact-check efficacy.” A typical sentence: “Adair’s approach in this position reflected a commitment to undiluted sourcing and causal analysis of policy impacts, influencing subsequent innovations in political journalism.”.

    Industry observers note that take a close look at that sentence and you’ll see it’s just a mush of buzzwords. I don’t know what “undiluted sourcing” is and have never used the phrase, nor would I refer to “causal analysis”…of anything. Grok is trying to impress us with an MBA vocabulary but is really just an epic bullshitter.

    Bernadette Meehan, CEO of the Wikimedia Foundation, which provides money and technical infrastructure for the encyclopedia, has called AI “an existential threat” to Wikipedia. The 25-year-old encyclopedia has long been a source and beneficiary of Google searches. Wikipedia provides the answers and in turn benefits from readers clicking through to read articles. But when people make a query to a chatbot, they often get the answer they need in an AI summary and don’t click through to read the encyclopedia article. That threatens donations because fewer readers see Wikipedia’s fundraising pitches. Wikipedia has banned content generated by LLMs, but that hasn’t stopped many contributors — some well-intentioned, some not — from dumping an avalanche of AI-written content on the site. That has put a huge burden on the site’s “Newly introduced pages patrol,” the editors who approve articles, because they must weed out the lousy content. (Wikipedia has a helpful guide of LLMs’ favorite words and phrases, such as “tapestry” and “meticulously” and sentences that start with “additionally.”) Still, terrible as it is, Grokipedia offers lessons in how AI can help Wikipedia. Grok’s voracious internet searches sometimes find things that human editors don’t. The long article about me includes a substantive discussion of my research about lying in politics and my work with fact-checkers around the world, neither of which are in the Wikipedia version. Grokipedia also provides some welcome balance. When it offers context, Grokipedia can be a little heavy with hype (“His work has been lauded for innovating transparency in media…”) But it also included a “Criticisms and Controversies” section that details complaints that PolitiFact is biased against Republicans. That section has a healthy back and forth about the critiques and my response. That kind of balance could be helpful for Wikipedia, which has taken heat from Musk and others for being too lefty. Musk’s encyclopedia also has a playful spirit that Wikipedia could learn from. Grokipedia’s homepage features random samples of recent edits that provide a glimpse at how the site is being improved. Another Grokipedia feature reads articles aloud in an AI voice you select: Eve, who sounds like a BBC anchor; Ara, a serious woman with crisp diction; Leo, who might have been a professor at Oxford; and Sal, whose name suggests a sports bar but whose voice is NPR. My significant takeaway from Grok is the importance of human judgment in curating knowledge. Grok is a bot trying to behave like a human editor. Its many mistakes and lousy writing show that AI is not ready to replace Wikipedia’s talented volunteers. Still, Grok shows that AI can be a tool that helps them research and write better articles. After seeing an AI encyclopedia up close through my experiences with Grok, I come away with hope. Yes, AI can be a sloppy researcher and an awful writer. But Grok’s performance, shaky as it was, highlighted AI’s readiness for higher-level responsibilities. Bill Adair, the Knight Professor of the Practice of Journalism and Public Policy at Duke University, is writing a book about how Wikipedia editors are adapting to the age of AI.

    #55258. Latest Update: A Trusted Optimizely Script Carried Malware To 178 Organizations via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1014 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Searchenginejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: A Trusted Optimizely Script Carried Malware To 178 Organizations via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1014 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that websites running Optimizely Web Experimentation served malicious JavaScript to visitors on Nov.
    • Scott Helme, founder of Report URI, a company that sells tools for monitoring the scripts that run on websites, reported finding the code in snippets belonging to 178 organizations, including Zoom, the BBC, CNN, Salesforce and GitLab.
    • Optimizely’s status page notes an unauthorized party “exploited a vulnerability in Experimentation” to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that websites running Optimizely Web Experimentation served malicious JavaScript to visitors on Nov. 16 after an attacker added it to their projects inside Optimizely. The code swapped crypto wallet addresses, looked for payment cards typed into sites’ own forms, and loaded exploit kits aimed at iPhones and iPads running older versions of iOS.

    Scott Helme, founder of Report URI, a company that sells tools for monitoring the scripts that run on websites, reported finding the code in snippets belonging to 178 organizations, including Zoom, the BBC, CNN, Salesforce and GitLab.

    Optimizely’s status page notes an unauthorized party “exploited a vulnerability in Experimentation” to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects. In a statement to BleepingComputer, the manufacturer noted the vulnerability was “in the Experimentation account signup flow” and that it has notified all affected customers. Teams running Optimizely Web have checks to make inside their own accounts, starting with every project’s custom code and everyone who can edit it, according to Helme.

    Sources indicate that the way Optimizely Web works is by having each client load a JavaScript snippet hosted on Optimizely’s Content Delivery Network (CDN). In addition to the client-specific experiment data, this snippet can have an optional Project JavaScript section which allows clients to input their own custom JavaScript that will run with every page load.

    Report URI found that the hacker had created malicious code within the Project JavaScript section but left everything else about the script intact; thus, even though the malicious code was present, the script still came from cdn.optimizely.com, a domain that every affected website already trusted. Affected were also scripts that clients served from their own domains, as well as those for optimizely.com and login.optimizely.com.

    Optimizely’s statement to BleepingComputer says the organization has “blocked access to the vulnerable path and deployed a fix” and has “ended active sessions, revoked tokens, and reset access for affected user accounts.”.

    In a recent development, helme found that the inserted code would load a second script which would replace cryptocurrency wallet addresses with the attacker’s. Starting at 1:43 p.m. UTC, it would watch the website’s own form fields for credit card information, expiration date and CVV, and attempt to submit this information to the attacker after receiving all three. Credit card information entered via hosted payment iframes (such as Stripe and Adyen) was outside the script’s reach.

    Helme’s team reviewed a total of 1,611 Optimizely snippet files, most of which came from Report URI’s own crawl data; 188 contained malicious code. Helme believes the actual number is likely greater than 188. Report URI first saw the code in a snippet on Nov. 16 at 4:21 a.m. UTC, and all of the infected files were clean as of 11:11 p.m. UTC the same day.

    Recent findings suggest that the Content Security Policy (CSP), as a header, tells the browser the scripts that a website can use (the script-src section) and to which locations it may transmit data (the connect-src section). Report URI then compared those policies for the affected organizations’ sites against those required by the malicious code. Out of the total of 159 organizations that were reviewed, 68 had no Content Security Policy at all and 50 did have a Content Security Policy that permitted both the malicious code and transmission of sensitive user information.

    Seventeen organizations permitted the malicious code to execute, but prevented it from transmitting the user’s information due to restrictions placed upon their connect-src directives. However, this did not prevent the malicious actor from substituting the intended recipient’s wallet address with the attacker’s. Additionally, 24 of the organizations, or 15%, completely blocked execution of the malicious code, and they differed from the other organizations studied in having a restrictive script-src directive.

    Helme wrote that listing Optimizely’s domain name within an organization’s Content Security Policy does not provide protection because the malicious code originated from that same domain. A common Content Security Policy setting, 'strict-dynamic', permits access to be granted to the malicious code if it is inserted into the content via the Optimizely snippet. Likewise, an 'unsafe-eval' setting allows an inline version of the malicious code to be executed when access to the original version has been denied.

    Industry observers note that optimizely’s Content Security Policy help page lists 'strict-dynamic' in the recommended script-src line. Certain Optimizely features such as audiences with custom JavaScript conditions are unavailable unless 'unsafe-eval' is used, and the page’s full sample Content Security Policy includes 'unsafe-eval'.

    Helme states the Project JavaScript in all of the Optimizely Web customer projects and the custom JavaScript in their experiments should be opened to find 1688360.cc, atob( and any other scripts that were written by someone other than the development team. You also need to review who has write access among your owners, API tokens and integrations and then rotate your credentials.

    The change history page from Optimizely indicates that each project’s History logs every Project JavaScript change and that you can filter the log entries based upon how they were made (via the REST API or via the Web Experimentation interface). There are no steps listed for customers on the status page.

    Optimizely’s documentation example below shows the History navigation item and the Type, Date and Source filters.

    Industry observers note that project JavaScript is run on every page that loads an Optimizely snippet, so this attack was able to hit visitors without changing anything on the affected sites’ own code. The change sat in customers’ Optimizely projects, which put your Optimizely account (which includes who can edit Project JavaScript and what API tokens exist) on the same audit list as your site.

    Optimizely told BleepingComputer it’s continuing to investigate and will publish updates on its status page, which listed the incident as Monitoring on the morning of Nov. 17. Its status page, X post and statement don’t say how many customer projects were affected or how a flaw in the signup flow let the attacker change existing customer projects. Until they do, the checks inside the account are the ones teams can run themselves.

On Friday, Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and Microsoft noted they would support a common robots.txt signal that, per OpenAI, “makes it easier for publishers and website operators to communicate the same preference to multiple participating providers at once.”.

    Anthropic engineer Kevin Kelley proposed the common signal as part of work for the Internet Engineering Task Force, and Anthropic is already supporting it. OpenAI claims it will do so “in the coming months,” and Google and Microsoft say they’ll do so next year.

    Meta VP of communications Andy Stone called the common signal “an crucial step,” writing in a tweet that the company supports “publishers’ ability to express preferences about how their content is used for foundational generative AI training.” Meta is under scrutiny for proposed commercial terms that would allow broad scraping; last week, it agreed to delay implementation of those terms.

    Date: Confirmed, Rating: Meets Expectations, Comments: None via @sejournal, @pedrodias

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2042 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has a name, a start time, and a note that the rollout may take up to two weeks.
    • I’ve watched this for most of 20 years.
    • In a recent development, when Google rolled out what the industry later called Panda, in February 2011, they wrote a post about it.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The routine is familiar by now. Google posts a sentence. It has a name, a start time, and a note that the rollout may take up to two weeks. Within the hour, somebody has published a “what we know so far.” By the evening, there’s a list of winners and losers. Before the week is out, with the rollout still running, there’s a recovery guide in seven steps.

    I’ve watched this for most of 20 years. The only part that has changed is the sentence. It used to be longer.

    In a recent development, when Google rolled out what the industry later called Panda, in February 2011, they wrote a post about it. The post remarked what the change was for: sites that add little, copy from others, or just aren’t very useful. It said how massive it was: 11.8% of queries. You could argue with the result, and plenty did, but there was a stated target to argue with.

    Industry observers note that here is the entry for the November 2026 core revision, which started on Nov. 10. It was released. It applies globally and in all languages. It may take up to two weeks. That’s the lot: three facts, none of them about your site.

    It has been revealed that google has been open about why. In a Q&A on Search updates, it mentioned it changes Search thousands of times a year and announces the ones it considers notable, about 10 a year when it last counted in public. Its core updates documentation adds that smaller core updates go out continually and aren’t declared at all. So a named update is a ranking change that Google decided to put on a calendar. The calendar entry tells you when. It tells you nothing about what changed, or about what happens in between.

    The announcement shrank to a timestamp, and the commentary expanded to fill the space.

    According to recent reports, the date does have a use. Google’s own guidance uses it: wait a week after the rollout finishes, then compare that week with the week before it started. The date draws a line through your data so you know where to look. Visibility trackers do a similar job across the market; they show which sites moved.

    Industry observers note that what neither of them shows is why. Which system changed, and why it moved your site in particular, is known inside Google and nowhere else. A rank tracker and a strong feeling won’t close that gap.

    Recent findings suggest that that hasn’t slowed anyone down. An obscure tool vendor published a winners-and-losers study of the November update within a day or two of the launch. It gave the wrong start date and called it the sixth core update of the year. Google’s dashboard lists three. I’d say the analysis was rushed, but that implies there was something to analyze.

    The closest thing I know to a core patch is the annual performance review.

    According to recent reports, anyone who has had a job knows the meeting. You walk in and get a rating that was settled long before the meeting was booked. It reflects the year you had. It also reflects the people you were measured against, because plenty of companies calibrate ratings across a team; you can do the same work as last year and drop a grade because three colleagues did better. Search works the same way. A page is ranked against every other page that could answer the query, so a site can lose ground without changing anything.

    Recent findings suggest that A core revision is review day. It’s when the rating becomes visible. Nobody sensible leaves that meeting and asks what changed about the meeting.

    Sources indicate that the comparison stops in one place. After a review you get a manager, written feedback and a chance to ask what went wrong. After a core upgrade you get a dashboard entry. That missing conversation is the entire market for update commentary: an industry of people offering to be the manager who explains your rating, none of whom were in the calibration room.

    Sources indicate that the strongest objection to all this is that the losses are real, and it’s correct. Companies do lose a large share of their organic revenue overnight, and people lose jobs over it. The practitioners who spend their time on recoveries are dealing with real businesses in real trouble.

    There’s also evidence that sometimes the reviewer gets it wrong. In October 2024, Google invited a group of independent publishers hit by the September 2023 helpful content update to its campus. According to people who were in the room, they were told their content wasn’t the problem, and that they shouldn’t count on getting their traffic back. That is an awkward fact for anyone, me included, who indicates most affected sites had it coming.

    Look at what it does to the recovery guide, though. If the content wasn’t the concern, “seven steps for improving your content” were never going to work. The publishers with the best case against Google are also the best evidence that nobody outside it could diagnose them.

    Now the less sympathetic group, which in my experience is the bigger one.

    Most of the affected sites I’ve been asked to look at over 20 years had the same history. Somebody decided what they could get away with before finding out what the market already offered. They hadn’t researched what customers needed or looked at how good the existing answers were. They picked keywords with volume, wrote about them, and launched.

    When that didn’t work, they went looking for a shortcut, and social media had plenty. A thread with a promise that was too good to be true, and was. A “hack” from somebody who discovered SEO in the summer and by autumn had a conference slot and a YouTube channel. In office terms, that’s career advice from the colleague who joined in August and already runs a workshop. They copied it without asking why it would work. Some of these tricks do work for a few months, which is the worst outcome available, because the fall then lands inside an patch window and gets blamed on the update.

    Recent findings suggest that then they hired SEO to make it work, as if rankings were a delivery service for businesses that forgot to have a product. I’ve written about the wall that approach runs into; it hasn’t moved.

    In a recent development, this is the employee who did the minimum all year and arrives at the review certain that the rating system has changed, and has brought printouts. In fairness to them, they have a problem that needs solving. “The algorithm changed” is something you can say to a board. “We built a site with nothing to say and then paid someone to get it found” tends not to make the deck.

    Industry observers note that so there’s a buyer for an outside cause, and the update coverage supplies one. It comes with a diagnosis nobody outside Google could have made and a retainer that renews before the next update can contradict it. The seller gets a client, and the client gets a story. The site stays exactly as useful as it was, which was the problem.

    This trade feels legitimate to the people in it because of how the industry thinks about quality.

    Take E-E-A-T. Google coined it for its quality raters, and Google’s own documentation indicates it isn’t a specific ranking factor. The industry read that and sold E-E-A-T audits anyway, with scores for a thing Google says it has no score for. Somewhere there is an author bio that was added to fix a business model.

    In a recent development, the traits themselves are older than the initialism. Peter Morville’s user experience honeycomb had “credible,” “useful,” and “valuable” in it in 2004, as facets of a product, with no ranking attached. The industry needed Google to hand it an initialism before it noticed that people prefer things they can trust.

    “JavaScript SEO” has the same shape: it’s progressive enhancement, which web developers were practicing before anyone gave it a conference track. I made that case in Stop Learning SEO and won’t repeat it.

    Industry observers note that if quality is a list of items to tick, then a core update is a latest edition of the list, and you need someone to tell you what’s on it. There is never a shortage of volunteers. Back in the office, that’s working to the KPIs. The person who works to the KPIs has to know the moment they change. The person who is good at the job mostly finds out on review day that they still are.

    So people who hold quality as a checklist need each enhancement explained; the announcement explains nothing, and so somebody makes one up.

    It has been revealed that the first question a business could ask after an enhancement is “What did this update change for my site?” Answering it would take the list of systems that changed, how much each one counts, and what every competing page did in the same fortnight. Nobody outside Google has those. You can still pay for an answer. It’ll arrive as a confident PDF with a traffic-light table, and it will tell you to improve content quality, show more expertise, and prune the thin pages.

    Now read the PDF from the revision before. It says the same thing. So will the one after the next update, because the advice was never derived from the update. If the remedy is the same whatever changed, the change taught nobody anything.

    Industry observers note that the second question is “what do the people I want as customers need that they can’t already get?” It’s a worse question to be asked. It has no villain and no deadline; it can’t be handed to a thread, and the answer may be that the business has nothing to add yet. It’s also slower and more expensive to answer than a PDF. But it can be answered by people you can find and talk to, and it could have been answered before the site released.

    The fair objection to the second question is Google. Google is in the business of taking in what other people know and serving it back as its own answer, and AI Overviews and AI Mode have made that the main event. The part of the web where people found you through a search result is being eaten, and Google is the one holding the fork. I’ve covered what that did to publishers’ traffic. So why polish anything for a channel that’s shrinking?

    Because the second question was never about the channel. A site is a product, and what people need from it doesn’t change when fewer of them arrive through Google. What does change is how much of what you know you should hand over for free. I’ve argued that publishing everything is a terrible business strategy, and I still think so. Holding back the method is sensible. Shipping a site that’s a bare outline of what you’re supposed to be good at is a different decision, and it fails the customer long before it fails a ranking system.

    Recent findings suggest that the line between those two is thin, and it’s meant to be. It sits in a different place for every business, and no revision, checklist, or thread will tell you where yours is. A search engine certainly won’t; it looks after its own interests, as it always has. The only people who know how much is enough are the ones you’re trying to sell to, which is one more reason to go and ask them.

    In the office, it’s the gap between “what did the calibration committee change this year?” and “what did I do this year?” Only one of those is yours to find out, and it’s the one that doesn’t come with somebody else to blame.

    It has been revealed that google will post another sentence soon enough. The recovery guide for it already exists. It’s the one from last time.

    “People are sick and tired of doomer content, and they also don’t like ‘climate stories.’”.

    Mongabay’s most successful videos are about weird animals.

    Recent findings suggest that but not every video from the environmental newsroom can be about strange — or strangely cute — animals. Some have to be about shrimp farm pollution. Or a deforestation crisis brought on by cacao farming in Liberia. That’s where the challenge comes in, Mongabay video managing editor Lucia Torres has found. Turning that kind of journalism into something people stop scrolling for isn’t easy.

    “Generally mass audiences are less interested in environmental content on YouTube [and] Instagram,” Torres mentioned. “We have to compete with recipes, music videos, etc.”.

    Recent findings suggest that mongabay publishes around 150 to 200 videos a year with a team of four full-time and one half-time producers. These include short vertical videos on YouTube Shorts and Instagram; evergreen explainers around “complex enviro-problems”; twice-monthly features; and lengthy investigations or short documentaries.

    Industry observers note that to reach latest audiences with its environmental journalism, Mongabay started experimenting with behind-the-scenes reels in late 2024. At the time, Mongabay’s Instagram reels averaged 2,000 to 3,000 views. Torres mentioned she was inspired by behind-the-scenes videos from National Geographic, The New York Times, ProPublica, and contributing creator Izzy Sasada. An early behind-the-scenes video — on pollution from those shrimp farms — drew about 14,000 views. Additional videos from California and Indonesia each got about 6,000 views. Mongabay started to dive deeper with videos that featured sources and reporters filming from the field.

    A post shared by Mongabay | mongabay.com (@mongabay).

    According to recent reports, from the initial tests, it became clear to Torres that the best-performing videos were ones with behind-the-scenes footage from investigations or collaborations. Putting reporters on camera — in the field or at their desks — worked.

    Recent findings suggest that “The content [on platforms like Instagram] is dominated now by individual content creators,” said Torres, who is right now a Knight Science Journalism Fellow at MIT. She said Mongabay is “still figuring out how we can create personalities or creators within the organization that represent what Mongabay does — that are good journalists but also good at talking in front of the camera.”.

    A post shared by Mongabay | mongabay.com (@mongabay).

    Sources indicate that another successful example came with Mongabay’s investigation into vanishing forests in Liberia. The piece ran as a long-form article, a lengthy YouTube video, and a behind-the-scenes short.

    A post shared by Mongabay | mongabay.com (@mongabay).

    According to recent reports, mongabay now intends its multimedia packages for major investigative stories from the beginning. “They require cross-team, high-level collaborations,” Torres said. “You really have to think about all the elements you are going to use before starting production so when you’re in the field you get everything you need.”.

    Not everything has panned out. Last year, Mongabay tried a data visualization series on climate data. It didn’t work. The lessons for the newsroom went beyond video.

    “People are sick and tired of doomer content, and they also don’t like ‘climate stories,’” Torres said. “The simple mention of ‘climate’ scares them away.”.

    CEO and founder Rhett Butler has seen the same thing across Mongabay’s journalism.

    In a recent development, “We’re seeing strong evidence that doomer stories are resonating less with our audiences,” he mentioned. “Climate stories — especially those focused on disasters or the climate emergency — tend to garner less interest than other topics.” The ones that do well, he added, have “an ecosystem or wildlife angle, give readers a sense of agency, or present a solution.”.

    Mongabay has responded by introducing more projects and series focused on solutions journalism, like Indigenous-led conservation, agroecology, and conservation technology.

    Recent findings suggest that RELATED ARTICLEAudience editors offer advice for “dispiriting” times in social and searchSarah ScireJanuary 16, 2025“We’ve also been sharing data with the newsroom about which kinds of framing are reaching more people right now, so writers and editors can consider whether they might want to incorporate how people are responding to problems into their stories,” Butler mentioned. “But we aren’t overly prescriptive, so ultimately it’s up to editors and writers how they use this information.”.

    Looking at the 3,422 articles published between June 1, 2025 and August 31, 2026, Butler found that the median story featuring hope or a solution got 41% more traffic than articles that only described the crisis or threat. (Articles classified as being about an “action confronting a threat” got 43% more.).

    Today, 71% of the 100 most-read stories on Mongabay’s English-language site can be classified as “hope / solution / agency” or “action confronting a threat,” Butler mentioned. Only 21% were “doom only.”.

    Recent findings suggest that the video team has done something similar. The environmental newsroom’s short series Stranger Creatures leads with “the wonder of wild creatures first,” Torres noted. The conservation or endangered species angle follows.

    “We’ve stopped framing stories as a climate problem, and started framing stories from a solutions-oriented, action-driven perspective, community-first, or fun-stuff first,” Torres stated. “Climate is implicit now in the stories.”.

    It has been revealed that what video won’t be, at least for now, is a revenue generator. Almost all of Mongabay’s revenue comes from contributions and grants, according to its annual report. (Events, licensing, and advertising “are insignificant at this point,” Butler stated.).

    Sources indicate that “I’m not bullish on video becoming a material source of revenue for Mongabay, given how the space has evolved and our position in it,” Butler mentioned. “Ten years ago I was a lot more optimistic on that front.”.

    Industry observers note that part of the problem, he remarked, is incentives. “Building a video strategy around advertising creates an incentive to prioritize views, which may not align with our broader organizational emphasis on impact,” Butler said. “The stories that attract the largest audiences aren’t necessarily those most likely to inform decisions or prompt action.”.

    #55250. Google Ads Surcharges Rise To 3% In France And Italy – Local US Advertisers Can Be Billed Too via @sejournal, @gregjarboe

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1343 w)

    AI & Tech 📈 Bullish 🌐 Searchenginejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    Google Ads Surcharges Rise To 3% In France And Italy – Local US Advertisers Can Be Billed Too via @sejournal, @gregjarboe

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1343 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • If you manage a Google Ads account, you probably got an email last week saying that ads served in France and Italy will carry a 3% Regulatory Operating Cost starting Jan.
    • Recent findings suggest that I found this out the practical way.
    • According to recent reports, I scanned them and moved on.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    If you manage a Google Ads account, you probably got an email last week saying that ads served in France and Italy will carry a 3% Regulatory Operating Cost starting Jan. 1, 2027. You may have deleted it because you don’t advertise in Europe. Don’t assume you’re off the hook. Google bills these surcharges based on where your ads are actually served, and its default location setting can serve your ads to people who have never set foot in your target area.

    Recent findings suggest that I found this out the practical way. I do some pro bono consulting for a retailer on the Upper East Side of Manhattan, and I have access to his Google Ads account. His campaigns are built to reach shoppers within a few miles of his store. On the morning of Nov. 11, his account received two notices from Google Payments, one headed “Surcharge Updates for Ads Served in Italy” and the other “Surcharge Updates for Ads Served in France.”.

    According to recent reports, I scanned them and moved on. Then I went back, because I suspected plenty of Search Engine Journal readers were asking the same question I was. Why is a neighborhood retailer in Upcoming York getting billing notices about two countries he isn’t targeting?

    The short answer is that the emails are a warning, not a bill. Whether they become a bill depends on settings most local advertisers have never opened.

    According to recent reports, google calls these charges jurisdiction-specific surcharges. Some are labeled Digital Services Tax (DST) fees and some are labeled Regulatory Operating Costs, but they work the same way. They are added to your invoice on top of your ad spend, and on top of any account budget you set.

    In a recent development, here is how the rates for Google Ads stand on Google’s help page, before and after Jan. 1, 2027.

    Two former entries are off the list. Google claims ads served in India stopped carrying a 2% charge on Sept. 1, 2024, and ads served in Canada no longer carry the 2.5% DST fee.

    The same increases apply to Display & Video 360, and Google’s help page notes YouTube placements bought on a reservation basis carry the surcharges too.

    In Italy, the jump is half a point. In France, it is a full point, which means the fee itself rises by 50%. Turkey moves the other way.

    See also: Ask A PPC: How Will The Tariffs Impact My PPC Campaigns?

    Google’s help page states the rule plainly. The charge applies every time an ad is served in one of these jurisdictions, “regardless of where your actual business is located.” The surcharge is calculated on the impressions or clicks served in each country, so an account that serves nothing in France pays nothing in France.

    That would seem to settle it for my client. But a few paragraphs further down, Google adds a warning that you might show ads to customers in a country you never targeted “because your business is in a location of interest for them.” Google also notes it is the advertiser’s responsibility to make sure campaign target settings are correct, and that it will not refund surcharges triggered by legitimate clicks and impressions served according to those settings.

    In plain English, if your settings let a shopper in Milan see your ad, you pay the Italy surcharge on that impression, and you don’t get it back.

    See also: 13 Google Ads Settings To Check When Running International PPC Campaigns.

    Google’s advanced location options give you two choices for who counts as being in your target area. “Presence or interest” reaches people who are in, regularly in, or who’ve shown interest in your targeted locations. “Presence” reaches only people who are in or regularly in them.

    It has been revealed that presence or interest is the default, and Google labels it as recommended. Google supports that recommendation with its own data, saying advertisers in travel, real estate, and education who switched to it saw 5% more conversions on Search campaigns. That is Google’s claim from Google’s internal data, and it covers three verticals, not retail.

    For a store on Madison Avenue, “interest” is where Europe gets in. Someone in Paris searching for shops on the Upper East Side has shown interest in Fresh York. Under the default, your ad can serve to that person, and the impression lands in France.

    According to recent reports, the controls have also been widening. Demand Gen campaigns picked up the same Presence or interest versus Presence choice in late 2025, and AI Max for Search has added options for reaching people based on locations of interest. More automation in where ads go means more chances to serve impressions in places you didn’t pick.

    Giovanni Perilli, a funnel marketing consultant who writes about European ad costs, published a breakdown the same day the emails went out. The France email he received did not mention Italy at all. In his words, the email “leaves out the change that matters most to anyone advertising in Italy.”.

    Recent findings suggest that that matches my own experience, with a twist. My client’s account got two separate emails, one per country. Advertisers who received only one should check the help page rather than assume nothing else changed.

    Sources indicate that perilli also turns the surcharge into numbers a PPC manager can use. Because the fee is added on top of what you spend, he multiplies a cost-per-acquisition by 1.03 and divides a return on ad spend by 1.03. A €40 CPA effectively becomes €41.20. A ROAS of four becomes about 3.88. If your break-even ROAS is 2.5, your real target in France and Italy is now about 2.58.

    Recent findings suggest that those are small numbers. On thin retail margins in the first quarter, they are not nothing.

    See also: Google States Changing tCPA & Budgets Won’t Reset Learning – 6 BFCM Takeaways.

    According to recent reports, google’s help page notes the France and Italy charges cover part of the cost of complying with digital services tax legislation in those countries. The tax news over the past year lines up with that.

    Recent findings suggest that french lawmakers voted in October 2025 to double France’s digital services tax from 3% to 6% for the largest platforms, but the budget bill carrying it was rejected a month later, and the rate remains 3%. Italy’s DST has applied at a 3% rate since 2020, and its 2025 budget law removed the domestic revenue threshold that had kept some companies out of scope. Turkey went the other direction, cutting its DST from 7.5% to 5% this year and to 2.5% on Jan. 1, 2027. Google’s Turkey surcharge falls to 2.25% on the same date.

    Recent findings suggest that google also has company now. Meta began charging its own location fees on July 1, 2026, at 3% in France, Italy, and Spain, as Bloomberg reported. From January, Google and Meta charge the same 3% in all three countries.

    Here’s my read. Digital services taxes were sold to voters as a way to make big tech pay. The platforms are now itemizing those taxes on advertisers’ invoices, and some of those advertisers are small businesses on another continent. Whatever you think of the policy, the bill has moved down the chain, and PPC managers are the ones who have to explain it to clients.

    Here are four steps I’m taking in my client’s account, and I’d suggest you take them in yours.

    I almost ignored these notices, and I’ve been reading Google Ads billing emails since 2003. My advice is to treat them as an audit prompt, not as spam. The surcharge itself is modest. The real story is how many local accounts may be serving ads in Europe without anyone deciding they should.

    My client’s ads are meant for the Upper East Side, not Paris or Milan. I’d rather confirm that in a report before Jan. 1 than discover it on a February invoice.

    All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    Sources indicate that we will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    College football already has an Orange Bowl, a Peach Bowl, and a Citrus Bowl, so on its face, there’s nothing outlandish about the concept of an Onion Bowl.

    But this matchup wouldn’t be titled to evoke some locale’s bumper crop, à la the Famous Idaho Potato Bowl. Instead it would market “America’s Finest News Source,” The Onion. (Today’s top headlines: Bain Capital Acquires Tibetan Buddhism For $35 Million; Abdul El-Sayed Makes History As First Physically Healthy Senator; Chuck Schumer Delivers Victory Speech To Previously Enthusiastic Crowd.).

    On Thursday morning, Onion CEO (and past Nieman Lab contributor) Ben Collins announced the publication’s quest to buy naming rights for a bowl game, both on Bluesky and on the podcast Pablo Torre Finds Out:.

    The Onion is extremely close to buying an honest-to-goodness, Division 1 college football bowl series bowl game.

    Yes, we're trying to pull off The Onion Bowl.

    A few days before Christmas, potentially in Texas.

    Industry observers note that but we've already been banned once. And we need your help.

    — Ben Collins (@bencollins.bsky.social) November 5, 2026 at 8:32 AM.

    It has been revealed that for those unfamiliar, American college football seasons traditionally end with a few dozen bowl games, scattered around the country (and occasionally outside it). Nearly all of these games sell naming rights to one company or another, leading to fun combinations like the Poulan Weed Eater Independence Bowl, the TaxSlayer.com Gator Bowl, and the Union Home Mortgage Gasparilla Bowl. Collins wants to buy the rights to one of the several bowl games that are still without a sponsor for their games next month.

    This absurdity — though no more absurd, I suppose, than the Snoop Dogg Arizona Bowl presented by Gin & Juice by Dre and Snoop — serves as the excellent marketing hook to get people to buy a $75/year print subscription, a major driver of The Onion’s revenue.

    Sources indicate that indeed, only three U.S. newspapers have a daily print circulation over 100,000 — The Wall Street Journal, The New York Times, and the New York Post; The Washington Post and USA Today have already fallen below that line. (At the risk of being pedantic, though, The Onion appears in print monthly, not daily, making it a bit of an apples-to-oranges comparison. Also, The Onion gets to make up its stories.).

    Collins says The Onion actually got quite close to buying the naming rights to the Upcoming Orleans Bowl, which last year lost its longtime naming sponsor, the…Ohio-based freight-shipping concern R+L Carriers? The Onion was prepared to pay “mid six figures.” But the organization that runs the bowl, the Greater New Orleans Sports Foundation, apparently said no deep into the process, a move Collins attributed to “politics.” (I reached out to the Greater New Orleans Sports Foundation for comment — a sentence I did not expect to type today — but did not hear back.).

    So the guys who sell bowl games ushered us to what we thought was a pretty good fit: The Fresh Orleans Bowl.

    Sources indicate that I love Fresh Orleans. I love having crawfish out of the back of a pickup truck at 3 a.m. The game would've been in the Superdome two days before Christmas. Good fit! Right? Right???

    — Ben Collins (@bencollins.bsky.social) November 5, 2026 at 8:38 AM.

    Then the folks who run the New Orleans Bowl, a commission that includes representatives of the city and state of Louisiana, found out our prepares to highlight our mascot:.

    — Ben Collins (@bencollins.bsky.social) November 5, 2026 at 8:39 AM.

    Despite getting all approvals from ESPN and scraping together the cash, right as we were about to sign the paper work to put The Onion Sports Bowl in Latest Orleans, their state-funded commission called us and remarked it straight up: "No.".

    Recent findings suggest that we asked why. They noted politics. And the Sickos Guy.

    — Ben Collins (@bencollins.bsky.social) November 5, 2026 at 8:40 AM.

    While the Fresh Orleans Bowl might be out, several right now-brand-free possibilities remain, including the Frisco Bowl in newly blue Texas — the state also home to The Onion’s rival to the death, Alex Jones.
