    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Searchenginejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    Rank Math SEO WordPress Plugin Hit By 16 Vulnerabilities In 2026 via @sejournal, @martinibuster

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (715 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sixteen vulnerabilities have been discovered in the popular Rank Math SEO plugin in 2026, setting a newly introduced record for vulnerabilities discovered, more than any other SEO plugin.
    • Industry observers note that rank Math’s 2026 vulnerabilities included potential pathways to website takeover, exposure of protected information, and unauthorized changes to WordPress content and data.
    • Although AI is making vulnerability disclosures more common, other SEO plugins like Yoast SEO did not have anywhere near that many vulnerability discoveries.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sixteen vulnerabilities have been discovered in the popular Rank Math SEO plugin in 2026, setting a newly introduced record for vulnerabilities discovered, more than any other SEO plugin.

    Industry observers note that rank Math’s 2026 vulnerabilities included potential pathways to website takeover, exposure of protected information, and unauthorized changes to WordPress content and data. All of these things could also have a negative impact on SEO.

    Although AI is making vulnerability disclosures more common, other SEO plugins like Yoast SEO did not have anywhere near that many vulnerability discoveries. The free version of Yoast SEO was reported by Wordfence to have a total of four vulnerabilities in 2026 and only two were discovered in the paid version.

    The sixteen vulnerabilities share certain issues in common but arguably the worst of them are:.

    Remote Code Execution (CVSS rated 8.8) Two vulnerabilities with a CVSS severity score of 8.8 were discovered that could enable attackers with Contributor or Author-level access to execute arbitrary code on the server, potentially leading to complete website compromise.

    It has been revealed that arbitrary File Upload (7.2) One of the vulnerabilities could potentially lead to a website takeover through malicious file uploads, although this vulnerability required Administrator privileges. CVE-2026-104752: Arbitrary File Upload, requiring Administrator-level access or higher. Disclosed October 8, 2026. CVSS 7.2 (High).

    Stored Cross-Site Scripting (7.2) An unauthenticated attacker could potentially execute malicious JavaScript in an Administrator’s browser. Depending on the circumstances, that could lead to privileged actions or account compromise. CVE-2026-66702: Stored Cross-Site Scripting, requiring no authentication. Disclosed July 31, 2026. CVSS 7.2 (High).

    It has been revealed that stored Cross-Site Scripting (7.2) An unauthenticated attacker could potentially execute malicious JavaScript in an Administrator’s browser. Depending on the circumstances, this could enable an attacker to make unauthorized changes to the website or take control of an Administrator’s account. CVE-2026-66702: Stored Cross-Site Scripting, requiring no authentication. Disclosed July 31, 2026. CVSS 7.2 (High).

    Industry observers note that these vulnerabilities could allow attackers to access protected content or sensitive website information without the necessary permissions. Unlike vulnerabilities that enable unauthorized changes, these primarily concern exposing information that should remain restricted, although SQL injection could also allow attackers to manipulate website data.

    Recent findings suggest that these vulnerabilities could enable attackers to make unauthorized changes to a WordPress website, including modifying content-related data, changing homepage settings, and deleting SEO information. Some could be exploited without logging in, while others required an account but allowed actions beyond that user level’s permissions.

    In a recent development, most vulnerabilities were discovered within a relatively short period. Eleven of the 16 vulnerabilities were discovered between August 27 and October 14, 2026. Of those vulnerabilities, late August and early September saw a concentrated cluster of vulnerability discoveries. Eight were reported between August 27 and September 3, within just eight days.

    Sources indicate that the disclosures continued into October. Five vulnerabilities were reported in October, including three disclosed on October 8 and the latest on October 27.

    It has been revealed that as previously stated, Rank Math’s direct competitor, Yoast SEO, only experienced four vulnerabilities during a year which saw an increase in vulnerability discoveries. The unusually high number of vulnerabilities leads to questions about Rank Math’s coding practices, code review, and quality control.

    The other problem in the sixteen vulnerabilities is that are repeated instances of the same kinds of exploits.

    In a recent development, missing authorization was the most frequently identified vulnerability category. Seven of the 16 entries explicitly mention inadequate permission checks, pointing to recurring problems with enforcing permissions before allowing actions.

    It has been revealed that some security problems could lead to complete website compromise. Two vulnerabilities carried CVSS scores of 8.8 and involved remote code execution, allowing attackers who met the required conditions to potentially execute malicious code on the server.

    Recent findings suggest that overall, the vulnerabilities involved a broad range of security weaknesses. They included unauthorized modifications, information exposure, cross-site scripting, SQL injection, arbitrary file uploads, and remote code execution. The vulnerability discoveries do not point to just one type of coding lapse; they point to a wide range of coding concerns.

    The full list of Rank Math vulnerabilities can be found at Wordfence, with links to a description page for each vulnerability.

    Camunda is the enterprise platform for agentic orchestration, enabling organizations to coordinate AI agents, people, and systems across complex, end-to-end business processes. With built-in governance, auditability, and human oversight, Camunda gives enterprises the control they need to move AI from pilots to production — safely and at scale. Trusted by over 700 organizations worldwide, including 9 of top 10 US banks, Camunda helps enterprises boost operational efficiency, accelerate time-to-value, and deliver better customer experiences.Fully remote and global, we are in the middle of something bigger: transforming into an AI-first organisation, built on our own platform. We use Agentic AI to automate, orchestrate intelligent processes, and elevate human contribution across every team.Named GP Bullhound’s Top 100 Next Unicorn list, 2025 Great Place to Work certified. Visionary in 2025 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Business Orchestration and Automation Technologies. ranked 3rd in Flexa's 2026 Most Flexible Companies, We’re growing fast and looking for top talent to join our team. If you want meaningful work, visible impact and put something genuinely rare on your CV, keep reading.

    According to recent reports, we are hiring a Sr. Manager, Total Rewards to lead the design, delivery, and continuous improvement of Camunda’s global compensation, benefits, and equity programs. This person will partner closely with the People team, Finance, and Legal to make sure our rewards are competitive, equitable, compliant, and easy to understand in every country where we operate. This is a hands-on, strategic role for a rewards leader who wants to build and run programs as a trusted business partner, not just administer them. The right candidate will bring deep technical rewards expertise, strong AI and analytical skills, and a passion for a great employee experience. We also expect this leader to be AI-forward in how we approach compensation strategy and job leveling, not only in how they use AI to get their own work done. That means using AI and data-driven methods to shape pay philosophy, benchmark and model market data, design and calibrate our job architecture and leveling framework, and make faster, more consistent, and more transparent rewards decisions.

    It has been revealed that own the global Total Rewards strategy across compensation, benefits, equity, and recognition, and make sure it helps Camunda attract, retain, and motivate top talent. Set an AI-forward vision for how Camunda designs and runs compensation, and turn it into a practical roadmap.

    Lead the annual compensation cycle, including merit, promotion, and equity planning, in partnership with People Business Partners, Finance, and business leaders.

    Industry observers note that own job architecture, leveling, and grading frameworks, and keep the Job Catalog accurate as the organization grows. Apply AI and data-driven approaches to job leveling, such as consistent role-to-level mapping, calibration, and level-drift detection, with human oversight.

    In a recent development, run market benchmarking and compensation analysis, and turn the findings into clear, data-driven recommendations for leadership. Use AI to speed up and improve benchmarking, pay modeling, and scenario analysis.

    Manage benefits programs and vendor relationships across regions, including EOR providers such as Remote.com, brokers, and equity administration platforms, with a clear view of cost, service levels, and employee value.

    Ensure compliance with pay transparency, pay equity, and local compensation and benefits regulations in every jurisdiction where Camunda operates.

    Partner with Finance on compensation budgeting and equity pool management, and track total rewards spend against a clear baseline.

    Advise People Business Partners and hiring managers on offers, pay decisions, and exceptions, balancing internal equity, market data, budget and capturing and retaining strong AI talent..

    Identify and adopt AI and automation tools that improve rewards analytics, benchmarking, and employee communications, and ensure AI use complies with local laws and regulations.

    Lead, coach, and develop the Total Rewards team, setting clear priorities and growth paths.

    It has been revealed that canada’s proposed federal budget includes some good news for local journalism. The federal government is extending its journalism tax credit by $501 million, expanding eligibility to audio and audiovisual news organizations, and renewing the Local Journalism Initiative, which supports journalism in underserved communities.

    Industry observers note that RELATED ARTICLEIn Canada, a government program to support local news tries to determine who’s most deservingSarah ScireMay 8, 2020Sarah wrote about the Local Journalism Initiative in its early days. A study earlier this year found that reporters paid with LJI funding believed they maintained their roles as watchdogs and wrote balanced stories, though two-thirds of interviewees were concerned about the perception of a conflict of interest. A growing number of journalists say the benefits of government subsidies for journalism outweigh the drawbacks.

    A recent report in The Tyee suggests government support is essential to the survival of local media in Canada. (The Tyee has received support from the Local Journalism Initiative.).

    “It’s either this or death, frankly,” LJI program director and Canadian Association of Journalists president Brent Jolly told The Tyee. “It’s not about local news editors getting their marching orders from the Prime Minister’s Office like some conspiracy theorists want you to think. It’s about infrastructure.”.

    Lisa Sygutek, publisher of the Crowsnest Pass Herald in Alberta, credited the LJI with growing the publication from “a 16-page paper to a 24-page paper.”.

    Read more in The Tyee’s look at Canadian local news here.

    • Enterprises need to think beyond rich results and develop the business context they publish for machines.
    • In 2027, schema markup has to be upgraded in order to maintain visibility in AI SERPs.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    AI is changing how customers discover and evaluate brands.

    Enterprises need to think beyond rich results and develop the business context they publish for machines.

    In 2027, schema markup has to be upgraded in order to maintain visibility in AI SERPs.

    Get a free, personalized AI-Ready Schema Markup Scorecard, Now →.

    The newly introduced job I see for schema markup is to help AI understand your business, not just make individual pages eligible for rich results. That means explicitly describing your products, services, people, and locations, showing how they connect, and keeping those facts and relationships accurate as your business changes.

    It has been revealed that one of the biggest questions I hear from enterprise marketing leaders today is: How do we make sure AI is getting our brand right? It’s a fair question.

    In a recent development, AI is increasingly influencing how customers discover, research, and choose businesses. Unlike traditional search, where customers could visit your website and form their own understanding, AI now brings information together from across the web to create answers on their behalf.

    In a recent development, that information might come from your website, a third-party directory, customer reviews, or an article published years ago. And not all of it is necessarily accurate, complete, or up to date.

    Sources indicate that here’s what I think is crucial for marketers to recognize: You can’t control everything AI says about your business. But you can take greater control of the information you give it, and that starts with your website.

    Your website is one of the most valuable sources of information you own. It’s where you define who you are, what you offer, the expertise you bring to market, and what you want your business to be known for.

    This is why I believe preparing the information you own for AI is one of the most key investments enterprise marketers can make today.

    And if your organization already has schema markup, you’ve already started building that foundation. The opportunity now is to think bigger about what it can do, and make sure your strategy is built for the job schema markup needs to do today and tomorrow, not just the one it did yesterday.

    The good news is that if you’ve already invested in schema markup, you’re not starting from scratch. But not all schema markup is created equal. Before you focus on doing more, ask whether what you already have gives machines a clear, connected understanding of your business.

    The opportunity is to assess the foundation you’ve built, identify where it could be stronger, and build from there.

    Here are three questions I’d encourage enterprise marketing leaders to ask.

    Pro Tip: Use a AI-Ready Schema Markup Scorecard to assess your current foundation and identify opportunities to strengthen how machines understand your business.

    Having schema markup across your website is a great start. But is it capturing the information that actually matters to your business?

    It has been revealed that think about your most crucial products, services, locations, and areas of expertise. Does your markup describe them accurately and in enough detail? Or is it simply meeting the minimum requirements for a search feature? The goal isn’t just more schema markup; it’s more meaningful markup.

    Recent findings suggest that it’s one thing for machines to recognize the individual parts of your business. It’s another for them to understand how everything fits together. Are your people, products, services, and locations consistently identified and connected? Can machines recognize when different pages are talking about the same thing?

    Recent findings suggest that think about a healthcare system. It might have schema markup describing its physicians, hospitals, and medical services. That’s a great start. But does that information clearly communicate which physicians specialize in which treatments? Where they practice? Which services are available at each location? And how all of those things connect back to the healthcare system?

    Move beyond describing individual pages to communicating a connected picture of your business.

    Your business is constantly evolving. Upcoming services, new locations, new expertise. And as your website content changes, your schema markup needs to keep up. Because it’s not enough for your website to tell one story to customers while your structured data tells another to machines.

    As your website evolves, does your schema markup keep pace, reflecting the same accurate information and maintaining the relationships that connect your business?

    According to recent reports, our Wells Fargo case study illustrates why this matters. Wells Fargo encountered an AI Overview that incorrectly identified a branch as permanently closed. By strengthening the structured information on its website, the team helped address that inaccurate answer.

    In a recent development, you can’t control every answer AI generates. But you can take greater control of the accuracy and consistency of the information you’re giving it to work with. And that requires governance to be part of your approach from the beginning.

    It has been revealed that we need to think differently about what we’re asking our schema markup to accomplish. We should question whether we’re giving machines the information and context they need to understand our business as a whole, and recognize our relevance to the topics that matter most.

    In a recent development, but here’s the challenge: Across large enterprise websites, that information is often spread across thousands of pages, managed by different teams, and constantly changing. Even when the information is accurate on individual pages, it doesn’t always tell a clear, connected story about the business.

    And sometimes, we’re contributing to the confusion ourselves. As Schema App’s CTO Mark van Berkel discusses in Forbes, AI doesn’t always need to hallucinate incorrect information. Sometimes, it works with conflicting information businesses have already published.

    If we want AI to understand our business, we need to give it more than individual pieces of information. We need to help it understand how those pieces fit together. And for large enterprises, that’s not a small challenge.

    According to recent reports, think about everything your organization publishes across its website. Your products and services, locations, your people and their expertise, the topics you want to be known for. All of that information helps tell the story of your business. But across thousands of pages, different teams, and constantly changing content, those connections aren’t always clear.

    Industry observers note that what if we started thinking about our website not just as a collection of pages, but as a connected source of truth about our business? That’s the opportunity I see with a Marketing Context Layer.

    A Marketing Context Layer is a governed foundation of information about your business that helps machines understand who you are, what you offer, what you’re known for, and how it all connects. It starts with the information you own and publish on your website.

    Through advanced schema markup, you can make important business facts and relationships explicit, connecting them into a Content Knowledge Graph that can be maintained as your business evolves.

    In a recent development, and this isn’t just a marketing conversation. Forrester has been exploring the importance of context layers in enterprise AI, recognizing the role of connected business knowledge in helping AI systems interpret and use information. I believe there’s an crucial opportunity to apply that same thinking to marketing. If enterprises are investing in governed business context to power AI internally, shouldn’t we also be thinking about the context we’re publishing for AI to understand us externally?

    Industry observers note that this is where schema markup becomes much more than an SEO tactic. It’s the starting point for building a connected, governed foundation of information about your business. One you can keep improving, maintaining, and putting to work as search and AI experiences evolve.

    As our CTO, Mark van Berkel, explores in Forbes, the organizations that want to make meaningful use of AI need to invest in the information foundations that support it.

    Industry observers note that I believe we’re at an exciting turning point for enterprise marketers. We’ve spent years investing in our websites, creating content, and building our presence in search. Now we have an opportunity to make those investments work harder by helping machines understand the business behind the content.

    And as AI continues to evolve, from search and answers to emerging agentic experiences, having clear, connected, and reliable business information will only become more vital.

    Sources indicate that because the goal isn’t just to be found. It’s to be understood. And that starts with taking ownership of the information we control.

    You may already have schema markup. But how well is it communicating the full story of your business?

    📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1649 w)

    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Niemanlab ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: AI is becoming an information gateway. Audiences still don’t want it making their news.

    📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1649 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Niemanlab

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing.
    • Sources indicate that we will never sell your address.
    • We have sent a confirmation link to .
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    Sources indicate that we will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    An average of 24% of respondents across nine countries said they’d seen a label noting that content was made with AI in the last week, and 20% had seen a bullet-point AI news summary.

    In my Nieman Lab prediction this time last year, I wrote that “in 2026, the use of AI as an information gateway will only rise further.”.

    As it turns out, I was right. In newly introduced research that I published with my colleagues Rasmus Kleis Nielsen and Richard Fletcher, one of our many findings is that generative AI systems are becoming ever more significant information intermediaries, both when intentionally used and when incidentally encountered.

    Industry observers note that for our newly introduced report, “Generative AI and News Report 2026: From Standalone Tools to Information Infrastructure,”  we surveyed audiences across nine countries, including the United States, on their use of AI in their everyday lives, what they think its impact will be on different sectors of society, and what they think about its use in news and journalism specifically. I obviously think you should read the whole report, but here are some of the major takeaways.

    The use of standalone conversational AI systems such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini continues to grow rapidly, with 51% of respondents across the six countries where we have past data saying they now use AI weekly (49% in the U.S.). That’s a faster spread, at least in the U.S., than smartphones or the internet saw.

    Many people also encounter AI through “incidental” AI exposure in the AI-infused services and platforms they’re already using. Search engines such as Google and Bing are key drivers: 57% of respondents across countries stated they saw or engaged with AI-generated answers or summaries in the last week. News media, too, drives AI exposure. An average of 24% of respondents across nine countries said they’d seen a label noting that content was made with AI in the last week, and 20% had seen a bullet-point AI news summary.

    In a recent development, despite all the talk about AI agents, we find that, so far, they haven’t broken into the mainstream. The vast majority of respondents across all nine countries (67%) said they had not used an AI agent in the last week. Fourteen percent used one for a real task and 13% tried one just to experiment.

    In a recent development, our data provides solid evidence that a broader transformation of the information environment is afoot. Conversational AI systems have arrived as information intermediaries. Trust is not the main reason people use them. Instead, people see conversational AI systems as friction-reducing machines that get them information more quickly.

    “Getting information” continues to be the most common use case. Thirty-eight percent of respondents across countries (35% in the U.S.) noted they had used generative AI for getting information in the last week, up from 24% in 2025 and 11% in 2024.

    We looked more closely at what people do when they say they use AI for getting information. Across the six countries we’ve surveyed since 2024, we primarily see a mixture of search-equivalent behaviors like “researching a topic” (24%) or “answering factual questions” (18%). People are also increasingly turning to AI for advice (20%).

    In a recent development, using AI directly for news, meanwhile, remains a niche activity, as we demonstrated in the Digital News Report earlier this year. But that use is increasing: 9% of respondents across our six core countries say they use AI for news, up from 6% in 2025 and 3% in 2024.

    Many people don’t hold clear or strong views about whether AI output is trustworthy. But people who do rely on it for information trust it. Across the nine countries, 75% of those who used AI to answer factual questions trusted the answers, as did 76% of those who used it for advice and 72% of those who used it for news. Only small minorities expressed distrust.

    In a recent development, at the same time, trust and trustworthiness do not, at this stage, seem to be central to why people rely on AI systems. Instead, people tend to see these systems as friction-reducing machines. The convenience of getting a faster and easier answer was chosen by 64% as the main reason they use AI, followed by the interactivity afforded by natural language interfaces (56%). Only a minority (21%) said they use AI because they get more reliable information from it than from other sources.

    Industry observers note that as AI systems become widely used, their growing popularity is likely to affect the use of legacy content offerings and digital platforms and services. As my coauthor Rasmus Kleis Nielsen put it on LinkedIn, rapid growth in AI use isn’t just eating into what news sites have to offer. It’s eating into search, too — with people who use AI for information saying they use not just news, but search engines less, too, and by a wider margin. Challenging times may be ahead not just for news publishers, but also for the incumbent digital giants previously seen as unassailable.

    As in previous years, we wanted to know what people think of AI’s use in journalism and news. We find that people’s attitudes here are remarkably entrenched and negative — though they also haven’t worsened significantly.

    People across countries remain uncomfortable with the use of AI in the newsroom, especially with the idea of news being made entirely or primarily with AI. On average across nine countries, just 12% of respondents say they are very or somewhat comfortable with news made entirely by AI. That figure rises to 19% if there is some human oversight. This has hardly changed since 2024, and the gap between human- and AI-made news appears in every country we surveyed.

    This also remains true regardless of whether it is breaking news or reporting. People are even more uncomfortable with AI being used for commentary or opinion — formats where the expectation that a human should share their view is strongest.

    Our findings raise several crucial questions for journalists and publishers navigating the rise of generative AI.

    First, generative AI is becoming an increasingly significant information intermediaries, with a number of possible knock-on effects on news. People are using AI to reduce friction by getting “good enough” outputs for some information needs — and skipping legacy platforms, established publishers, and the time and effort it takes to find the best available information. Discovery, brand attribution, data collection, and monetization all grow more challenging for publishers in this context.

    Second, even though use continues to grow, the public remains skeptical of AI in news. This isn’t just a challenge for newsrooms’ internal adoption. It also highlights that publishers using AI need to communicate to audiences what’s in it for them.

    In a recent development, third, beyond news, our findings speak to wider debates about AI’s societal impact. As in other studies on this topic, we find that uptake of AI is uneven. Weekly use is more common among people in professional occupations than those in entry-level or service occupations. Most people rely on free — usually less advanced — AI models.

    According to recent reports, the differences in how — not just whether — people use AI may become a new dividing line. As AI researcher and OpenAI cofounder Andrej Karpathy recently argued, there is a widening “gap in shared understanding of LLM capability,” with most people not seeing what has left those inside AI firms both excited and worried.

    Expectations of what AI will do differ far more between daily consumers and people who have never used it than between any other groups in our survey. When two groups form very different views of the same technology because they have such different starting points, there will likely be consequences.

    This doesn’t matter just for people’s individual choices around whether and how to make use of AI in their own lives. It also matters where AI is adopted and governed through collective decisions — in public services, for example — that apply to those who do not use it.

    Felix Simon is the research fellow in AI, information, and news at the Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism and a research associate at the Oxford Internet Institute (OII) at the University of Oxford.

    When the Covid-19 pandemic normalized remote work, a second trend caught on: shutting down physical newsrooms.

    A report from Northwestern University’s Local News Initiative, published Tuesday, looks at the cultural losses that news outlets face when their staff stops working together under one roof. Here’s LNI contributor and Columbia College Chicago journalism professor Jackie Spinner:.

    As pandemic-era safeguards that necessitated working from home waned, some have championed the technological advances that allow many journalists to report, edit and publish from basically anywhere with stable Internet access. But the cost savings from a smaller or nonexistent physical presence isn’t the only consideration. Less clear-cut is the impact on the elements of journalism that never appear on budgets, such as the training absorbed from looking over someone’s shoulder or the institutional knowledge gained and passed by working in proximity to others over time.

    During the pandemic, several news outlets downsized their offices — from city high-rises to co-working spaces — due to financial constraints and latest hybrid work schedules.

    On Tuesday, I spent time looking for the local news outlets that have foregone or reduced office space and opted for primarily remote work in recent years. Here are some:.

    #55215. Latest Update: How To Find The Questions Your Customers Ask AI (And Your Keyword Tools Miss)

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1841 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Searchenginejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: How To Find The Questions Your Customers Ask AI (And Your Keyword Tools Miss)

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1841 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In my last article, I made the case that search volume is screening out your best content opportunities.
    • So, this is the practical follow-up.
    • I always start here, because it’s the source most teams overlook, and it’s usually the best one.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In my last article, I made the case that search volume is screening out your best content opportunities. The short version is that the highest-intent questions your buyers ask are increasingly being noted to an AI assistant, and they rarely show up in a keyword tool. Near the end of that piece, I listed a few places to find those questions instead: People Also Ask, forums, your own sales calls and support tickets, and the assistants themselves. That list was only four bullet points, and the most common reply I’ve had since is some version of “OK, but how do I actually do that?”.

    So, this is the practical follow-up. I’ll go through how I collect these questions, how I use Search Console to check which ones are already reaching a site, and how I turn the whole lot into something a content team can work from.

    I always start here, because it’s the source most teams overlook, and it’s usually the best one. Sales calls, discovery calls, support tickets, live chat logs, and the messages people send before booking a demo are all people describing their problem in their own words. That’s very close to how they’d describe it to ChatGPT or Gemini.

    Here’s a real example from a recent discovery call of mine (anonymized, with the details changed enough that you couldn’t identify the business). The prospect was a furniture retailer, and this was roughly how they opened the call:.

    According to recent reports, “We moved to Shopify a couple of years ago and lost a massive chunk of our rankings. Some of it came back, and then we dropped again this year. Is that still the migration, or are our own collection pages competing with each other?”.

    A few minutes later, they asked a second question:.

    Industry observers note that “We sell exactly the same products in France and Germany, but those sites barely get any traffic. Do we need completely separate content for each country?”.

    Recent findings suggest that neither of those would ever appear in a keyword export. The closest you’d get is something like “shopify migration SEO” or “international SEO,” which tells you almost nothing about the actual situation. But if you look at those two questions as a content brief, they’re incredibly specific: a platform, a timeline, two possible causes, and a decision to make.

    This is exactly the kind of question a buyer takes to an assistant, and it’s the kind of question your content should be able to answer.

    If you record your calls (I use Fireflies, but most call recorders produce a transcript you can export), I’d take the last three months of sales and discovery calls and run them through an AI assistant with a prompt like this:.

    “From these call transcripts, list every question the prospect asked or implied. Rewrite each one the way they would phrase it to an AI assistant, and keep their constraints, such as organization size, budget, timeline, platform, and what they’ve already tried. Group similar questions together and note how many calls each group came up in.”.

    The final instruction here is critical. If the same scenario comes up in five separate calls, that’s the closest thing to demand data you’ll get for a question with no search volume, and it’s a lot more persuasive in a meeting than “I think people are asking this.”.

    Recent findings suggest that you want to be careful with a couple of things here. Strip out names, manufacturer details, and anything identifying before transcripts go into a third-party tool, and make sure your call recording consent covers this kind of use. Also, sales calls skew toward people who are already close to buying, so I’d add support tickets and pre-sale inquiries into the mix to capture earlier-stage questions too.

    It has been revealed that your own calls only tell you about people who already found you. Forums help with everyone else.

    Industry observers note that reddit is the obvious one, but Quora, industry Slack and Discord communities, Facebook groups, and review sites such as G2 or Trustpilot can all be just as useful depending on your market. The value usually lies in the opening post, where someone explains their constraints in full, and in the replies, where other people ask the follow-up questions an assistant would also need answered before it could give a decent response.

    Sticking with the migration example, a search like site:reddit.com shopify migration rankings dropped should bring up plenty of threads where store owners describe the same problem in their own words, often with details my prospect didn’t mention, such as redirect concerns or how long they waited before panicking.

    Industry observers note that I copy the most relevant threads into a document and run the same extraction prompt over them. That way, forum questions and sales questions end up in the same format, and you can group them together later.

    See also: The Review Gap: Finding Client Opportunities In Competitor Feedback.

    Once you have a set of real questions, the next step is working out what an AI assistant would actually search for when answering them.

    It has been revealed that google is open about the fact that AI Overviews and AI Mode may use a query fan-out technique, issuing multiple related searches to build a single response. You can’t see those searches for a real AI Mode session, but you can get a reasonable approximation through the Gemini API.

    Recent findings suggest that when you use Grounding with Google Search, the API response includes a field called webSearchQueries, which lists the searches the model ran to answer your prompt. Google’s own documentation describes it as useful for understanding the model’s reasoning process.

    Industry observers note that if you feed in the first migration question from earlier, you’d expect to see sub-queries covering things like how long rankings take to recover after a Shopify migration, how to check redirects after a re-platform, and how to spot keyword cannibalization between collection pages. Your own output will vary from run to run, but each sub-query is effectively a section your page would need to cover to be useful as a source.

    Industry observers note that you don’t need to be technical for this. Go Fish Digital published a walkthrough that runs it through Screaming Frog with a copy-and-paste custom JavaScript snippet and an API key from Google AI Studio. Their version sends each page’s H1, but swapping in your own list of questions is straightforward.

    According to recent reports, I want to be clear about what this output is, though. It indicates you how a Gemini model expands a question, which is a fair proxy for Google’s AI features, but it isn’t a record of what AI Mode ran for an actual user. I treat it as a coverage checklist, and I wouldn’t present it to a client as anything more definitive than that.

    In a recent development, for ChatGPT, Perplexity, and the other assistants, the manual route still works fine. Ask each one your question, note which sub-topics it decides to cover and which sources it cites, and compare that against the page that’s supposed to answer it.

    See also: The 2003 Framework That Was Already Doing Query Fan-Out.

    Search Console is better as a validation step than a discovery tool for this, because it highlights you which of these questions are already finding their way to your site.

    Long conversational queries do turn up in the Performance report. Suganthan Mohanadasan has already covered four ways to surface them in a lot of detail, so I’d recommend checking that out if you haven’t already. For a quick look, I use the Custom (regex) option in the Query filter. This pattern returns queries of eight words or more:.

    And this one returns queries that start with a question word:.

    Then I compare what comes back against the questions from calls and forums. If the migration scenario indicates up as a long query, that’s good confirmation that real people are bringing it to Google. If it doesn’t show up, it could be a coverage gap, or the queries may simply be too rare for Google to show you.

    Recent findings suggest that that last point is significant because Google anonymizes rare queries, and conversational queries are rare almost by definition. Suganthan found that 57.7% of his impressions sat in the anonymized pool over a 59-day period, so anything you find here is an undercount.

    If you have access to the generative AI performance report, the pages view is worth a look too. It highlights which of your URLs are already appearing in AI Overviews and AI Mode. There’s no query data in it (yet), and sites with few AI impressions may not see the report at all, but it does tell you which pages Google is already comfortable using as a source.

    According to recent reports, by now, you’ll have a messy list of questions from several sources. To get it into a shape a content team can actually use, I put everything into one sheet. Here’s how a single row might look, using the migration example:.

    Recent findings suggest that for the priority column, I use the same proxies from my previous column: business value, evidence that the question is being asked, how massive the coverage gap is, and whether you can answer it with real specifics. The frequency column feeds straight into the second one.

    Recent findings suggest that once the sheet is filled in, you’ll usually notice that most of the questions cluster around a handful of situations. Those clusters are your content strategy. In my experience, most of them can be handled by strengthening a page you already have, which is quicker than publishing something new and tends to perform better too.

    I’m aware this is a lot less tidy than sorting a spreadsheet by volume, so I think it’s worth being up front about the limitations.

    Sources indicate that you still won’t have a volume figure next to any of these questions, which means you’re prioritizing on judgment and frequency. Your own calls are biased toward people who already know you exist, so questions from audiences you don’t reach yet will be underrepresented. The Gemini fan-out is an approximation of Google’s behavior, and Search Console only indicates you part of the picture because of anonymization.

    However, I don’t think any of that is a reason not to do it. It just means you should present the output as a well-evidenced shortlist, particularly to stakeholders who are used to seeing a number next to every target or goal.

    If you want somewhere to start right now:.

    Recent findings suggest that keyword tools are still useful for understanding what people type into a search box. But a growing share of the questions that decide whether a buyer picks you are being asked in a conversation with an assistant, and the good news is that plenty of them are already sitting in your inbox and call recordings.

    💡 Key Takeaways

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    According to recent reports, we have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    According to recent reports, the latest budget would make a local reporting program permanent and extend a 35% tax credit on newsroom salaries. The support makes “a massive, massive difference.”.

    A Canadian program to place local reporters in underserved communities has lived from renewal to renewal. Publishers who relied on the Local Journalism Initiative couldn’t be sure whether the money would be there again.

    That changed last week when Canada proposed a federal budget that would make the Local Journalism Initiative permanent. The 2026 budget would increase LJI funding to $134 million over four years with $41 million in annual ongoing funding after that. (Figures are, naturally, in Canadian dollars.) For the budget to be finalized, it must pass Parliament. With Prime Minister Mark Carney’s party in the majority, it’s expected to.

    Expanding the LJI is not even the biggest piece of federal help for newsrooms, according to Paul Deegan, president and CEO of the news industry advocacy group News Media Canada. The same budget extends a 35% tax credit on newsroom salaries through 2028 and opens it to radio and television newsrooms for the first time. The tax credit will cost $501 million over the next five years, according to the budget. Thanks to the Online News Act, Canadian newsrooms also get funding from Google. And then there’s Canadian investment in public media; the 2026 budget added $300 million over two years to CBC/Radio-Canada “to strengthen its capacity to meet the evolving needs of Canadians across the country.”.

    I asked Deegan: How did Canadian publishers secure so much federal funding for news?

    Sources indicate that “We have a government that ‘gets it,’” Deegan said. “They see what Massive Tech monopolists have done to local news. They know the labor tax credit is the leading driver of maintaining and growing newsroom headcount.”.

    RELATED ARTICLECalifornia’s massive local news bill becomes lawLaura Hazard OwenOctober 1, 2026There have been similar proposals and experiments in the United States, including a new tax credit in California. But Canada is much further down the road. The country can offer lessons on what it looks like when a federal government commits to supporting journalism.

    The labor tax credit refunds 35% of a newsroom employee’s salary, up to $29,750 per journalist per year. The percentage had been scheduled to fall to 25% at the end of 2026.

    “In terms of employing the [largest] number of journalists and keeping newsroom employment stability, the labor tax credit is number one,” Deegan remarked.

    There’s also the Online News Act which has brought in $100 million of Google money annually. Of that amount, $63 million is set aside for news publishers. (Meta blocked news on Facebook and Instagram in Canada rather than pay under the Online News Act.) Publishers receive around $17,000 per journalist per year.

    It has been revealed that “That’s about $47,000 per journalist per year from those two measures,” Deegan said. “That just makes a massive, massive difference.”.

    Recent findings suggest that in the U.S., some ideas for funding local journalism have been criticized as helping large chain newspapers — including chains that have hollowed out local newsrooms for years. Deegan — whose news industry group counts Postmedia and Torstar as members — acknowledged that the largest share of tax credit dollars goes to the largest employers.

    Recent findings suggest that but News Media Canada also represents small and digital-only publications, and Deegan noted the smallest Canadian outlets face another problem. To qualify for the tax credit, an organization must produce original news content and regularly employ at least two journalists “at arm’s length” from its owners. An advisory board found the second rule excludes small “mom-and-pop” newsrooms.

    According to recent reports, the Local Journalism Initiative is a more targeted program than the tax credit. Launched in 2019, it was designed to support local and community news in underserved areas. The LJI program supports about 470 reporting positions in roughly 1,000 communities across Canada.

    Even generous government subsidies have not stopped losses in local news completely. But early results demonstrated the LJI increased reporting capacity and local news in “news poverty” communities with limited local news offerings. The same evaluation identified reaching “news deserts” — communities with no existing local news outlets — and Indigenous communities as obstacles.

    “Since LJI is demand driven, funding allocation across the country varies and gaps remain in some areas, such as news deserts,” the report reads. Later, the report notes that allowing news startups “could better support attraction and retainment of journalists” in the neediest communities.

    According to recent reports, many of the newsrooms receiving the LJI funding are small. Deegan described family-owned weekly newspapers with circulations as low as 800. Funding provides a local journalist to report on “cops, courts, city hall, and the school board.”.

    “Without those LJI journalists in some of those communities, those things simply wouldn’t be covered,” he noted.

    Some underserved communities, particularly in northern Canada, struggle to hire reporters given high living costs and remote locations. “Even with the grant, it’s just hard to recruit and find people,” Deegan noted.

    Industry observers note that deegan points to two factors that have made Canada’s federal funding for news work. The first is distance. Publishers get LJI money from one of three administrator organizations: News Media Canada, Community Radio Fund of Canada, or the Consortium of Official Language Minority Community Media. These organizations — not the government itself — administer the funds and an independent board advises on who qualifies for the tax credit.

    “To avoid perceptions of conflict of interest, the government ensured that third parties adjudicate who receives local journalism initiative reporters and who is eligible for the labor tax credit,” Deegan said.

    The second factor applies to the Online News Act and, more generally, to Canadian politics.

    “When it comes to holding those platforms to account, one of the reasons we have been successful is that we have a ban [on] corporate political financing at the federal level in Canada,” Deegan said. “These companies sprinkle goodies around to friendly academics, think tanks, and other useful idiots to do some of their bidding, but our government sees through that nonsense.”.

    We’re hiring an Account Executive to ASEAN (singapore, malaysia, SEA) across our commercial and enterprise segments. You’ll sell to founders, engineering leaders, and technical buyers. We’re after someone who has done this before, enjoys the technical depth of the work, and wants to help define how Supabase sells in the region.

    Own the full sales cycle from first conversation to close, including multi threaded enterprise deals.

    Run technical discovery and tie it to business outcomes the buyer cares about.

    Work with Sales Engineers and Product on demos, proofs of concept, and architecture reviews.

    Build and run your own territory initiative, including pipeline, forecasting, and account strategy.

    Work with AWS and regional partners and resellers to open and progress deals.

    Handle data residency, security, and procurement conversations with enterprise and public sector buyers.

    Hand off to Customer Success so customers onboard well and expand.

    5+ years in a technical sales role, ideally selling developer tools, databases, cloud infrastructure, or open source.

    A record of consistently beating quota, with numbers you can walk us through.

    Experience closing both fast moving commercial deals and longer enterprise cycles with procurement, security, and legal involved.

    Enough technical fluency to hold a credible conversation with an engineer without bringing a Sales Engineer to every call.

    Comfort selling to founders, CTOs, and platform teams.

    Experience with Postgres, or a competing backend or database platform.

    An existing network across the ASEAN startup, scale-up, and developer ecosystem.

    Experience with cloud marketplace or co-sell motions, particularly AWS.

    Familiarity with ASEAN compliance expectations, such as Singapore PDPA, Malaysia PDPA, or financial services and government requirements.

    We hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

    Every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the organization. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

    Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

    Industry observers note that we move fast, build in public, and use what we ship. If it’s in your project, we probably use it in ours too. We believe deeply in the open-source ecosystem and strive to support—not replace—existing tools and communities.

    • ONA, OpenNews, and others see troubled times ahead, so it’s goodbye to “rubber chicken dinners.”.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    In a recent development, we have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    ONA, OpenNews, and others see troubled times ahead, so it’s goodbye to “rubber chicken dinners.”.

    According to recent reports, RELATED ARTICLEWe know coronavirus has wrecked the events business for media in 2020. But will it come back post-virus?Joshua BentonMarch 25, 2020When the pandemic forced conferences to go virtual, the question was whether people would come back in person post-Covid.

    For a while, they did. For a couple years after the pandemic, people were excited to be in person together again. U.S. journalism organizations saw their revenue climb, as sponsors and funders spent generously.

    At the end of 2026, though, the situation is less rosy. Combine surging jet fuel prices, inflation, media companies cutting costs, and declining sponsor and funder dollars, and the future appears grim not just for journalism conferences but, in some cases, for the organizations behind them.

    Revenue is the total revenue line on each organization’s IRS Form 990. The 990s are from ProPublica’s Nonprofit Explorer. ONA’s 990 for 2025 was not available as of November 12, 2026.

    The Online News Association said on Tuesday that it is “pausing” its 26-year-old conference and laying off its five staffers.

    “Before the pandemic, the annual conference was ONA’s biggest source of revenue, and together with grants, it sustained the organization. This is no longer true,” Niketa Patel wrote. “The costs of large convenings have climbed sharply while professional development and sponsorship budgets have shrunk.”.

    Industry observers note that LION Publishers said in September that it’s getting out of the large conference business for now. “Philanthropy is famously fickle, and funding priorities have shifted, making this kind of conference a very tough lift,” executive director Chris Krewson added.

    In a recent development, LION barely broke even on the conferences it held in 2025 and 2026, Krewson told me. The organization may still hold smaller events next year, it’s not cutting staff or programming, and it’s expanding its Audit program. But it “won’t be taking on the responsibility for an independent event at a hotel with a food and beverage minimum and hotel room block for 400-plus people.”.

    “Every dollar I spend on rubber chicken dinners and microphones/WiFi for three days is money I can’t spend on programs that make publishers’ businesses stronger,” Krewson noted.

    OpenNews remarked in October that it’s switching into “emergency mode”1 and cutting back on “work that distills journalism craft: no more community calls or Source articles for at least the rest of 2026 and maybe longer.”.

    Industry observers note that the future of OpenNews’s annual conference, SRCCON, is uncertain. “We usually make our decision about SRCCON at about this time every year, but this year is different as we consider the news from both LION and ONA and the funding pressures that we know all too well,” Jessica Morrison, co–executive director of OpenNews, told me in an email. “We are opening a community conversation today — emails going out very soon — to gather input about SRCCON, our other programs, and where we go next with OpenNews.”.

    The three-year-old Organization for Accessible Journalism said Thursday that it is shutting down. “Financial support never reached a level that allowed us to build beyond an all volunteer effort — including my full-time effort,” founder Stacy Kess wrote.

    In a recent development, journalism conferences in the United States are certainly not gone. IRE and NICAR will hold their annual data journalism conference in Denver in March. The Institute for Nonprofit News is “talking about what INN Days will look like in 2027” and will know more by early next year. And the International Symposium on Journalism is on for 2027 — its 28th year, founder (and Nieman Foundation board member) Rosental Alves told me. But things have gotten harder, he said. “It’s not only the difficulty of finding sponsors, but also the rising costs of venues, hotels, airfares, etc., compounded by shrinking travel budgets in newsrooms and even the problems international attendees face in coming to the U.S.,” he told me in an email. ISOJ cut costs, in part by moving to a different venue, and it benefits from being relatively small. “It’s very sad that foundations and corporations that funded journalism conferences in the past have pulled back their support,” Alves added. “The need for these gatherings is as great as ever.” a play on Emergency Mode for News, its initiative to support journalists working during disasters [↩].

    #55208. Industry News: How I’m Approaching AI Search (And How You Should To)

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2844 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Searchenginejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: How I’m Approaching AI Search (And How You Should To)

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2844 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In focusing on citation tactics and cheap visibility tricks, we’re missing the bigger picture.
    • There’s nothing inherently wrong with it.
    • In a recent development, I don’t have the energy or the wherewithal to play catch-up every year or two.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    AI is strangely simple. And we’re overcomplicating it.

    In focusing on citation tactics and cheap visibility tricks, we’re missing the bigger picture. As an industry, we’ve got away with poor content for years. Updating the same “best spoons” article three times a week because some other idiot is doing exactly the same thing.

    There’s nothing inherently wrong with it. It’s just too SEO-y. We’re missing a much bigger opportunity by framing it through a really narrow lens.

    In a recent development, I don’t have the energy or the wherewithal to play catch-up every year or two. So I think of AI search as the ultimate synthesis of your marketing efforts.

    Your positioning, reputation, expertise, content, and presence across the internet are all potential inputs into how AI systems understand and represent you.

    It’s not just about your website anymore.

    It has been revealed that I’ve spent a lot of time recently working on AI search, information retrieval, audience research, and discoverability strategies. The more I do, the more convinced I become that we need to approach this as marketers, not SEOs.

    But don’t build your entire “marketing” strategy around it. I use marketing in the loosest possible sense of the word.

    If you’re in dire need of a refresher, here’s a few parts on the fundamentals of modern information retrieval:.

    There’s one other concept I haven’t written about in detail: query fan-out. Not because it’s not important, more just because a) it’s pretty dull and b) it isn’t a upcoming concept for SEOs. We’ve been using tools like AlsoAsked for years to understand related questions, adjacent information needs and the wider context surrounding a search.

    Image Credit: Harry Clarkson-Bennett.

    But we also need to distinguish between three things:.

    They’re related, but they aren’t interchangeable. Being crawled doesn’t guarantee inclusion in training data. Being retrieved doesn’t guarantee a citation. And a citation doesn’t guarantee commercial value.

    Industry observers note that understanding these mechanisms is vital – mainly just so you can answer the brain-dead questions people ask you about AI. Building your entire marketing strategy around their current implementation is the action of a halfwit.

    Industry observers note that models, retrieval systems, and interfaces will change. An owned audience is a considerably more durable investment. So build one.

    It has been revealed that this is the biggest change I’ve made to my approach. Not just for AI search, but for traditional SEO.

    Industry observers note that I don’t begin by asking which prompts a brand should appear in. Or how much search volume a keyword or even topic has. Mainly because my trust in search volume and all forms of visibility is at rock bottom.

    So I use SparkToro to investigate where audiences spend time, which websites they visit, who influences them, and which platforms they’re disproportionately likely to use compared with the wider population.

    For this audience, I know that if I want to influence them, LinkedIn is a non-negotiable (Image Credit: Harry Clarkson-Bennett).

    Industry observers note that I combine that with traditional search research, AI search behaviour and an assessment of the brand’s existing positioning. You don’t need to overcomplicate this – ask a number of different LLMs about insert brand and record the responses.

    I want to answer some relatively straightforward questions:.

    This research should inform two things.

    In a recent development, first, our owned platforms. We use what we’ve learned to improve the way we position ourselves, the services we offer, the language we use, and the content we create.

    Let’s try to make things under our control as human and well-targeted as possible.

    In a recent development, second, our wider marketing strategy. We identify the publications, communities, creators, platforms, and people capable of influencing that audience, and decide how to reach them.

    Audience affinity with specific Subreddits, via SparkToro (Image Credit: Harry Clarkson-Bennett).

    You need to know this. Not because it might get your brand mentioned as part of the training data. But because this is where you should be marketing.

    Made-up prompt data is out. Real, human-led marketing is in. If we want SEO to be taken seriously, this is the proper evolution.

    It has been revealed that the goal isn’t to manufacture mentions for an AI model. It’s to build a brand people want to discover, engage with, and recommend.

    It has been revealed that if those activities also increase your representation in AI systems, wonderful. But that’s a delicious byproduct, not the reason for doing them.

    While audience research informs the wider strategy, your website needs to be accessible, understandable, and representative of who you are. That is something reasonably competent SEOs can lead.

    Sources indicate that can the relevant search and AI crawlers access your content? Can they render it? Are you inadvertently blocking systems you want to reach?

    This means reviewing bot management, robots directives, rendering, indexability, internal linking, site architecture, and the usual technical SEO fundamentals.

    A traditional SEO-type audit with a few improvements.

    One that understands that not all AI bots serve the same purpose. Training crawlers, search crawlers, and user-triggered retrieval systems can have different access requirements and commercial implications.

    Crawlers do different things (Image Credit: Harry Clarkson-Bennett).

    Especially important if you’re working for – or with – a publisher. Someone whose business may depend on you understanding the wider context.

    If you’re restricting access to your content, you need to understand what you’re giving up, what you’re protecting, and where the value might exist instead.

    Perhaps that’s content licensing, direct audience relationships or proprietary products.

    The role of the SEO changes considerably in an environment where you’re not maximising access. You’re helping the business understand the trade-offs between visibility, intellectual property and commercial value.

    Sources indicate that it’s like a paywall. You’re restricting reach for commercial purposes. It’s the correct move if played properly.

    See Cyrus Shepherd’s excellent test to understand how much search traffic was truly influenced by Google’s AI proposition.

    This is where I think modern information retrieval methods and SEO intersect perfectly. I’ve written about how to approach this in Entities Are the Foundation of Modern SEO.

    This framework is relatively simple:.

    Image Credit: Harry Clarkson-Bennett.

    This isn’t about adding some structured data and hoping ChatGPT tries to hump your leg. Spoiler: It won’t.

    It’s about making sure that your owned presence accurately represents your positioning and that the wider internet provides credible, independent evidence to support it.

    Recent findings suggest that so, we know who we are. We’ve represented ourselves properly. Now we have to rely on *shudders* other people to corroborate this message.

    We have to build an off-site presence.

    This references a podcast I did with Andy Francos and an article I wrote for Lumar two years ago (Image Credit: Harry Clarkson-Bennett).

    We’re talking actual, real marketing (not SEO). PR, partnerships, content and audience development.

    If the people you’re trying to reach spend their time reading particular publications, following particular experts or participating in particular communities, those are the places worth investing in.

    Bollocks to a citation. Your audience is there. You know, people you could actually sell something to.

    That might mean publishing original research, collaborating with influential people, appearing on podcasts, creating genuinely useful resources or contributing expertise to relevant publications.

    Some of those activities will generate links. Others will generate mentions, relationships, conversations and brand demand – a real representation of site quality in Google.

    Recent findings suggest that the more consistently you’re associated with the right subjects, people and organizations, the stronger your wider digital presence can become. That is, in essence, how training data and entity relationships work.

    Image Credit: Harry Clarkson-Bennett.

    If you’re lucky, some of that evidence may eventually influence how AI systems represent you.

    But you won’t care, because you’ll have been making sales by marketing to actual customers.

    Modern methods of information retrieval across SEO and AI search share many, if not all of the same fundamentals.

    Arguably, AI search has a longer tail to it. But it’s not sustainable, nor sensible, to create a page for every possible thought your audience may have. To perpetuate a false Henry Ford quote:.

    “If I had asked people what they wanted, they would have noted faster horses.” H. Ford, Never.

    So you need to strike a balance. No one cares about visibility without impact. At least not for long.

    Industry observers note that there is room to try and test things. Good things. Things real people will care about.

    Industry observers note that people like Jan-Willem Bobbink and Dan Petrovic highlight some really brilliant things you can test that are eminently sensible for SEO and AI search. Surprise, surprise, they work for people too. It’s marketing.

    According to recent reports, let me give you an example. Maybe more accurately, let me steal one of Jan’s:.

    Sources indicate that “I spent the last three weeks on SEO / GEO work for B2B clients, and the changes that made the biggest difference were mostly about information that was missing or hard to find. Buyers run into the same problems on these sites, so you can usually get these fixes approved without having to explain SEO to anyone.”.

    Image Credit: Harry Clarkson-Bennett.

    Being explicit, consistent, and accurate is not an AI hack. It’s just pretty sensible.

    Industry observers note that adding pricing pages, case studies, and telling people why you are the best in the business are always good ideas. Even if your pricing pages just say something like prices starting at x, that is a better way of finding the right audience.

    And if you want to feature in AI responses, for god’s sake don’t hide your case studies. You need to provide a clear reason for your inclusion. Hard if your best work is hidden.

    In a recent development, statements like “Client Y saw a 30% improvement in deliverability metrics” can noticeably improve your citation rate because a model is literally looking for a reason to include you. You need to give them one. Just as you would a person.

    According to recent reports, experience. Expertise. Authority. Trust. Not so stupid after all.

    Measurement’s been broken for a decade anyway. It’s just nice for the C-suite to have numbers to report on – even if they’re complete hokum.

    You try and figure this out (Image Credit: Harry Clarkson-Bennett).

    AI visibility’s not much better. A hugely flawed metric given the personalization, lack of prompt data, and completely individual prompts. But it’s better than nothing. Indicative at best, but you need to use something.

    Industry observers note that people still want to know how they’re represented in AI systems. And so they should – it’s a valuable channel. My preference is to establish a representative set of prompts across four areas:.

    Track these consistently across the systems that matter to your audience.

    Look at whether you’re mentioned, how you’re described, which competitors appear, and which sources are being used. Find out when you start to appear for certain terms and see if it matches your positioning.

    I always track my mentions with Alertmouse (Image Credit: Harry Clarkson-Bennett).

    I appear in AI recommendations around news SEO expertise despite having done nothing specifically to optimize for AI search.

    What I have done is spend years working in the industry, publishing, building relationships, contributing expertise, and establishing a reasonably clear on-site and off-site identity.

    Not a bad list, although I am not sure ChatGPT is quite nailing the profile pictures for us… (Image Credit: Harry Clarkson-Bennett).

    I guarantee you, if you ask Barry Adams, he’ll tell you he’s done nothing special for AI either.

    I’ve written what I think are high-quality articles on third-party websites and podcasts, featured in roundups, and built my own distribution platform. It just also happens to work for featuring in AI systems.

    AI systems don’t necessarily need to send you traffic to influence commercial outcomes. Which is a good thing, because ChatGPT sends less than 1% of Google’s traffic.

    Similarweb’s research found that users who received a brand recommendation in ChatGPT were 2.5 times more likely to visit that brand’s website within the following seven days than users who were recommended a competitor.

    Much of that activity happened through subsequent branded searches rather than direct AI referrals. One of those measures of site quality that should be monitored.

    In a recent development, AI search can and does function as a brand discovery and consideration channel. I think referral traffic is, at best, a secondary measure of success from LLMs. While they’ve engineered the exit out, you cannot deny the reach these systems have.

    Sources indicate that unfortunately, our attribution systems can’t cope with “I saw it here once.” We need to focus on incremental change. The outcomes attributable to marketing.

    According to recent reports, establish a baseline. Run a campaign. Measure changes in branded demand, direct visits, conversions, leads, and commercial outcomes. Compare with appropriate benchmarks or control groups where possible.

    Keep tracking AI visibility, referrals and citations, but use them as supporting indicators.

    Our objective is to establish whether said marketing activity is creating additional business value, not whether ChatGPT has linked to your homepage.

    For businesses whose models depend on monetizing information and attracting a click, AI search presents a very different challenge.

    Sources indicate that they are monetizing other people’s work for their own ill-gotten gain. That is an irrefutable commercial dilemma. Hence all the protectionism. So we need to establish what that cost is and try to find alternative methods of monetization.

    In The Generative AI Report Sucks – Let’s Make It Brilliant, I outlined how publishers can combine AI visibility data with traffic dependency, commercial value, audience resilience, and server logs.

    We can go some way toward solving actual business problems.

    According to recent reports, always, always, always a good thing to do. Regardless of your job.

    Sources indicate that this opportunity is no different, especially for organizations (like publishers) with substantial authority across particular subjects. They have influence within the wider information ecosystem.

    That influence can have commercial value.

    Industry observers note that publishers Should Think About AI Visibility. Content licensing, data partnerships, research collaborations, and other commercial arrangements offer opportunities to monetize expertise and proprietary information.

    But this needs careful handling.

    Industry observers note that selling links or undisclosed editorial influence is not a sustainable AI strategy. It introduces reputational, editorial, and search-policy risks.

    The more sustainable opportunity is to understand the value of your existing content, expertise, audience, and distribution – and build legitimate commercial products around those assets.

    Lots of companies are selling or actively considering selling their archived assets or data to AI companies:.

    In a recent development, for publishers in particular, this is an opportunity to rethink the value they create beyond the click. See the Daily Mail’s approach to GEO monetization here.

    Sources indicate that if you’re more on the glass half full side, you’ll be able to sniff out commercial opportunities. Ideally ones that don’t ruin the brand or fall foul of Google’s link payment guidelines.

    General advice: If something smells a bit off, it probably is.

    If you’re a business looking to take this seriously, there’s an organizational question you need to answer.

    Who is responsible for all of this?

    Because as great as we can be, it shouldn’t just be your SEO.

    In a recent development, this touches technical infrastructure, audience research, brand positioning, content, PR, distribution, commercial partnerships, and measurement. That requires someone who understands the entire ecosystem and, crucially, how to influence people.

    Recent findings suggest that nobody is an expert at all of these things. They’re too different. Too complex.

    For larger businesses, I’d be thinking about a Head of Marketing or Head of Discoverability with responsibility for coordinating these activities. Someone who at least knows the basics of each and can herd a clowder of cats.

    They need the authority to bring different teams together, allocate resources, challenge existing assumptions and measure outcomes against business objectives.

    There’s a reason SEOs rarely graduate to marketing lead positions. We don’t understand wider marketing because we’ve rarely had to. SEO was always the best channel… According to wonky data, anyway.

    AI search gives us a very good reason to change that.

    And for anyone working in SEO, I think there are three particularly interesting directions.

    It has been revealed that all three have tremendous value. Limiting yourself to SEO, particularly as a collection of search-engine or LLM-specific tactics, is increasingly short-sighted.

    Industry observers note that discoverability has been changing for a decade. We need to think much more broadly about how audiences discover and engage with content. The opportunity is to bring those disciplines together.

    A little rebrand and refocus on what you want from your career may be the best thing you ever do.

    Stop trying to engineer your way into an AI response. Build a brand worth recommending, an audience worth owning, and a business that benefits whether the citation comes or not.

    Enjoy yourself. This will be a better era for marketers and marketing. Your competition is lazy and inept. They’re just faster.

    Featured Image: LariBat/Shutterstock.
