    #55180. Latest Update: WordPress 7.2 Arrives Dec. 8 – Last-Minute Changes Still Being Made via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2654 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Searchenginejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: WordPress 7.2 Arrives Dec. 8 – Last-Minute Changes Still Being Made via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2654 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • This version has, in beta, turned on a new public address on updated sites.
    • Sources indicate that this feature is on by default.
    • That makes /random/ the 7.2 change most sites will need to decide on before updating.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    WordPress 7.2 is due on Dec. 8. This version has, in beta, turned on a new public address on updated sites. /random/ directs you to a random published post. Versions of the address also do this within categories, tags, author archives, or eligible custom post types.

    Sources indicate that this feature is on by default. Switching it off will require coding, as there are no settings available via the WordPress dashboard to disable this feature. Further, in the November roundup of the WordPress Developer Blog, the filter name listed doesn’t match the actual filter name used in the code. Copying the name from the Developer Blog will have no effect.

    That makes /random/ the 7.2 change most sites will need to decide on before updating. The new Secrets API, a way for plugins to store credentials, was removed from 7.2 on Nov. 17. That came days after Matt Mullenweg, who leads the release, sided with a request to pull it.

    Core’s upcoming AI pieces are tools for developers and plugins, and none of them adds an AI feature visitors or editors will see.

    Beta five is the latest test release, and WordPress states not to run it on production sites. The first release candidate (RC1) is due Nov. 17, so details can still change before the final release.

    Aaron Jorbin’s developer note opens, “A request to example.com/random/ will lead end customers to a randomly selected published post. The feature is on by default.”.

    Recent findings suggest that the /random/ path and its category, tag, author, and post type versions use the default base with pretty permalinks. The base is translatable, and a new field on the Permalinks screen changes it. The development code also responds to a random query variable, so ?random works too on the home page and archives. Since a Nov. 16 change, a search URL that includes it redirects to the same search without the parameter.

    It has been revealed that by default, posts are eligible. Pages and attachments aren’t. Custom post types are considered eligible if they’re publicly queryable, have archives and the developer hasn’t registered them with 'randomable' => false. The code filters for only published posts (with no password).

    Recent findings suggest that it uses a 302 redirect. The development code sends no-cache headers and includes the header X-Robots-Tag: noindex, follow with the 302 redirect response. This header covers the original /random/ request, but not the post this redirects to. If there is no match to the query, the request will return a 404.

    Recent findings suggest that if you’ve created a published page with the slug “random,” then this will override the redirect. The same thing happens if you create a post with the slug “random,” when permalinks are set to use the post name. Peter Wilson confirmed this in the comments after Daniel Iser raised it, and recommended using a base like “shuffle” instead.

    Random queries run from the main WP_Query, so pre_get_posts callbacks that change archives will also affect their random redirect. Developers wishing to target random requests only should use wp_is_random_content_query().

    Recent findings suggest that turning this feature off is done by adding the one-line mu-plugin shown in the note, add_filter( 'wp_enable_random_content_redirect', '__return_false' );. This will prevent WordPress from generating rewrite rules for random content, hide the base field on the Permalinks screen, and ignore the query variable. The code’s documentation indicates that flushing the rewrite rules is necessary after changing the filter value.

    The roundup’s version, wp_enable_random_content_direct, isn’t used anywhere in the code.

    Random redirects made their initial appearance in the code on Sept. 21; at this point they were an optional ?random query that needed sites to return true for a filter called enable_random_content_redirect if they wanted them to be active.

    According to recent reports, they were reverted two days after that. The commit message mentioned of the feature, “The feature is intended to land in WordPress 7.2 but will need some work.”.

    On Oct. 16, they returned as /random/ rewrite rules turned on, with the filter name changed and the default for the filter set to true. They were added to Beta 1 on Oct. 20.

    Jorbin’s post drew a long thread of objections. Joost de Valk wrote, “This is a horrible idea to turn on by default.” In a later reply, he added, “Now I fear people will randomly end up on invoices, offers, client specific pages, etc.” Responding to another commenter, Jorbin wrote, “The WordPress Philosophies mean that opt-out options are not added for every feature, otherwise the options pages would become unusable.”.

    Mullenweg replied to a commenter whose site already has a page named “random,” writing, “I agree it should not use page URL structure.” In a separate comment, he wrote, “I don’t think this should be an appended pretty URL; the request was just for /?random, just at root.” He also addressed concerns about performance and exposure, saying query strings, searches, and REST calls offer “far more ways” to exhaust a site’s resources.

    As of Nov. 17, no one maintaining the feature had posted a change to its default or its URL structure. Since the note, code changes from Nov. 12 to Nov. 17 have adjusted when the redirect fires, how it treats searches and how it picks a post.

    See also: Web Almanac Data Reveals CMS Plugins Are Setting Technical SEO Standards (Not SEOs).

    The Secrets API would have allowed plugins to save API keys, tokens and more via libsodium encryption, and would have utilized the options tables, which hosts could replace with their own keyring or storage utilizing a secrets.php drop-in.

    WordPress reverted the API on Nov. 17. The commit points to feedback on the announcement that questioned the design, including whether one API should both write secrets and read the ones a host supplies. Peter Wilson had also found that the API never checked its manage_secrets and manage_network_secrets capabilities when secrets were set. The commit message opens, “Removes the Secrets API from WordPress 7.2 to allow more time for the API to mature before it ships in a future release.”.

    Earlier, Ryan McCue, a contributor, had commented that he believes secrets managed outside WordPress should only be readable and never writable to WordPress and that allowing writes to be part of this feature and easy to accomplish makes the API “likely to ossify” around that design. He argued that, under this design, a secrets store backed by hardware security modules offered no additional protection over an already encrypted database. He concluded, “I am a strong -1 on this feature, and I think this should be backed out of core for 7.2 until the above is resolved.”.

    Mullenweg replied, “I agree with @rmccue here.” Two minutes later, he wrote, “It’s also not a great time to be making ourselves a target for very sensitive things like that.”.

    Eric Mann, the writer of the developer note, responded to the encryption point, writing, “Encryption at rest protects against someone walking off with the disk. It does nothing about SQL injection, a leaked mysqldump, a misconfigured backup bucket.” Mann initially wanted to leave the API in 7.2 and referenced a proposed solution for how the AI plugin handles failed write operations, one of the items that was mentioned by McCue.

    It has been revealed that after Wilson’s finding, Mann replied, “I’m not excited about it but agree more time will help us ship a more solid foundation here. I’d still like to target at least 7.3 if possible.”.

    The AI plugin version 1.5.0 (released Oct. 29) moved its opt-in Key Encryption experiment into a bundled version of the Secrets API which stores the plugin’s AI service keys. Its maintainers had a pull request open to upgrade it to the version planned for core. After the revert, Jeffrey Paul, who had approved it, wrote that the plugin should “use an approach here that leverages the functionality outside of core” instead. The pull request was still open on Nov. 17, and 1.5.0 was still the latest release.

    See also: When The WordPress Plugin Update Is The Security Risk: Why SEOs Should Pay Attention.

    WordPress put AI building blocks into core before this release. Roger Montti reported in May that 7.0 shipped four of them, including the WP AI Client and a Connectors screen for AI services. In October, he reported that WordPress had released a canonical MCP Adapter plugin for connecting AI systems through the Model Context Protocol (MCP).

    WordPress 7.2 is set to add three new read-only abilities, which are registered actions called by other applications. The new read-only abilities allow other applications to query content, users, and WordPress settings. A developer will be able to build an embedding, a numeric representation of text, through the AI client to provide similarity search functionality.

    In addition to adding the three read-only abilities, the WordPress core team has marked those abilities as exposed to clients such as the WordPress core REST API, MCP, or AI agents. According to the documentation, “Exposure flags do not grant execution permission.” The content query ability requires a logged-in user and checks if the user has read permission for the returned posts. There is right now no MCP server included in the WordPress core.

    According to a post released about version 1.5.0 of the AI plugin, the AI plugin provides versions of these latest abilities that are expected to be identical to the versions “coming in WordPress core with 7.2 this December.” Additionally, the post says there are breaking changes in how existing integrations work because of this update.

    Sources indicate that the AI features editors will experience live within the AI plugin itself, where they are currently being tested as opt-in experiments with different requirements; two examples include text-to-speech and revision summaries where content is sent to the site’s selected AI provider. In addition, Content Verification identifies C2PA Content Credentials, a standard for providing provenance information for digital media. However, according to the release post, Content Verification “does not yet perform cryptographic verification” of C2PA Content Credentials. Another feature, MCP Access, decides what the plugin makes available over MCP.

    The AI plugin’s screenshot highlights the “Unverified” notice displayed when Content Credentials are detected.

    The AI plugin flags detected Content Credentials as unverified. Screenshot: WordPress AI.

    Industry observers note that supporting broader types of agents in the future is part of intends for the next release. WordPress’s agentic-web proposal indicates, “Agents can already accomplish a lot with WordPress through WP-CLI, the REST API, and file management. However, these approaches often require local access or more advanced configurations.” The agentic-web proposal plans to implement support for WordPress 7.3 and is planning to develop foundational elements during the 7.2 cycle.

    Admin and login screens in 7.2 separate the combined JavaScript and style sheets they once had into individual assets. According to the roundup, this means each asset is loaded separately by WordPress, which has also included prefetching of the assets needed for the next screen it thinks you’ll be viewing. load-scripts.php and load-styles.php have been deprecated in this version. This change applies to the admin and login screens only.

    The new SVG icons in the admin bar and menu replace the ones previously made available via the Dashicons font. So if your plugins used CSS to add additional styling to those icons’ ::before content, you may want to review them. Beta 5 introduced notification emails when an application password was created. Also according to WordPress, 7.2 aims to include full support for PHP 8.6.

    The preview below highlights the upcoming icons in the WordPress admin menu.

    It has been revealed that upcoming icons in the WordPress 7.2 admin menu. Screenshot: WordPress Developer Blog.

    In a recent development, whether to keep /random/ active is probably the decision most WordPress sites will have to make by Dec. 8. Unless /random/ is turned off, all published posts without a password (including content from a custom post type that is publicly queryable with an archive) can randomly appear. Some commenters on Jorbin’s post thought that would be true for some testimonial or client page custom post types they had created, even though those are not included in the site’s navigation links. First, check which of your custom post types are publicly queryable and have an archive. Then, for any of those custom post types that shouldn’t appear, set 'randomable' => false so that they won’t show up through this method.

    The noindex header isn’t applied to the posts /random/ points to, and the selection made by WordPress doesn’t automatically skip posts an SEO plugin has set to noindex. There was still no response as of Nov. 16 to a commenter who questioned that in the developer notes. Owners of SEO plugins that prevent access to posts via search engines may want to determine if /random/ will still be able to reach those posts.

    On sites behind a page cache or CDN, /random/ can return a 404 right after the upgrade. According to the hosting team, that lasts until rewrite rules are flushed, which core does on the first wp-admin request after the upgrade, per site on multisite. On the platform the team tested, a cached 404 stayed after the upgrade until the cache was purged. One tester using shared hosting without a page cache found the rules already in place. To help prevent a stale 404 from being served, purge the page cache after the first admin visit.

    Industry observers note that mcCue raised the load that the selection’s random ordering could put on large sites, especially if bots hit /random/ repeatedly. Jorbin said on Nov. 10 that he had opened a ticket to look at performance on very large sites, and a fix landed on Nov. 17. It looks up random post IDs instead of sorting the archive at random, a method the commit states “keeps the cost of a request independent of the number of posts”. Archives whose posts are too sparse among the post IDs fall back to a cached pool of up to 1,000 randomly ordered posts. Building that pool still reads every eligible post. Sites with a persistent object cache can reuse the pool for 10 minutes. Mullenweg’s view is that searches and REST calls already offer more ways to strain a site. Teams with large archives can watch for repeated hits on /random/ in their logs after the update.

    Agency managers running multiple sites will likely handle /random/ in the same way across their entire fleet using a mu-plugin with the correct spelling of the filter.

    Plugin developers can opt public post types out of /random/ where a random visit makes no sense. They’ll also want to check admin CSS for the icon change and update any integration that calls the content, user, and settings abilities.

    Recent findings suggest that mullenweg’s /random/ comment about URL structure could lead to changes to the original /random/ plan. Many commenters (on the developer note) are opposed to the default.

    When the Secrets API returns, and with what design, is now open too. Sites using the AI plugin’s Key Encryption will need to see how its next release handles the revert.

    Sources indicate that whether /random/ will honor SEO plugins’ noindex settings is still an open question. The release date itself has two values on WordPress.org. The release schedule indicates Dec. 8, while the roadmap still lists Dec. 10.

    RC1 on Nov. 17 will include the Field Guide and the 7.2 branch. This should help identify where /random/ ended up. RC2 is set to be released Nov. 24, and RC3 Dec. 1. A dry run and code freeze for Dec. 7 precede the scheduled release on Dec. 8. Agent connection work, broader than just connecting an MCP, along with authorization work in core, is targeted for WordPress 7.3.

    To test if /random/ can access your content and how this impacts caching, you’ll need to install RC1 onto a staging version of your website.

The metro area of more than 3 million people is home to The Minnesota Star Tribune, public radio powerhouse MPR, local TV stations, and multiple successful nonprofit startups, from nearly two-decade-old MinnPost to Sahan Journal (whose founder, Mukhtar Ibrahim, also launched The Somali Brief this fall).     Sources indicate that “There is a healthy degree of vitality in local news in the Twin Cities. The story elsewhere is ‘news deserts’ and little original journalism,” University of Minnesota professor Benjamin Toff told St. Anthony. While local institutions like the Star Tribune have survived, he added, “it’s not immune to industry forces, including the veritable disappearance of print.”.

    Recent findings suggest that wordPress confirmed the release of version 7.1.5, a security update that fixes 18 vulnerabilities plus two security improvements. The update addresses several types of vulnerabilities, including cross-site scripting and SQL injection, as well as an unauthenticated flaw that could lead to remote code execution.

    WordPress 7.1.5 fixes 20 issues covering a range of vulnerabilities across WordPress core. One of the vulnerabilities in particular stands out because it could lead to remote code execution (RCE), a type of flaw that can result in a site takeover.

    Sources indicate that the first one that stands out is an unauthenticated privilege escalation vulnerability affecting the Template Part block attributes which could lead to remote code execution (RCE), a type of flaw that can result in a site takeover. There is no authentication required to exploit this vulnerability, and it could lead to RCE. That combination is the worst-case scenario for a CMS.

    Sources indicate that A remote code execution (RCE) is a vulnerability that enables an attacker to run their own code on someone else’s server from somewhere else, usually over the internet. For a WordPress site, that means the attacker can make the web server execute commands of their choosing. From there they can read or change files and make entries to the database, create admin accounts, install backdoors, or inject malware.

    Multisite Administrator to Super Admin takeover (Customizer menu previews). This vulnerability requires an Administrator account, but on a multisite installation that means that an attacker who achieves admin level credential on one site can attain control of the entire network of sites.

    Industry observers note that unauthenticated stored XSS via shortcode attributes in comments. No login is needed to exploit it. Stored XSS is a type of flaw that can run malicious code in the browser of anyone who views the affected comment, including administrators, which can lead to account takeover.

    Two SQL injection vulnerabilities:.

    According to recent reports, wordPress urges site owners to update to version 7.1.5 immediately to address security vulnerabilities. The update is available through the WordPress dashboard or as a download, with automatic updates supported. Security fixes are also available for older affected WordPress versions, although only the latest version is actively supported.

    All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    The local journalism that has long powered the 169-year-old firm is no longer a viable business model, executives told McClatchy employees during a virtual town hall this month.

    Two months after McClatchy Media laid off more than 90 journalists nationwide, executives at the storied local newspaper chain offered a blunt assessment of its future.

    The award-winning local journalism that has long powered the 169-year-old firm was no longer a viable business model, executives told McClatchy employees during a virtual town hall this month, and its survival depended on a wholesale reinvention — centered entirely around artificial intelligence.

    From the rollout of newly introduced lifestyle websites that feature AI-generated articles and sponsored content to legal review and finance, executives revealed how AI is now integrated into virtually every part of the company. The demonstration comes after McClatchy, one of the nation’s largest newspaper conglomerates, carried out deep staff cuts in September at the Miami Herald, The Kansas City Star, and more than a dozen other local news outlets. An anonymous “person close to the executive decision-making” told The New York Times the layoffs were not about AI and were instead about “business performance in some areas.”.

    A companywide blueprint presented during the meeting highlights how McClatchy is systematically outsourcing the infrastructure for local news to AI agents — and rebranding around lifestyle verticals for sports fans, outdoor enthusiasts, and true-crime junkies.

    It has been revealed that dubbed “Project Catalyst,” the companywide restructure will create an “AI-native operating model” that takes “repeated tasks off of humans” and embeds AI agents “directly into the daily workflow,” Jeff Dorsey, McClatchy’s chief operating officer, noted at the town hall. Dorsey described the initiative as an effort to automate “non-core as well as core functions,” “get rid of things that just don’t offer the same value” they once did, and “provide cash, frankly, to keep the business afloat.”.

    McClatchy, which operates 29 daily newspapers across 14 states, didn’t respond to multiple requests for comment.

    Central to the rebrand is the launch of four new websites: Crime Hunter, a site devoted to “real-life crime and justice”; Saltwater South, which “celebrates the places, people and experiences that make the coastal South unlike anywhere else”; Camp & Country, a “national outdoor destination”; and Student Section, billed as “the home of the college sports fan.”.

    Each of the sites is “powered by Trend Hunter,” a company McClatchy acquired in 2024 that uses AI “to glean insights into consumer trends” and sell consumer goods like $33.91 rosemary oil “to support a healthy scalp environment,” a $249 red light therapy cap to regrow hair “without the hassle of messy serums” and $34.99 “MAGIC Mushroom Coffee” for “clarity, balance and natural energy.”.

    Little discussed, however, were the company’s local news ambitions. Kristine Sherred, chair of the Washington State NewsGuild and the food and dining reporter at The News Tribune in Tacoma, Washington, mentioned that she and other journalists were left to wonder “why we were even invited.”.

    “Our takeaway was that it wasn’t about news,” Sherred mentioned. “The future McClatchy appears to be building does not seem aligned with the mission of journalism.”.

    The meeting this month offered the clearest roadmap to date about McClatchy’s all-in approach to AI as one of the nation’s largest newspaper conglomerates navigates traffic declines, shifting consumer habits, and heavy debt obligations. It also comes at a critical moment for a media industry that seeks to modernize with AI — technology simultaneously blamed for gutting web traffic and touted as a tool to cut costs.

    “There is no sector that has not been disrupted this year by AI — everyone is going through extraordinary disruption,” Hunter mentioned. Through a laser focus on AI-powered efficiencies, he said, the company can turn around its fortunes. “We can win — not with yesterday’s solutions, though.”.

    For McClatchy, which has undergone aggressive cost-cutting efforts since it was acquired by New Jersey-based hedge fund Chatham Asset Management in 2020, its pivot toward AI-generated content over the last year has been met with internal pushback and, from some readers, ridicule.

    In May, journalists at The Sacramento Bee, the Miami Herald, and other McClatchy-owned papers withheld their names from articles that were produced with its “content scaling agent,” a chatbot that repackages human-written news articles at varying lengths for different audiences — complete with reporters’ names.

    In a recent development, similar resistance has played out at other news outlets. Earlier this month, for example, reporters at the Akron Beacon Journal in Ohio withheld their bylines for two weeks to protest a tool that generates AI summaries of articles that, the journalists allege, undermines their work and provides readers false information.

    Sources indicate that many news organizations prohibit the publication of AI-generated articles. But for McClatchy, they’ve become a core part of its business strategy and, according to Hunter, a key part of its “company-wide effort to agentify the entire enterprise.” During a contentious virtual meeting in May, Hunter pleaded with skeptical journalists to get on board or find another job.

    Anyone at McClatchy can now build AI tools to support their workflows, Rajiv Pant, McClatchy’s chief product and engineering officer, noted earlier this month.

    Recent findings suggest that “In every one of these, humans are at the command center, they aren’t just checking the technology’s work,” Pant noted. “They set the direction, make the calls and own the results. The technology lets each one of them do more of the work that only they can do.”.

    Sources indicate that trend Hunter content — including AI-generated posts — now appears regularly across McClatchy’s local publications and social media feeds, including articles with little connection to the communities those outlets have historically served. Recent examples include a post about winter “barn jackets” in the Miami Herald and a feature about collegiate football in Texas for the Kansas City Star.

    Other posts highlight obscure beauty products and questionable health trends, including how nugget ice “has become the craze worth understanding,” how saunas have “reshaped social wellness,” and “what your poop color, shape and frequency say about your gut health.”.

    Or, as one Kansas City Star reporter put it, the layoffs have created news websites where it’s “city reporters out, shitty reporters in.”.

    “They’re trying to kind of go toward these buzzy-type topics instead of local journalism that holds people to account,” said the reporter, who spoke on the condition of anonymity due to retaliation concerns.

    Readers, an overwhelming majority of whom are skeptical of AI use in newsrooms, have also taken notice. In a post on X, one social media user wrote that “people want the news” not “AI generated slop.” Another called into question McClatchy’s decision to publish an article — across numerous local news brands — about why the actress Scarlett Johansson “changed her magnesium supplement routine after a spray left her feet feeling dry.”.

    In a recent development, this AI slop is what McClatchy forced a bunch of its newspapers to publish in unison a few weeks ago. Who needs real human reporters when you can have this? https://t.co/Z82Vg67WtH.

    — James (@jameslineky) September 10, 2026.

    Given the rapid spread of AI-generated content online, McClatchy executives see the brand credibility of its legacy publications as a differentiator. Over time, Hunter said, the market will reward trust — and McClatchy is well positioned to capitalize on its local news audiences.

    “It is important that we have credible, accurate and relevant content,” Hunter stated. “We are not running from our standards, but we’re running toward a fresh model to help customers make better decisions.”.

    In recent months, as much as 20% of articles published by McClatchy newspapers were AI-generated, according to data from AI-detection company Originality.ai. (AI detection tools like Originality are imprecise in distinguishing synthetic writing from human-authored content.) Rather than building fresh audiences, McClatchy’s use of AI-generated content could erode trust among readers, said Jon Gillham, Originality’s founder and CEO.

    According to recent reports, such a reality is already playing out in Washington, said Sherred of the Washington State NewsGuild. Sherred’s union went on strike in May to demand “ethical limits” around the firm’s use of AI. The guild said in a statement at the time it was negotiating for “freedom to write hard-hitting news stories that take time, and not be punished if we don’t churn out clickbait.”.

    According to recent reports, “We hear this from people in the community all the time: They don’t want short snippets, they don’t want rehashed work and they don’t want AI telling them the news,” Sherred said. “The only way you get high-quality local news is by having high-quality local reporters actually out there making it.”.

    Less than a week after McClatchy laid off journalists nationwide in September, executives sent the remaining staff an emoji-laced email announcing “fresh talent”: several executives, two reporters and three editors for its “Content Innovation Lab” — the engine behind its fresh AI-powered lifestyle verticals.

    A recent job listing for innovation lab writers notes the “organization’s future depends” on an embrace of AI and the innovation lab is its “next-generation approach to content” where emerging technologies are leveraged to “fuel experimentation and productivity.”.

    According to recent reports, “From barbecue to bourbon, water sports to hiking, and golf to college sports, we are going to develop a steady stream of reader-focused, high-quality content for national and regional audiences,” according to the job listing. Producers will use AI to launch fresh brands “tied to dedicated communities of interest around travel, food, outdoor recreation, sports and even crime.”.

    The insights into the firm’s future editorial direction come on the heels of its steepest staff reduction in years, with layoffs of investigative reporters, government watchdogs, and other journalists focused on local news.

    “The city of Tacoma no longer has a city reporter,” Sherred noted. “What’s the purpose of a local paper if you have no one covering your local government?”.

    According to recent reports, hired to lead the Content Innovation Lab is Patrick Stiegman, a 20-year ESPN digital veteran who, during the meeting this month, turned to sports media lingo to describe the goal behind Saltwater South, Camp & Country, and its other AI-powered lifestyle brands. By “cultivating passionate fans” around obsessive lifestyle niches, he remarked, the company seeks to leverage reader data “and monetization opportunities” to guide coverage decisions.

    Perhaps nobody put McClatchy’s pivot in starker terms than Ariel Storch, recently hired to lead an AI-powered rebrand of its video strategy.

    “We make entertainment — not content, entertainment,” Storch stated during the Nov. 6 meeting. “Think about a late-night show. Nobody tunes in to be informed, they tune in to laugh. The by-product is you leave knowing about a new movie, a new book, a new product.”.

    Recent findings suggest that building new audiences is critical as the company works to claw itself out of debt, noted Joe Settineri, McClatchy’s chief financial officer. Stabilizing McClatchy’s core business is necessary, he said, for the Content Innovation Lab and its other AI initiatives to be successful.

    Industry observers note that “Today, most of that profitability is already spoken for because, like most companies, we have a sizable amount of debt,” Settineri remarked. “Like a loan on a house, we have to pay it down or you lose the house.”.

    Latest Update: Federal funding for public media is coming back, one way or another. But is it time for a deeper rethink?

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1977 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Niemanlab

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways

    All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    According to recent reports, we will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    Congressional Democrats will have to determine whether they want to revive the old system Donald Trump defunded or build something more attuned to today’s media ecosystem.

    Sources indicate that it was 318 days ago that the Corporation for Public Broadcasting — the primary funder of public media in the United States since 1967 — officially ceased to be, the victim of Republican budget cuts and years of attacks from Donald Trump. CPB is not “on pause” or “in hibernation” — it’s dead. As its final CEO Patricia Harrison put it: “CPB’s final act would be to protect the integrity of the public media system and democratic values by dissolving, rather than allowing the organization to remain defunded and vulnerable to additional attacks.”.

    You may have heard, however, that we had some elections in the U.S. recently, and the Republicans who defunded NPR and PBS will no longer control the House of Representatives or Senate as of January 3. In their place will be Congressional Democrats much more favorable to public media. So it seems quite likely that the federal government’s next budget will re-fund it rather than de-fund it.

    But with CPB officially no more, Democrats will have a rare opportunity to rethink the system from scratch instead of just prescribing minor tweaks to funding levels. The media environment of 2027 will, it goes without saying, be radically different from 1967’s. Over-the-air broadcasting is no longer America’s dominant medium. The immensely profitable newspapers that were the bedrock of news back then are shells of their former selves. And what was once a highly localized information ecosystem has been thoroughly nationalized and globalized, with access to news increasingly determined by a few large tech platforms. Democrats could just revive the old LBJ-era model — but should they instead build something new?

    These questions will dominate the next year of discourse around public media, and interested parties are already laying out intends. This morning, the Roosevelt Institute released a newly introduced white paper titled “Creating a New U.S. Public Media System: Normative Arguments and Policy Options.” Written by Penn professor (and past Nieman Lab contributor) Victor Pickard, it argues for a thorough reinvention:.

    Sources indicate that taken together, the 2025 federal defunding of American public media, the ongoing collapse of local journalism, growing media oligarchy, a multitude of social harms arising from unregulated platforms and AI technologies, and other political and economic challenges to our media and democracy demonstrate the need for robust public media systems. Fundamental flaws — especially its funding mechanisms — are baked into the historical U.S. public media model, and they must be structurally addressed. The current crisis presents a unique opportunity to create an entirely new kind of public media system based on a local “Public Media Center” model. Pickard lays out three core ideas: de-privatization, democratization, and localization. De-privatization means more thoroughly removing “public” media from the interests of the private sector. No more sponsorship messages from Monsanto or ExxonMobil, no more need to pitch corporations or beg listeners for the funds needed to pay reporters. Pickard wants the public media system to be entirely publicly funded, to the tune of roughly $30 billion a year. That would be a massive increase — almost 60×! — from the pre-Trump level of federal funding, which was around $500 million a year. Even if you include all non-federal sources of revenue, $30 billion would still represent a public media system 8 to 10 times larger than what exists today. (Pickard dreams massive!) RELATED ARTICLEDo countries with better-funded public media also have healthier democracies? Of course they doJoshua BentonJanuary 24, 2022But the fact that $30 billion sounds enormous is mostly about how small U.S. public media has always been compared to its international peers. Before defunding, the U.S. spent roughly $3 per person per year on public media. Compare that to countries like Norway ($110), Finland ($101), Denmark ($93), the U.K. ($81), France ($76), Czechia ($60), Japan ($53), Australia ($36), and Canada ($27). If Pickard got his $30 billion wish, U.S. public media funding would sit at about $88 per capita — BBC territory, roughly speaking. But even getting to the level of Canada or Australia would mean a huge increase. By democratization, Pickard means confronting criticism that public media systems’ output often skews toward the interests of elites — either the incumbent government in a case like Viktor Orbán’s Hungary or the sort of “latte-sipping NPR liberals” that conservatives have inveighed against for decades: Endeavoring to democratize public media institutions, therefore, is not only ethically sound but also strategic: Democratization can help ensure bipartisan trust, structural resilience, and journalistic independence. Toward this aim, a public media system should not be public in name only but actually owned and controlled by local communities. To encourage trust and community investment, this collective ownership and governance must translate to public participation in all stages of media production and dissemination. In fact, public media institutions are often cross-ideological islands of trust in an otherwise dismal landscape. This trust in public media can be further deepened through direct public ownership and participation, perhaps through community action programs, participatory budgeting, or some similar bottom-up model of democratic governance. Local media bureaus — rotating oversight boards that are locally elected or randomly selected — could help ensure additional public accountability.

    Pickard lays out three core ideas: de-privatization, democratization, and localization.

    Sources indicate that de-privatization means more thoroughly removing “public” media from the interests of the private sector. No more sponsorship messages from Monsanto or ExxonMobil, no more need to pitch corporations or beg listeners for the funds needed to pay reporters.

    Recent findings suggest that pickard wants the public media system to be entirely publicly funded, to the tune of roughly $30 billion a year. But even getting to the level of Canada or Australia would mean a huge increase.

    By democratization, Pickard means confronting criticism that public media systems’ output often skews toward the interests of elites — either the incumbent government in a case like Viktor Orbán’s Hungary or the sort of “latte-sipping NPR liberals” that conservatives have inveighed against for decades:.

    According to recent reports, endeavoring to democratize public media institutions, therefore, is not only ethically sound but also strategic: Democratization can help ensure bipartisan trust, structural resilience, and journalistic independence. Toward this aim, a public media system should not be public in name only but actually owned and controlled by local communities.     Industry observers note that this trust in public media can be further deepened through direct public ownership and participation, perhaps through community action programs, participatory budgeting, or some similar bottom-up model of democratic governance. Local media bureaus — rotating oversight boards that are locally elected or randomly selected — could help ensure additional public accountability.

    And for Pickard, localization is a logical response to the de-localization of media that the internet hath wrought. Many public radio and TV stations primarily serve as distributors of national content, in large part because funding is nowhere near robust enough to create enough local programming to fill each day. And no matter how much you like Ken Burns or All Things Considered, sending the same programming nationwide can limit the range of a community’s residents who might be interested. He advocates pushing more control away from a federal-level entity like CPB and toward states, counties, and cities via block grants.

    Pickard describes the nodes of this system as Public Media Centers: “multimedia hubs that are federally guaranteed but locally owned and democratically governed,” which “would provide journalism, broadcasting, digital media, and other information services based on community needs.”11“Public Media Centers” is also what Pickard called them in one of his first public articulations of the idea, in his 2021 prediction here at Nieman Lab. Some might be housed in existing public radio or TV stations, others in post offices or libraries. And individual communities would be able to determine which media formats work best for them, rather than being locked into the expensive broadcast infrastructure required to reach audiences in 1967.

    In a recent development, I am obliged to note that there are a huge number of barriers to Pickard’s vision becoming reality. Most obviously: $30 billion a year is a lot of money. That’s around the annual budget of the federal school lunch program ($32 billion), FEMA ($32 billion), or NASA ($25 billion). Secondly, the commercial media industry would not sit quietly while the federal government funds an enormous latest rival that doesn’t need to sell ads or subscriptions. (For context, the entire U.S. newspaper industry pulls in around $20 billion a year in revenue.) And American suspicion of “state-funded media” goes deep enough that I can’t imagine Democrats looking to retake the White House in 2028 deciding this is the hill to die on.

    Recent findings suggest that but the newly introduced Congress is still weeks away from convening, and the next federal fiscal year starts more than 10 months from now. This is the season for massive dreams, for expanding the edges of the Overton window, and in that sense, Pickard’s ideas should give newly empowered policymakers a lot to think about.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • 17, Chrome 158 rolls out to the majority of desktop and mobile people and drops support for client-side XSLT (Extensible Stylesheet Language Transformations).
    • For years, WordPress core and major SEO plugins, including Yoast SEO, Rank Math, and All in One SEO (AIOSEO), have referenced an .xsl stylesheet inside their XML sitemaps.
    • Without XSLT support, opening a WordPress sitemap in Chrome 158 displays raw, unstyled XML markup alongside a browser console and page warning.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, on Nov. 17, Chrome 158 rolls out to the majority of desktop and mobile people and drops support for client-side XSLT (Extensible Stylesheet Language Transformations).

    For years, WordPress core and major SEO plugins, including Yoast SEO, Rank Math, and All in One SEO (AIOSEO), have referenced an .xsl stylesheet inside their XML sitemaps. When a person opened a sitemap URL in a browser, Chrome executed that XSLT file to transform the underlying XML code into a clean, clickable HTML table.

    Without XSLT support, opening a WordPress sitemap in Chrome 158 displays raw, unstyled XML markup alongside a browser console and page warning.

    Screenshot from author, November 2026.

    Industry observers note that search engines do not use XSLT. Googlebot, Bingbot, and other web crawlers fetch and parse the raw XML nodes (, ) at the source. Crawlers avoid browser-side stylesheets, meaning indexing, crawl efficiency, and search rankings remain unaffected.

    Recent findings suggest that because Chrome 158 lands while Google’s November core update, which began on Nov. 10, is still rolling, site owners and clients checking their domains during routine ranking audits may panic when they see raw XML in place of the familiar formatted table.

    Depending on your site configuration, WordPress serves its sitemap index from one of two primary URLs:.

    If you open either URL in Chrome 158 or a newer release, seeing a wall of XML tags confirms the browser skipped the XSLT stylesheet, not that the sitemap file is corrupt or broken.

    Screenshot from author, November 2026.

    To verify, or prove to a nervous client, that Google reads the sitemap without trouble, check Google Search Console:.

    As long as Search Console reports “Success,” Google parses the XML structure without error.

    XML sitemaps exist for machine consumption, and search engine bots read the underlying and tags. Dropping visual styling changes nothing about URL discovery, crawl budget, or search visibility.

    Because Chrome 158 arrives alongside the November core patch, clients or stakeholders who inspect their sitemap URLs will spot unformatted XML code and assume a site outage or plugin failure caused ranking fluctuations.

    Recent findings suggest that chrome logs a deprecation warning in DevTools whenever a page invokes an .xsl stylesheet. Automated site-health crawlers or QA tools that monitor browser console errors may flag sitemap URLs until plugins or WordPress core drop the stylesheet reference.

    Editors and junior marketers who relied on opening /sitemap_index.xml in Chrome as a quick directory of site URLs lose that visual table unless they switch browsers (such as Firefox or Safari, which retain XSLT for the time being) or use a dedicated HTML sitemap.

    Because search crawlers ignore XSLT, you don’t need to rush to make emergency fixes. Choose from the steps below based on your role and client needs:.

    Note: This is only a visual change. Chrome 158’s removal of XSLT support only affects how sitemaps render in human browsers. Search engine crawlers process raw XML directly and are completely unaffected.

    According to recent reports, organic performance, indexing, and rankings remain safe. WordPress 7.2 will remove the stylesheet reference and, with it, the Chrome warnings, leaving core sitemaps as plain XML. Yoast SEO 28.9 will restore a styled view using CSS, while Rank Math and AIOSEO have not confirmed a change.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, camunda is the enterprise platform for agentic orchestration, enabling organizations to coordinate AI agents, people, and systems across complex, end-to-end business processes. With built-in governance, auditability, and human oversight, Camunda gives enterprises the control they need to move AI from pilots to production — safely and at scale. Trusted by over 700 organizations worldwide, including 9 of top 10 US banks, Camunda helps enterprises boost operational efficiency, accelerate time-to-value, and deliver better customer experiences.Fully remote and global, we are in the middle of something bigger: transforming into an AI-first organisation, built on our own platform. We use Agentic AI to automate, orchestrate intelligent processes, and elevate human contribution across every team.Named GP Bullhound’s Top 100 Next Unicorn list, 2025 Great Place to Work certified. Visionary in 2025 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Business Orchestration and Automation Technologies. ranked 3rd in Flexa's 2026 Most Flexible Companies, We’re growing fast and looking for top talent to join our team. If you want meaningful work, visible impact and put something genuinely rare on your CV, keep reading.

    Hi there! We're hiring an Information Security Engineer with a focus on Application Security to join our Information Security team at Camunda.

    Industry observers note that we are a team that takes security seriously without making it feel like a locked door. We work in a transparent, straightforward way, and we care about doing the work right rather than just checking a compliance box.

    It has been revealed that you will work side by side with our R&D engineers: reviewing designs, threat modeling new features, digging into code and helping teams make good, risk-based decisions about the vulnerabilities that come in. You'll also help build the internal tools that make this work scale, including our CVE registry and the LLM-assisted workflows we use to analyse code and triage findings.

    Camunda is an AI-first company, and InfoSec is no exception: AI agents are part of how we review code, assess vulnerabilities, and build our tools. You will help shape how that works.

    Industry observers note that this is a hands-on role for someone who already has solid AppSec foundations and wants to grow. We are a generalist team, so you will also take part in our on-call rotation and incident response, and get exposure to other areas of security. But most of your time will be spent with engineers and building and maintaining internal tools and processes.

    Vulnerability management: triage findings from SCA, container and code scanning, external reports and internal security testing; assess whether Camunda is actually affected; agree fix / mitigate / accept with engineering and follow through to release.

    Threat modeling and security reviews: run threat modeling sessions and design reviews with R&D teams for new features and architecture changes, and turn the results into concrete, prioritised actions.

    Code analysis with LLMs: use and improve LLM-assisted tooling (agents, prompts, reusable skills) to review code, validate findings and reproduce challenges, while applying your own judgement to know when the model is wrong.

    Recent findings suggest that build internal security tooling: contribute to the CVE registry and related automation that connects scanners, engineering teams, and customer communication. Much of it is built on Camunda itself.

    Help engineers do the secure thing by default: answer questions, review pull requests, improve guidelines and occasionally run a session or workshop.

    On-call and incident response: share the InfoSec on-call rotation with the other engineers and help investigate and resolve security incidents.

    Support the wider team: help write security advisories for our customers, answer customer security questions and support audits.

    What You Will Bring to the Role.

    Around 3+ years in security or software engineering, with at least 2 of them working on application or product security (AppSec, product security, pentesting, or a security-focused developer role all count).

    Experience at a SaaS or software product company, working closely with engineering teams that ship often through modern CI/CD and cloud environments.

    Hands-on vulnerability triage: you've worked with tools like Snyk, Trivy, Semgrep, CodeQL or similar, can tell a real issue from a false positive, and can explain how exploitable something actually is in context (CVSS, exploitability, configuration).

    Threat modeling and design review experience (e.g. STRIDE) on real systems, ideally web apps, APIs, or distributed services.

    Industry observers note that you read and write code. You're comfortable reading Java (Camunda is built on it) well enough to follow a data flow and spot a security bug. You can write scripts and small tools and contribute to an existing codebase with review.

    Sources indicate that you build with AI, not just chat with it. You use AI coding agents (Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot or similar) in your daily work to write tools, analyse code or automate tasks. And you know their output still needs a second look, especially when it comes to security.

    According to recent reports, clear, friendly communication with engineers. You see yourself as an enabler, not a gatekeeper, and you can explain risk to people who aren't security specialists.

    Some Python and/or JavaScript experience, or experience building internal tools.

    Willingness to learn and use Camunda, since we build a lot of our own security automation on it. Prior BPMN / workflow experience is a plus.

    Experience responding to security incidents or being part of an on-call rotation.

    Exposure to security advisories, CVE disclosure or bug bounty programmes.

    Knowledge of AI/LLM security risks (OWASP Top 10 for LLMs / agentic apps, prompt injection, tool abuse).

    Experience securing Kubernetes or container-based workloads, or open-source / B2B software.

    This role is an existing vacancy.

    Sources indicate that all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    According to recent reports, we will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    It has been revealed that we have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    Stations in Newly introduced Hampshire, Wisconsin, Massachusetts, and Utah all climbed in our regular ranking of public radio stations between July and September.

    Sources indicate that more than a year ago, NHPR reporter Todd Bookman started asking questions about “an irregular personnel maneuver” involving the chief justice of Upcoming Hampshire’s Supreme Court. Bookman’s reporting ultimately became “Exhibit A” in the ethics probe that led to the justice’s resignation in September.

    It has been revealed that the bombshell resignation news was NHPR’s biggest story in September — and of 2026 to date. The story helped push NHPR up several spots in our regular ranking of public radio websites. NHPR saw visits rise 22% that month, according to Similarweb visit figures compiled by Nieman Lab.

    RELATED ARTICLECollaborations and primary elections boosted traffic to public media sites this quarterNeel DhaneshaJuly 29, 2026At the very top of the list, not much moved. The Chicago Sun-Times, owned by Chicago Public Media, held onto the top spot, followed by Gothamist (from WNYC) and Minnesota Public Radio. As Nieman Lab senior writer Joshua Benton wrote when introducing the rankings, which we’ve also done for local newspapers and local nonprofit news sites, not all markets are created equal. Public radio stations serving major metropolitan areas with lots of college graduates have a bigger potential audience than stations serving smaller communities and areas with fewer resources. And, of course, Similarweb provides an estimate; internal metrics may differ. Still, the rankings are a valuable window into some industry-wide trends, and often an opportunity to highlight local news organizations punching above their weight.

    Like several public media sites on our list, election season provided a bump to NHPR. Upcoming Hampshire held its primary on Sept. 8 and the statewide public radio station saw a traffic boost from results pages and campaign coverage, said NHPR director of audience engagement Casey McDermott. She described September as a solid month, not an outlier. “But what makes September an exceptionally cool case study is that it reflects two fundamentals at the heart of our mission: a commitment to fresh, local reporting and a renewed internal investment in digital publishing,” McDermott said. “[Bookman’s piece] wasn’t just a standard breaking news item — it was the culmination of months of meticulous accountability reporting,” McDermott added. On the audience side, McDermott said that, in addition to a boost from NHPR’s partners at NPR and Google News, the chief justice story benefited from X (formerly known as Twitter). A post by NHPR president and CEO Jim Schachter caught on and inspired “a stream of supportive comments about the importance of local journalism.” BREAKING: Fearless reporting by New Hampshire Public Radio results in the resignation of the chief justice of the New Hampshire Supreme Court. #NHPolitics https://t.co/6DtIeEIwdp — Jim Schachter (@jimschachter) September 15, 2026 WBUR, one of two Boston-based public media stations, grew every month this quarter, moving from 1.45 million visits to 2.1 million in September, according to Similarweb. WBUR had the biggest raw gain of any station in September. Tiffany Campbell, WBUR’s executive editor for digital audience and news, said organic search traffic and Google Discover helped. “We’ve been working on building out many referral streams,” Campbell said, “but in early September Google delivered a lot of organic search audience via a couple of strong stories.” “Our referral diversification aims to be less reliant on Google organic search but it’s also important to take advantage when it delivers,” she added. Those strong stories? An explainer on the insanity defense during jury deliberations in Lindsay Clancy’s murder trial, results from the Massachusetts primary held on Sept. 1, and a Here & Now interview with Associated Press photographer Richard Drew — who took the “Falling Man” photo — on the 25th anniversary of 9/11. All three stories drew both local and national readers, Campbell said. Campbell credited the steady rise in traffic to “things we’re always doing: in-depth local coverage, comprehensive reporting on a closely watched election (which was an early indication of interest in the general election in November) and relevant enterprise reporting.” The Milwaukee-based WUWM was the fastest climber in the top 25 this quarter. The station nearly doubled its visits between June and September, rising in our ranking from No. 31 to No. 15. According to Similarweb, the station’s visits rose 32% in August and by another 17% in September. Michelle Maternowski, WUWM audience innovation manager, said the surge started with Wisconsin’s August 11 primary. “We published our Voter Guide in time for that and saw a decent amount come to our meet the candidate posts,” she said. Readers were especially interested in news and information on the lesser-known races. “We see lots of traffic to the down ballot, statewide races — like state treasurer and secretary of state.” And then there’s the gift that keeps on giving. Published in 2019, WUWM’s segment on the 150th birthday of the periodic table still ranks “really high in search results.” “I think once the school year started up again, a lot of students were searching their periodic tables,” Maternowski said. “It is very silly that this story continues to get so much traffic.” If you only look at the top 25 stations, you’ll miss some impressive jumps. The Salt Lake City-based KUER, for example, took the biggest leap in ranking of any station in July. The station’s visits rose 122% that month, according to Similarweb’s numbers. “The numbers don’t lie,” Jim Hill, digital manager in the KUER newsroom, confirmed. “July was a monster for us.” Hill had expected a “plateau or small retreat” after a record year in 2025 — which included the Charlie Kirk killing and a shooting at a No Kings Protest in Utah. Instead, the news site has been ahead of last year’s pace. Total customers are up 19% over last year, even after attempts to filter out bots, and social media referrals falling by 54%. (Hill noted the station’s social media producer was laid off and that KUER is attempting to “pivot to video/reels.”) The station saw “some runaway Google Discover success” last year but, in 2026, clicks from Google Discover are “less than half” of its 2025 figures. Hill credited “engagement reporting and audience-valued topics” that have “kept audiences reading” despite the headwinds. KUER also grew its “owned” email audience and drove 34% more users to the website compared to 2025, according to Hill. All in all, July was “very hit-heavy,” Hill said. The top 10 stories — led by Donald Trump’s decision to dramatically shrink two Utah national monuments — accounted for 64% of the month’s views. The station also saw a major boost from NPR, including multiple stories from a week-long hearing in the Charlie Kirk case. “Our newsroom was the ground team for NPR, so the network highlighted web coverage nationally,” Hill said. Most of the audience came from outside Utah. Hill said NPR can be directly attributed for 32% of sessions, Google Search 14%, and Google News 13.5%. Two wildfire stories also gave major traffic boosts. But audiences especially loved hearing about Utah getting full-color specialty license plates. The story was KUER’s top Google Discover story in July and also got a significant bump (14% of visits) from Reddit. “We affectionately refer to stories like this as license plate news,” Hill said. “It always hits with the audience.” Sure enough, a second plate story, on Utah cracking down on the infamous “Montana loophole,” ended the month as the No. 2 Discover story.     In a recent development, sure enough, a second plate story, on Utah cracking down on the infamous “Montana loophole,” ended the month as the No. 2 Discover story.

    #55161. Latest Update: Google’s Next Patch Won’t Touch The Index, And Nobody Will Announce It via @sejournal, @DuaneForrester

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1740 w)

    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Searchenginejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: Google’s Next Patch Won’t Touch The Index, And Nobody Will Announce It via @sejournal, @DuaneForrester

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1740 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The viral version of Google’s latest research post says the model makes itself smarter, and the post itself says something more useful to anyone whose job depends on what Google remembers about their organization.
    • In March I argued that the training data cutoff had become a ranking factor, because content on the two sides of the cutoff lives in different systems with different confidence behavior, and I suggested timing important claims to land before major training runs.
    • The post describes a two-phase lifecycle.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The viral version of Google’s latest research post says the model makes itself smarter, and the post itself says something more useful to anyone whose job depends on what Google remembers about their organization. On Oct. 27, Ali Behrouz and Vahab Mirrokni of Google Research published the sleep framework, a method that gives a language model a scheduled offline phase in which it moves what it picked up during use into its long-term weights, then rehearses on data it generates for itself. The viral framing is wrong in a specific way: the post states that the method operates within a fixed architecture under human-defined training rules, so nothing is modifying itself without supervision. What that framing misses is the part that matters here. If this design ships, the knowledge inside Google’s models stops being frozen at a cutoff and starts updating on a cycle that nobody outside Google will see.

    In March I argued that the training data cutoff had become a ranking factor, because content on the two sides of the cutoff lives in different systems with different confidence behavior, and I suggested timing important claims to land before major training runs. That advice assumed the cutoff was a wall with a date on it. This paper describes a wall that moves on its own schedule, without a date, and the right way to read it is as the next form of the Google update: one that changes what the model believes rather than how the index is ranked, and that arrives with no announcement because there is no event to announce.

    The post describes a two-phase lifecycle. During a wake phase, the model takes input and holds newly introduced information in fast, short-term memory components, which is roughly what context does today. During a sleep phase, it stops taking input and runs two stages. The first is consolidation. The model unlocks new, previously dormant low-rank experts inside a mixture-of-experts layout, assigns them to slower-updating memory blocks, and distills the short-term traces into them through a process the authors call knowledge seeding, which in plain terms means the new facts get their own fresh parameters rather than being written over old ones. Then the temporary parameters are reset so the capacity can be reused. The second stage is what the authors call dreaming. The model generates synthetic samples by randomly routing across its experts so that knowledge from different domains mixes, filters those samples with a gradient-based selection method, and fine-tunes on the ones that survive.

    Industry observers note that the reported results come from four settings: sequential translation into languages the model had never seen, where standard fine-tuning and in-context approaches forgot earlier languages, and the sleep model held a near-zero performance drop; recall on a long-context benchmark out to ten million tokens; factual knowledge incorporation from document passages, where the sleep model beat supervised fine-tuning and a prior self-editing method; and math reasoning on an open 8-billion-parameter base model. The underlying paper has been on arXiv since June and on OpenReview since September 2025, so the blog post is Google deciding to say this out loud, not Google discovering it.

    This is not a one-off. The same authors published Nested Learning in November 2025 with the Hope architecture and the idea of a continuum memory system, a chain of memory blocks that update at different frequencies, with the fast blocks holding short-term information and the slow blocks holding durable knowledge. The sleep framework is what you build once you have blocks that update at different rates: a schedule for moving information from the fast ones to the slow ones. Titans came before Hope, Hope came before sleep, and the arc now runs about two years. The autoregressive ranking paper I covered in September closed a five-year arc on how results get ordered. This one is younger and just as deliberate.

    It is research, not a product. The post makes no statement about deployment, timelines, or which Google models might use it. The experiments run on open Qwen models at 1.7 and 8 billion parameters, not on Gemini. No compute cost is reported for a sleep cycle, and no one outside the team has replicated the results. In the experiments, the upcoming facts arrive as documents, not as user conversations or crawled web pages, so anyone claiming the model learns from your chats is extrapolating past the paper.

    It has been revealed that those caveats are real and they do not change things. Google publishes research arcs and then ships pieces of them, and that pattern has held often enough that the practitioner question is not whether this exact method lands but what the design tells you about the direction. The direction is a model whose long-term memory is rewritten on a cycle.

    According to recent reports, anyone who has done this work for more than a few years lived through the first version of this shift. Google says it updates Search thousands of times a year and shares only the ones it considers notable, and in a 2022 interview Danny Sullivan put the previous year’s experiments and quality tests above 800,000. The named core updates are the handful that get a dashboard entry. Everything else lands continuously and silently, and the industry adapted by building a diagnostic ritual around the named few: traffic moves, you check the date against the enhancement trackers, and attribution follows.

    Industry observers note that retrieval already took the same path for freshness. AI Overviews and grounded answers pull fresh pages daily with nothing announced, so a claim that silence is new would be wrong. What the sleep framework changes is which layer goes silent. Retrieval changes what the model can look up. Consolidation changes what the model believes without looking anything up. Those are different things for a brand. A retrieved fact is cited, hedged, and replaceable the next time the page is fetched. A consolidated fact is spoken with the confidence of something the model knows, and the March piece covered why that confidence difference shapes how a brand appears in an answer.

    Industry observers note that so the shape practitioners already know, revealed core updates on the outside and unannounced tweaks between them, gets a second copy one layer down: announced model versions on the outside, unannounced consolidation accumulating between them. The ranking stack does not go away and this does not replace it. It sits on top of it, in the model that writes the answer.

    It has been revealed that the detail in the post I keep returning to is that consolidation is selective. The authors say the model is not asked to copy every detail from its short-term traces into its parameters, and the dreaming stage scores its own samples with a gradient-based filter before anything is trained on. That is a ranking function. It decides which facts the model will carry forward as durable knowledge and which it will let expire with the temporary parameters. Being seen during wake is not being learned. Being learned is what being indexed used to mean, and the thing deciding it is a loss calculation nobody outside Google can inspect.

    Three consequences follow, and the first two are my inference from the design rather than claims the paper makes.

    Sources indicate that first, the filter will favor facts that are consistent across sources. A gradient-based selection method keeps samples that reduce error broadly, and a fact that agrees with everything else the model has seen reduces error more reliably than one that contradicts a competitor’s page, a stale directory listing, or your own older content. Conflicting versions of your tech giant are no longer only a conflation risk at retrieval time, which I covered when German courts started holding the platform responsible for false answers, but a consolidation risk, because the version that gets learned is the one that fits best, not the one you prefer.

    Recent findings suggest that second, dreaming means the model rehearses on data you never published. The synthetic samples are generated by mixing experts across domains, so the model’s representation of a manufacturer can shift through rehearsal with no upcoming input from anyone. No competitor moved, no page changed, no update ran, and the answer about you is different anyway. This is a candidate mechanism for a question I have been asked repeatedly this year, which is why an answer changed when nothing observable changed.

    Third, and this one sits in the paper’s design directly, there is a window. Between a fact entering the fast memory and the next consolidation, a correction is cheap because nothing durable has been written yet. After consolidation, fixing a false fact is no longer a matter of updating a page and waiting for a recrawl. It is unlearning, and removing one specific fact from a model’s weights without damaging the rest remains an open research problem. The term I would use is the consolidation window, the period in which a wrong fact can still be caught before the model commits it, and the uncomfortable property of the window is that its length and timing are unknown to you.

    If no Google model announcement within roughly 18 months references periodic updates between releases, continual learning in production, or anything resembling a consolidation cycle, this stays a research direction, and the cutoff stays a wall. If the compute cost of a sleep cycle turns out to be comparable to a training run, the economics kill the cadence idea even if the method works. And if Google chooses to publish consolidation events the way it publishes core updates, the silence argument fails and the diagnostic ritual survives with a new row on the dashboard. I think the third is the least likely of the three, because Google has never published its unnamed changes and has mentioned plainly that it does not intend to.

    The useful response is to stop building process around an event that may stop existing.

    Industry observers note that the cutoff-aware calendaring I suggested in March still holds for the next major training run, because those will keep happening. What changes is the half-life of the word parametric. The safest assumption is that what the model knows about you is being revised on a schedule you cannot see, by a filter you cannot inspect, and that the only observable is the answer itself.
